وَأَمَّا زَيْدُ بْنُ أَسْلَمَ وَوَهْبُ بْنُ مُنَبِّهٍ وَنَحْوُهُمْ فَحَاشَاهُمْ مِنْ مِثْلِ هَذَا؛
 فَإِنَّهُمْ كَانُوا مَنْ أَعْظَمِ النَّاسِ تَعْظِيمًا لِلْأَمْرِ وَالنَّهْيِ وَالْوَعْدِ وَالْوَعِيدِ وَلَكِنْ قَصَدُوا الرَّدَّ عَلَى الْمُكَذِّبِينَ بِالْقَدَرِ الْقَائِلِينَ:
 بِأَنَّهُ يَشَاءُ مَا لَا يَكُونُ وَيَكُونُ مَا لَا يَشَاءُ.
 وَهَؤُلَاءِ حَقِيقَةُ قَوْلِهِمْ:
 إنَّهُ لَا يَقْدِرُ عَلَى تَعْبِيدِهِمْ وَتَصْرِيفِهِمْ تَحْتَ مَشِيئَتِهِ فَأَرَادُوا إبْطَالَ قَوْلِ هَؤُلَاءِ وَنِعْمَ مَا أَرَادُوا لَكِنَّ الْكَلَامَ فِيمَا أُرِيدَ بِالْآيَةِ.
 وَقَوْلُ أُولَئِكَ الْإِبَاحِيَّةِ يُشْبِهُ قَوْلَ مَنْ قَالَ:
 إنَّ الْعَارِفَ إذَا شَهِدَ الْمَشِيئَةَ سَقَطَ عَنْهُ الْمَلَامُ وَإِنَّهُ إذَا شَهِدَ الْحُكْمَ - يَعْنِي الْمَشِيئَةَ -
 لَمْ يُسْتَحْسَنْ وَلَمْ يُسْتَقْبَحْ سَبَبُهُ وَنَحْوُ هَذَا مِنْ أَقْوَالِ هَؤُلَاءِ الَّذِينَ تُشْبِهُ أَقْوَالُهُمْ أَقْوَالَ الْمُشْرِكِينَ الَّذِينَ قَالُوا:
 
{لَوْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ مَا أَشْرَكْنَا وَلَا آبَاؤُنَا وَلَا حَرَّمْنَا مِنْ شَيْءٍ}
 كَمَا قَدْ بُسِطَ الْكَلَامُ عَلَيْهِ وَبَيَّنَ أَنَّ إثْبَاتَ الْقَدَرِ السَّابِقِ حَقٌّ لَكِنَّ ذَلِكَ هُوَ الَّذِي يَصِيرُ الْعَبْدُ إلَيْهِ لَيْسَ هُوَ الَّذِي فُطِرَ عَلَيْهِ كَمَا قَالَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ 
{كُلُّ مَوْلُودٍ يُولَدُ عَلَى الْفِطْرَةِ فَأَبَوَاهُ يُهَوِّدَانِهِ أَوْ يُنَصِّرَانِهِ أَوْ يُمَجِّسَانِهِ كَمَا تُنْتِجُ الْبَهِيمَةُ بَهِيمَةً جَمْعَاءَ هَلْ تُحِسُّونَ فِيهَا مِنْ جَدْعَاءَ}
 . فَقَدْ بَيَّنَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ بِمَثَلٍ ضَرَبَهُ أَنَّ الْبَهِيمَةَ تُولَدُ سَلِيمَةً ثُمَّ تُجْدَعُ وَالْجَدْعُ كَانَ مُقَدَّرًا عَلَيْهَا؛ كَذَلِكَ الْعَبْدُ يُولَدُ عَلَى الْفِطْرَةِ سَلِيمًا ثُمَّ يَفْسُدُ بِالتَّهَوُّدِ وَالتَّنْصِيرِ وَذَلِكَ كَانَ مَكْتُوبًا أَنْ يَكُونَ. وَصَاحِبُ هَذَا الْقَوْلِ إنَّمَا قَالَهُ لِيُبَيِّنَ مَا خُلِقُوا لَهُ وَقَدْ قَصَدَ هَذَا طَائِفَةٌ
translated_text:
As for Zayd ibn Aslam, Wahb ibn Munabbih, and others like them, far be it from them to hold such a view! They were among those who held the divine commands and prohibitions, promises and threats in the greatest reverence. Rather, they intended to refute those who denied divine decree, claiming that Allah wills what does not happen and that things happen which He does not will. Their position effectively amounts to saying that He is unable to subject them to servitude and direct them according to His will. Zayd and the others therefore sought to refute their position—and how commendable their intention was! The question, however, concerns what the verse means.

The position of those antinomians resembles the statement that when the gnostic beholds the divine will, he is no longer subject to blame, and that when he beholds the decree—meaning the divine will—its cause is judged neither good nor bad. These and similar statements resemble those of the polytheists who said:

“If Allah had willed, neither we nor our fathers would have associated partners with Him, nor would we have forbidden anything.”

This has already been discussed at length. It has been explained that affirming Allah’s prior decree is right, but that it concerns the state the servant eventually reaches, not the disposition upon which he was created. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Every child is born upon the natural disposition. Then his parents make him a Jew, a Christian, or a Zoroastrian, just as an animal gives birth to a sound, whole animal. Do you see any mutilation in it?”

Through this analogy, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained that an animal is born sound and is subsequently mutilated, although that mutilation had been decreed for it. Likewise, the servant is born sound upon the natural disposition, then becomes corrupted by being made a Jew or a Christian, although it had already been written that this would happen.

The proponent of this view stated it only to explain what they were created for. This was also the intent of a group

فَسَّرُوا الْعِبَادَةَ بِأَمْرِ وَاقِعٍ عَامٍّ وَلَيْسَتْ هِيَ الْعِبَادَةَ الْمَأْمُورَ بِهَا عَلَى أَلْسُنِ الرُّسُلِ فَفِي تَفْسِيرِ ابْنِ أَبِي طَلْحَةَ الْمُضَافِ إلَى ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ:
 إلَّا لِيُقِرُّوا بِالْعُبُودِيَّةِ طَوْعًا وَكَرْهًا وَهَذِهِ الْعُبُودِيَّةُ كَقَوْلِهِ: 
{وَلَهُ أَسْلَمَ مَنْ فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ طَوْعًا وَكَرْهًا}
 وَقَوْلِهِ: 
{وَلِلَّهِ يَسْجُدُ مَنْ فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ طَوْعًا وَكَرْهًا}
 وَفَسَّرَتْ طَائِفَةٌ 
" الْكَرْهَ "
 بِأَنَّهُ جَرَيَانُ حُكْمِ الْقَدَرِ فَيَكُونُ كَالْقَوْلِ قَبْلَهُ وَالصَّحِيحُ أَنَّهُ انْقِيَادُهُمْ لِحُكْمِهِ الْقَدَرِيِّ بِغَيْرِ اخْتِيَارِهِمْ، كَاسْتِسْلَامِهِمْ عِنْدَ الْمَصَائِبِ وَانْقِيَادِهِمْ لِمَا يَكْرَهُونَ مِنْ أَحْكَامِهِ الشَّرْعِيَّةِ فَكُلُّ أَحَدٍ لَا بُدَّ لَهُ مِنْ انْقِيَادِهِ لِحُكْمِهِ الْقَدَرِيِّ وَالشَّرْعِيِّ فَهَذَا مَعْنًى صَحِيحٌ. قَدْ بُسِطَ فِي غَيْرِ هَذَا الْمَوْضِعِ لَكِنْ لَيْسَ هُوَ الْعِبَادَةَ.
 وَكَذَلِكَ قَالَ بَعْضُهُمْ:
 إلَّا لِيَخْضَعُوا لِي وَيَتَذَلَّلُوا قَالُوا: وَمَعْنَى الْعِبَادَةِ فِي اللُّغَةِ - التَّذَلُّلُ وَالِانْقِيَادُ وَكُلُّ مَخْلُوقٍ مِنْ الْجِنِّ وَالْإِنْسِ خَاضِعٌ لِقَضَاءِ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى مُتَذَلِّلٌ لِمَشِيئَتِهِ. لَا يَمْلِكُ أَحَدٌ لِنَفْسِهِ خُرُوجًا عَمَّا خُلِقَ. وَقَدْ ذَكَرَ أَبُو الْفَرَجِ قَوْلَ ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ هَذَا.
 قَالَ:
 وَبَيَانُ هَذَا قَوْلُهُ: 
{وَلَئِنْ سَأَلْتَهُمْ مَنْ خَلَقَهُمْ لَيَقُولُنَّ اللَّهُ}
 وَهَذِهِ الْآيَةُ تُوَافِقُ مَنْ قَالَ: إلَّا لِيَعْرِفُونِ؛ كَمَا سَيَأْتِي. وَهَؤُلَاءِ الَّذِينَ أَقَرُّوا بِأَنَّ اللَّهَ خَالِقُهُمْ لَمْ يُقِرُّوا بِذَلِكَ كَرْهًا بِخِلَافِ إسْلَامِهِمْ وَخُضُوعِهِمْ لَهُ فَإِنَّهُ يَكُونُ كَرْهًا وَأَمَّا نَفْسُ الْإِقْرَارِ فَهُوَ فِطْرِيٌّ فُطِرُوا عَلَيْهِ وَبَذَلُوهُ طَوْعًا.
translated_text:
who interpreted worship as a reality common to all, rather than as the worship enjoined through the messengers. Thus, in Ibn Abī Talha’s commentary attributed to Ibn ‘Abbās, it is explained as:

“Except to acknowledge their servitude, willingly or unwillingly.”

This servitude is like that mentioned in His words:

“To Him submits whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly.”

And His words:

“To Allah prostrates whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly.”

Some interpreted “unwillingly” as referring to the operation of divine decree, which would make this interpretation equivalent to the preceding one. The correct interpretation, however, is their submission to His decree without their choosing to do so, as when they surrender in times of calamity, and their compliance with those of His religious rulings that they dislike. Everyone must inevitably submit to His decree and His religious rulings. This is a sound meaning, discussed at length elsewhere, but it is not worship.

Likewise, some said:

“Except to submit to Me and humble themselves.”

They said: “The linguistic meaning of worship is humility and submission. Every created being among the jinn and humankind is subject to Allah Most High’s decree and humbled before His will. No one has the power to escape what he was created for.”

Abū al-Faraj mentioned this statement of Ibn ‘Abbās. He said: “This is explained by His words:

‘If you ask them who created them, they will surely say, “Allah.”’”

This verse accords with the interpretation, “Except to know Me,” as will be discussed below. Those who acknowledged that Allah was their Creator did not acknowledge this unwillingly, unlike their submission and subjection to Him, which may be unwilling. As for the acknowledgment itself, it is innate: they were created with it and offered it willingly.

A fourth view has also been advanced. Ibn Abī Hātim narrated from Zā’idah, from al-Suddī, concerning His words:

“I did not create the jinn and humankind except to worship Me.”

He said: “He created them for worship. Some worship is beneficial, and some is not. ‘If you ask them who created the heavens and the earth and subjected the sun and the moon, they will surely say, “Allah.”’ This acknowledgment on their part is worship, but it does not benefit them while they associate partners with Him.”

This meaning is sound. However, the polytheist worships Satan and whatever he sets up as an equal to Allah; Allah is not being worshipped. Merely acknowledging the Maker while associating partners with Allah is not called worship of Allah. Rather, one should describe it as He does:

“Most of them do not believe in Allah without also associating partners with Him.”

Their belief in the Creator is thus coupled with their association of partners with Him. As for worship, the hadith states: “Allah says: ‘I am utterly free of any need for partners. Whoever performs a deed in which he associates someone else with Me, I disavow him, and that deed belongs entirely to the one he associated with Me.’”

Thus, although the polytheists devote some of their worship to Allah, He accepts none of it. Rather, all of it belongs to those they associate with Him. They have therefore not worshipped Allah, glorified is He.

Similar to this is the interpretation of those who said: “Except to affirm My oneness. The believer affirms His oneness in both hardship and ease, whereas the unbeliever affirms His oneness in hardship and affliction, but not amid blessings and ease. This is illustrated by His words: ‘When they board a ship, they call upon Allah, devoting their worship sincerely to Him.’”

A fifth view has also been advanced. Ibn Abī Hātim related it from Ibn Jurayj, who said: “To know Me.” He said: “It was also reported from Qatādah.” Al-Baghawī attributed it to Mujāhid, saying: “Mujāhid said: ‘Except to know Me.’” He then said: “This is a sound interpretation, for had He not created them, His existence and oneness would not have been known. Its evidence is His words:

‘If you ask them who created the heavens and the earth and subjected the sun and the moon, they will surely say, “Allah.”’”

The response is: This meaning is sound; the fact that He was known only through His creation of them implies

“And when your Lord took from the children of Adam…”

But this is not worship. These “four views” represent the position of those who recognized that the verse is general and therefore sought to interpret it as referring to a form of worship encompassing all humans and jinn. They believed that interpreting it as worship in its familiar sense—obedience to Allah and obedience to His messengers—would necessarily imply that such worship actually occurred among them, whereas it did not. They therefore sought to interpret it as a form of worship that actually occurred. They thought that interpreting it as worship that did not occur would commit them to the position of the Qadariyyah: that He created them to worship Him, but they disobeyed Him independently of His will and power. Thus they sought to avoid the position of the Qadariyyah, and they are excusable for seeking to avoid it.

Yet they interpreted the verse in a way that was not intended. This happens to many people concerning verses whose apparent meanings the people of innovation invoke as evidence. For example, the Rāfidah invoke His words:

“And wipe your heads and your feet”

as evidence for wiping the tops of the feet. We then find their opponents advancing weak explanations. One says that “your feet” takes the genitive case through proximity to an adjacent word, as in the expression juhr dabbin kharib (“a ruined lizard’s burrow”), and other similarly weak explanations. The same applies to what they have said concerning the statement, “Thus Adam prevailed over Moses in argument,” and similar texts.

The “sixth view”—although Abū al-Faraj mentioned only four views concerning the verse—is the position held by the majority of Muslims: Allah created them to worship Him, meaning to do what they were commanded to do. Hence Muslims, past and present, are found citing this verse as evidence for this

meaning, even in their exhortations, reminders, and accounts, as in the account of Ibrāhīm ibn Adham: “You were not created for this, nor were you commanded to do this.” A report from the Israelite tradition states:

“O son of Adam, I created you to worship Me, so do not occupy yourself with play. I have undertaken to provide for you, so do not wear yourself out. Seek Me and you will find Me. If you find Me, you have found everything; if you miss Me, you have missed everything. I am dearer to you than everything else.”

This is what has been transmitted from the Commander of the Faithful, ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib, and other early Muslims. They relate that ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib said: “Only to command them to worship Me and call them to My worship.” They said that this is supported by His words, Exalted is He:

“They were commanded only to worship Allah, sincerely devoting their worship to Him.”

And His words:

“They were commanded only to worship one God.”

This is the interpretation preferred by al-Zajjāj and others. It is also the interpretation known from Mujāhid through an established chain of transmission. Ibn Abī Hātim said: “Abū Sa‘īd al-Ashajj narrated to us, saying: Abū Usāmah narrated to us, from Shibl, from Ibn Abī Najīh, from Mujāhid, concerning:

‘I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me.’

He said: ‘To command them and forbid them.’” Likewise, al-Rabī‘ ibn Anas is reported to have said: “I created them both only for worship.”

This is also indicated by such statements as His words:

“Does man think that he will be left without purpose?”

Meaning: without being commanded or forbidden. And His words:

“What would my Lord care for you were it not for your supplication?”

That is, were it not for your worship. And His words:

“What would Allah gain by punishing you if you are grateful and believe?”

And His words:

“O company of jinn and mankind, did there not come to you messengers from among you, relating My verses to you and warning you of the meeting of this Day of yours?”

Through to His words:

“While their people were unaware.”

And His words:

“Did I not enjoin upon you, O children of Adam, that you should not worship Satan—for he is clearly your enemy—and that you should worship Me? This is a straight path.”

And the following verses.

and what follows them.

When the jinn heard the Quran, they said:

“O our people, we have heard a Book revealed after Moses, confirming what came before it, guiding to the truth and to a straight path.”

“O our people, respond to the caller of Allah and believe in him.”

This verse and those that follow.

The jinn also said:

“Among us are those who submit to Allah, and among us are the unjust. Those who submit have sought out right guidance.”

This verse and those that follow.

In several places in the Quran, He says:

“O mankind, worship your Lord.”

“O mankind, fear your Lord.”

Thus, He commanded them to do that for which He created them. He sent messengers to mankind and the jinn, and Muhammad was sent to both mankind and the jinn. He recited the Quran to the jinn, and it is reported that when he recited Sūrat al-Rahmān to them, each time he recited:

“Then which of your Lord’s favours will you both deny?”

they would say: “We deny none of Your favours, our Lord; to You belongs all praise.”

This, then, is certainly the meaning intended by the verse. It is what the great majority of Muslims understand from it and cite it to establish. They acknowledge that Allah created them to worship Him, not to neglect His right.

In the two Sahīh collections, Mu‘ādh ibn Jabal reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to him:

“O Mu‘ādh, do you know Allah’s right over His servants?”

He replied: “Allah and His Messenger know best.”

He said: “Allah’s right over His servants is that they worship Him and associate nothing with Him. Do you know the servants’ right over Allah if they do that?”

I said: “Allah and His Messenger know best.”

He said: “Their right over Him is that He not punish them.”

In the Musnad, Ibn ‘Umar reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“I have been sent with the sword before the Hour, so that Allah alone is worshipped, without any partner. My provision has been placed beneath the shade of my spear. Humiliation and abasement have been laid upon those who oppose my command. Whoever imitates a people is one of them.”

 إنَّهُ شَاءَ إلَّا بِمَعْنَى أَمَرَ فَعِنْدَهُمْ مَا لَيْسَ طَاعَةً مِنْ أَفْعَالِ الْعِبَادِ مَا لَا
translated_text:
Those who hold this view then divide into two groups: Ahl al-Sunnah, who affirm divine decree, and those who deny it. Thus, there are “seven” views concerning the verse and “five” concerning divine wisdom.

Ahl al-Sunnah, who affirm divine decree, say that His words:

“I did not create jinn and mankind except to worship Me”

do not necessarily mean that they will actually worship Him, as the proponents of the preceding views have maintained. Nor do they entail denying what is divinely decreed—that something should exist in His dominion which He does not will, or that He should will something which does not come to pass—as the Qadariyyah maintain. The latter say that the purpose for which He created them was not realized because He wills things that do not happen, and things happen that He does not will.

The former said: “If whatever He wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass, then whatever has not occurred was not willed by Him. Thus, whatever worship has not occurred was not willed by Him.” This reasoning is sound. They then said: “Whatever He created them for, He must will to create. Since He did not will to create this, He did not create them for it.”

The fundamental error of both groups is their assumption that He wills the occurrence of whatever He created them for. The former say that He wills to create it, while the latter say that He wills it to occur on their part, meaning that He commands them to do it. They do not acknowledge any will of His concerning human actions apart from His command, which people disobey.

For this reason, they said: “Things happen that He does not will, and He wills things that do not happen,” just as they say: “People do what He has forbidden them and neglect what He has commanded them.” This meaning is correct if what is intended is His religious command.

However, the Qadariyyah, who deny divine decree, understand “He willed” only to mean “He commanded.” Thus, in their view, human actions that are not acts of obedience are things He does not

will, for, in their view, He does not create them. If He does not create something, He has not willed it, for all Muslims agree that whatever He wills to create, He creates.

The Qadariyyah do not dispute this. They do not dispute that whatever He Himself wills to do, He does, and that He is able to do whatever He wills to do. However, in their view, human actions do not fall within His creation, His power, or His will, nor within what He wills to do Himself. Rather, His will concerning them means only His command. They therefore say: He created them to worship Him—that they themselves should perform this worship—and He has commanded them to do so. If they do not perform it, this amounts to disobeying His command.

Those who affirm divine decree, however, say: Whatever He wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass. He, glorified be He, is the Creator of all things:

“Had your Lord willed, He would have made mankind one community.”

“Had Allah willed, they would not have fought one another.”

“Had your Lord willed, they would not have done it.”

And there are other similar passages. Thus, if He created them for the worship He has commanded, yet they do not perform it, He has not willed that it take place. For had He willed it to take place, He would have brought it about. Nevertheless, He has commanded them to perform it, loves and approves of their doing so, and wills that they do so in the religious sense—a will embodied in His command to worship.

This makes the meaning of the verse clear. His words:

“I did not create jinn and mankind except to worship Me”

are similar to His words:

“So that you may complete the prescribed period and glorify Allah for guiding you,”

and His words:

“Thus He has subjected them to you, so that you may glorify Allah for guiding you,”

and His words:

“So that it may not circulate solely among the wealthy among you,”

and His words:

“That is so you may know that Allah knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on earth

and that Allah has knowledge of all things,”

and His words:

“Allah is the One who created seven heavens, and of the earth their like,”

and the rest of the verse. Likewise, His words:

“We sent no messenger except to be obeyed by Allah’s permission.”

He sent the messenger only to be obeyed, yet he may be obeyed or disobeyed. Likewise, He created them only for worship, yet they may worship or may not.

There are many similar passages in the Quran explaining that He did what He did so that they would magnify Him, act justly and not commit injustice, know His attributes, and fulfil the other things Allah has commanded His servants, loved for them, and approved of from them—things in which their happiness, perfection, well-being, and success lie if they do them. Yet some of them do so, while others do not.

He, glorified be He, did not say that He performed the first act so that He Himself would perform the second, or so that He would bring about the second in them. Thus, He did not state that He created them in order to make them worshippers. For when He brings about means to ends that He Himself is to accomplish, He must inevitably accomplish those ends. It is impossible for Him to do one thing in order to do a second, yet not do the second. Rather, He stated that He performed the first act so that they would perform the second. They would therefore be the ones performing it, and through their action they would attain their happiness and what He loves and approves for them. Thus, both what He loves and what they love would be attained. As explained earlier, the ultimate purpose of everything He creates and commands is beloved to Allah and His servants. It embodies wisdom on His part and mercy toward His servants.

Thus, had they done that for which He created them, it would have brought about both what He loves and what they love. But they did not do it, and so they deserved what is deserved by one who disobeys Him, opposes His command, and neglects to do that for which he was created: the punishment of

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

To explain the distinction, in “will,” “permission,” “writing,” “judgment,” “decree,” “prohibition,” and similar matters, between what pertains to religion and accords with Allah’s love, pleasure, and revealed command, and what pertains to creation and accords with His will concerning creation.

He replied:

Praise be to Allah.

These matters—will, permission, writing, judgment, decree, prohibition, and others such as commanding, raising up, and sending—fall into two categories in the Book of Allah:

The first concerns religious matters that Allah Most High loves and is pleased with. He rewards those who observe them, admits them to Paradise, and grants them victory in this worldly life and in the Hereafter. Through these matters, He supports His servants: His pious allies, His successful party, and His righteous servants.

The second concerns events within creation that Allah has ordained and decreed, which encompass believers and disbelievers, the righteous and the wicked, the people of Paradise and the people of Hell, Allah’s allies and His enemies, those who obey Him—whom He loves and who love Him, and upon whom He and His angels send blessings—and those who disobey Him, whom He hates and abhors, and whom Allah curses and those who curse also curse.

translated_text:
Whoever considers these matters from this perspective perceives the reality of creation and existence: he sees all things as created by Allah, governed by His will, and subject to His wisdom. Whatever Allah wills occurs, even if people do not will it; and whatever He does not will does not occur, even if people will it. None can overturn His judgment or repel His command. He sees that Allah, glorified be He, is the Lord and Sovereign of everything; to Him belong creation and command.

Everything other than Him is subject to His lordship, governed and subdued, possessing no power over its own harm or benefit, death, life, or resurrection. Rather, it is a servant utterly in need of Allah Most High in every respect, whereas Allah has no need of it, just as He has no need of any created being. This perception is itself true. Yet “one group” has fallen short of it—the Magian Qadariyyah—while “another group” has stopped at it—the polytheistic Qadariyyah.

As for the former, they are those who claim that some created things, such as human actions, fall outside Allah’s power, will, and creation. The extremists among them denied His eternal knowledge and His prior recording of events. These were the first of the Qadariyyah to arise in this community, and the Companions and the early generations of the community refuted them and disavowed them.

As for “the second group,” they are worse than the former. They comprise various groups devoted to spiritual wayfaring, aspiration, worship, Sufism, spiritual poverty, and the like. They perceive this reality and recognize that Allah is the Creator of all created things, and thus the Creator of human actions, and that He wills everything that occurs. Yet beyond this, they make no distinction between faith and disbelief, recognition and denial, truth and falsehood, the rightly guided and the misguided, the upright and the wayward, a prophet and a pretender to prophethood, or an ally of Allah and an enemy; nor

between one with whom Allah is pleased and one who incurs His displeasure; nor between one whom Allah loves and one whom He detests; nor between justice and injustice, dutifulness and disobedience, the deeds of the people of Paradise and those of the people of Hell, or the righteous and the wicked. For they perceive what all beings share: the prior decree, the unfailingly effective will, the all-encompassing power, and the creation of all things. They perceive what created beings have in common but are blind to what distinguishes them.

Thus they become among those addressed by His words, Most High:

“Shall We then treat the Muslims like the criminals?”

“What is the matter with you? How do you judge?”

And His words, Most High:

“Or shall We treat those who believe and do righteous deeds like those who spread corruption on earth? Or shall We treat the God-fearing like the wicked?”

And His words, Most High:

“Or do those who commit evil deeds think that We will make them like those who believe and do righteous deeds?”

“And your Lord’s gracious word was fulfilled for the Children of Israel because of their patience.”

Another example is the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“I seek refuge in the perfect words of Allah, beyond which neither the righteous nor the wicked can pass, from the evil of what He has created, brought forth, and fashioned; from the evil of what descends from heaven and what ascends into it; from the evil of what He has brought forth in the earth and what emerges from it; from the evil of the trials of night and day; and from the evil of every visitor by night, except one who comes with good, O Most Merciful.”

The words beyond which neither the righteous nor the wicked can pass are not His commands and prohibitions in religious law, for the wicked have disobeyed His commands and prohibitions. Rather, they are the words through which things come into being.

As for the words pertaining to religion, which contain His commands and prohibitions in religious law, these include the divine scriptures: the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and the Quran. And He said:

Most High:

“He made the word of those who disbelieved the lowest, while the word of Allah is the highest.”

And the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“You have made marital relations with them lawful through the word of Allah.”

As for His words, Most High:

“And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice,”

they encompass both kinds.

As for “sending forth” in the first sense, it occurs in passages such as His words, Most High:

“Then, when the promise concerning the first of the two came to pass, We sent against you servants of Ours endowed with great might.”

The second sense occurs in passages such as His words, Most High:

“He is the One who sent among the unlettered a Messenger from among themselves.”

And His words, Most High:

“Our Lord, send among them a Messenger from among themselves.”

And His words, Most High:

“We have certainly sent a messenger to every nation, proclaiming: ‘Worship Allah and shun false gods.’”

As for “sending” in the first sense, it occurs in passages such as His words, Most High:

“We have sent the devils against the disbelievers, inciting them relentlessly.”

And His words, Most High:

“And We sent the winds to fertilize.”

In the second sense, it occurs in passages such as His words, Most High:

“Indeed, We sent Noah to his people.”

And His words, Most High:

“Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bearer of glad tidings and a warner.”

And His words, Most High:

“Ask those of Our messengers whom We sent before you.”

And His words, Most High:

“We did not send any messenger except to be obeyed by Allah’s permission.”

And His words, Most High:

“We did not send any messenger before you without revealing to him: ‘There is no deity except Me, so worship Me.’”

And His words, Most High:

“Indeed, We have sent to you a Messenger as a witness over you, just as We sent a messenger to Pharaoh.”

“But Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger, so We seized him with a severe punishment.”

translated_text:
He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

“Some people say, ‘Allah’s will applies to both the past and the future,’ while others say, ‘The will applies to the future, not the past.’ Which is correct?”

He replied:

The past unfolded by Allah’s will, and the future will not come to pass unless Allah wills it.

Whoever says concerning the past, “Allah created the heavens, if Allah wills,” or “He sent Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, if Allah wills,” is mistaken. Whoever says, “Allah created the heavens by His will and sent Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, by His will,” or something similar, is correct.

Whoever says that anything comes into existence without Allah’s will is mistaken. Whoever says, “Whatever Allah wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass,” is correct.

Everything that has already occurred has certainly occurred by Allah’s will. Allah certainly created the heavens by His will and certainly sent Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, by His will. Every human being in existence has certainly been created by Allah through His will. If Allah wills to change a created being from one state to another, He is able to do so. Thus, whatever He has created has certainly come into being by His will; and if Allah wills to change it, He certainly changes it by His will.

And Allah knows best.

translated_text:
What do the esteemed imams of the Muslims say concerning a group who disagree about Allah’s decree and predestination, both its good and its evil? Some of them hold that good comes from Allah Most High, whereas evil comes solely from one’s own self. Give us a ruling, and may you be rewarded.

The shaykh—may Allah be pleased with him—replied:

The doctrine of the people of the Sunnah and the community is that Allah Most High is the Creator, Lord and Sovereign of all things (*). There is no Lord besides Him and no Creator other than Him. Whatever He wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass. He has power over all things and knowledge of all things.

The servant is commanded to obey Allah and His Messenger and forbidden to disobey Allah and His Messenger. If he obeys, that is a blessing; if he disobeys, he deserves blame and punishment. Allah has the conclusive argument against him, while no one has any argument against Allah Most High. All of this occurs by Allah’s decree, predestination, will and power. Yet He loves obedience, commands it, rewards those who practise it for doing so, and honours them. He hates disobedience, forbids it, punishes those who commit it, and humiliates them.

Whatever blessings come to the servant, Allah has bestowed them upon him; and whatever evil befalls him is because of his sins
translated_footnote:
(*) Shaykh Nāsir ibn Hamad al-Fahd stated (p. 69):
This same fatwa is reproduced in (8/242–243), but the version there differs from this one. There, the fatwa begins: “Abū al-‘Abbās Ibn Taymiyyah was asked about good and evil, the universal decree, and religious commands and prohibitions. He replied: Praise be to Allah. Know that Allah is the Creator, Lord, and Sovereign of all things…”
Comparing the two passages reveals minor differences, the three most important being:
1 – On p. 63: “If he obeys, that is a blessing [from Allah bestowed upon him, and he receives reward and recompense through Allah’s grace and mercy]; if he disobeys, he deserves blame and punishment.” The words in square brackets are omitted here but appear in the other passage (p. 242).
2 – On p. 64: “Whatever sorrow, humiliation, and evil befall you are due to your sins and misdeeds.” On p. 242, the wording is “Whatever drought befalls you,” with “drought” replacing “sorrow.” This reading appears more likely to be correct, since it contrasts with “plenty” in the preceding statement: “Whatever plenty, victory, and guidance come to you, Allah has bestowed them upon you.”
3 – On p. 64: “And that the servant be certain of Allah’s law and command.” On p. 243: “And that the servant believe in Allah’s law and command.” The two readings are close in meaning, but the second appears more likely to be correct. Allah knows best.

translated_text:
and acts of disobedience, as Allah Most High says:

“Whatever calamity befalls you is because of what your own hands have earned.”

And He says:

“Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself.”

That is, whatever prosperity, victory or guidance comes to you is a blessing Allah has bestowed upon you; and whatever sorrow, humiliation or evil befalls you is because of your sins and misdeeds. All things come to pass through Allah’s will, power and creation. The servant must therefore believe in Allah’s decree and predestination and have certainty in His law and commands.

Whoever considers the reality of divine predestination while disregarding the commands and prohibitions, the promises of reward and threats of punishment, resembles the polytheists. Whoever considers the commands and prohibitions but denies divine decree and predestination resembles the Magians. But whoever believes in both, praising Allah Most High when he does good and seeking His forgiveness when he does wrong, while knowing that this occurs by Allah’s decree and predestination, is among the believers.

When Adam—peace be upon him—sinned, he repented, and his Lord chose him and guided him. Iblīs, however, persisted and sought to justify himself, so Allah cursed him and banished him. Whoever repents follows Adam’s way, while whoever persists and invokes predestination as an excuse follows the way of Iblīs. Thus, the blessed follow their father, while the wretched follow their enemy, Iblīs.

We therefore ask Allah to guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom He has bestowed His favour: the prophets, the steadfastly truthful, the martyrs and the righteous. Amen, O Lord of all worlds.

{إنَّ اللَّهَ قَبَضَ قَبْضَةً فَقَالَ: إلَى الْجَنَّةِ بِرَحْمَتِي وَقَبَضَ قَبْضَةً فَقَالَ: إلَى النَّارِ وَلَا أُبَالِي}

 - وَفِي لَفْظٍ -

When He creates a man for the Fire, He causes him to perform the deeds of the people of the Fire until he dies performing one of their deeds, and thereby admits him to the Fire.’”

In the hadith narrated by al-Hakam ibn Sufyān, from Thābit, from Anas ibn Mālik, he said that the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Allah took a handful and said, ‘To Paradise, by My mercy.’ And He took a handful and said, ‘To the Fire, and I care not.’”

This hadith and others like it concern two matters.

The first is the prior divine decree: Allah, glorified be He, knew who would belong to Paradise and who would belong to the Fire before they performed their deeds. This is a truth in which one must believe. Indeed, the imams, including Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, explicitly stated that whoever denies this has disbelieved. Rather, one must believe that Allah knew everything that would happen before it happened. One must also believe what He has told us: that He wrote it down and made it known before it came to pass. Thus, in Sahīh Muslim, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr narrated that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Allah decreed the destinies of all creatures fifty thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth, and His Throne was upon the water.”

In Sahīh al-Bukhārī and elsewhere, ʿImrān ibn Husayn narrated that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Allah existed, and nothing else existed. His Throne was upon the water. He wrote everything in the Record and created the heavens and the earth.”

In another wording:

“Then He created the heavens and the earth.”

translated_text:
In al-Musnad, al-ʿIrbād ibn Sāriyah narrated that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“I was recorded with Allah as the Seal of the Prophets while Adam still lay in his clay. I shall tell you how this began: the supplication of my father Abraham, the glad tidings announced by Jesus, and my mother’s vision when she gave birth to me: she saw a light emerge from her that illuminated the palaces of Syria.”

In the hadith of Maysarah al-Hurr, he said:

“I asked, ‘O Messenger of Allah, when were you recorded as a prophet?’—or, in another wording, ‘When were you a prophet?’ He replied, ‘While Adam was between spirit and body.’”

In Sahīh al-Bukhārī and Sahīh Muslim, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

“The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him—who is truthful and trustworthy—told us: ‘The creation of each of you is brought together in his mother’s womb for forty days as a drop of fluid. Then he becomes a clot for a similar period, then a lump of flesh for a similar period. Then the angel is sent to him and commanded concerning four matters. He is told: “Write down his provision, his deeds, his lifespan, and whether he will be wretched or blessed.” Then the spirit is breathed into him.’ He said: ‘By Him in whose Hand is my soul—or he said, “By Him besides whom there is no god”—one of you may perform the deeds of the people of Paradise until only a cubit separates him from it, but then what has been written overtakes him, and he performs the deeds of the people of the Fire and enters the Fire.’”

In Sahīh al-Bukhārī and Sahīh Muslim, ʿAlī ibn Abī Tālib, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

“We were with the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, at a funeral in Baqīʿ al-Gharqad. He said, ‘There is not one of you whose place in the Fire and whose place in Paradise have not already been written down.’ They asked, ‘O Messenger of Allah, should we not then rely on what has been written and give up deeds?’ He replied, ‘Perform deeds, for everyone will be enabled to do that for which he was created. Those who are among the blessed will be enabled to perform the deeds of the blessed; but as for those who are among the wretched

, they will be enabled to perform the deeds of the wretched.’ Then he recited the words of the Most High:

‘As for the one who gives and fears Allah, and believes in the best reward, We will make easy for him the way of ease. But as for the one who withholds and considers himself self-sufficient, and denies the best reward, We will make easy for him the way of hardship.’”

It is also reported in the Sahīh:

“He was asked, ‘O Messenger of Allah, is it already known who will be among the people of Paradise and who will be among the people of the Fire?’ He replied, ‘Yes.’ He was then asked, ‘What, then, is the point of deeds?’ He said, ‘Perform deeds, for everyone will be enabled to do that for which he was created.’”

Thus the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, explained that Allah knows who will be among the people of Paradise and who will be among the people of the Fire, and that He has recorded this. He forbade them to rely on this record and abandon deeds, as those who deviate from the truth do. He said that everyone will be enabled to do that for which he was created: the blessed are enabled to perform the deeds of the blessed, and the wretched are enabled to perform the deeds of the wretched. This is among the clearest explanations possible.

Allah, glorified and exalted be He, knows things as they truly are. He has appointed causes through which things come about, and He knows that they will come about through those causes. For example, He knows that a man will have a child by having intercourse with a woman and causing her to conceive. If that man were to say, “If Allah knows that I will have a child, there is no need for intercourse,” he would be foolish, for Allah knows that the child will come into being through the intercourse He decrees.

Likewise, He knows that a person’s crops will grow through the water with which he irrigates them and the seeds he sows. If that person were to say, “If He knows that this will happen, there is no need to sow,” he would be ignorant and misguided, for Allah knows that it will happen through those means. Likewise, if Allah knows that one person will satisfy his hunger by eating, another will quench his thirst by drinking, and another will die by being killed, then the causes through which Allah knows these things will occur must necessarily take place.

translated_text:
Likewise, if Allah knows that one person will be blessed in the Hereafter and another wretched, we say: That is because the latter performs the deeds of the wretched. Allah knows that he will become wretched through these deeds. To say, “He will be wretched even if he does not perform them,” would be false, for Allah admits no one to the Fire except on account of his sins. As the Most High says:

“I will surely fill Hell with you and all those among them who follow you.”

Thus He swore that He would fill it with Iblīs and his followers. Whoever follows Iblīs has disobeyed Allah Most High. Allah does not punish a servant for what He knows he will do until he actually does it. Thus, when the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was asked about the children of the polytheists, he said:

“Allah knows best what they would have done.”

This means that Allah knows what they would have done had they reached maturity. It has been reported that a messenger will be sent to them on the Day of Resurrection: whoever obeys him will enter Paradise, and whoever disobeys him will enter the Fire. The obedience or disobedience that Allah knew of them will thereby become manifest.

Likewise, Allah created Paradise for those who believe in Him and obey Him. Whoever He has decreed to be among them, He enables to believe and obey. If someone says, “I will enter Paradise whether I am a believer or a disbeliever, if Allah knows that I am among its people,” he is fabricating a lie against Allah. For what Allah knows is that he will enter it through faith. If he has no faith, he is not the one whom Allah knows will enter Paradise. Rather, whoever is not a believer but a disbeliever is known to Allah as one of the people of the Fire, not one of the people of Paradise.

For this reason, He commanded people to supplicate, seek Allah’s help, and employ other such means. Whoever says, “I will neither supplicate nor ask, relying instead on divine decree,” is also mistaken, because Allah has made supplication

If He decrees that a servant will obtain some good through supplication, it will not be obtained without supplication. Whatever Allah has decreed and known concerning His servants’ circumstances and ultimate outcomes, He has decreed through causes. He brings decreed events to pass at their appointed times. Nothing in this world or the Hereafter occurs without a cause, and Allah is the Creator of causes and their effects.

For this reason, some have said:

“Relying on causes is to associate partners with Allah, contrary to belief in His oneness; denying that causes have a causal role is a deficiency of reason; and disregarding causes altogether undermines the revealed Law.”

Causes alone do not necessarily produce their effects. When rain falls and seeds are sown, that alone is insufficient for plants to grow. There must also be a wind that fosters growth by Allah’s permission, and their failure to emerge must be averted. All the necessary conditions must therefore be fulfilled and all impediments removed, and all of this occurs by Allah’s decree and predestination. Likewise, a child is not born merely because semen is deposited in the vagina. How many men have ejaculated without fathering a child! Rather, Allah must will the child’s creation, so that the woman conceives and nurtures it in her womb, together with all the other conditions and the removal of impediments necessary to complete its creation.

The same applies to the Hereafter: a person does not attain blessedness through deeds alone; rather, deeds are a cause. For this reason, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“None of you will enter Paradise by his deeds.” They asked, “Not even you, O Messenger of Allah?” He replied, “Not even I, unless Allah envelops me in mercy and bounty from Him.”

Yet He has said:

“Enter Paradise for what you used to do.”

Here, the preposition bi- indicates causation—that is, “because of your deeds.” What the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, negated was bi- indicating exchange, as when one says, “I bought this in exchange for that.” In other words, deeds are not sufficient payment or a sufficient price for entering Paradise. Rather, there must also be Allah’s pardon

translated_text:
and His bounty and mercy. Through His pardon He erases sins, through His mercy He brings good things, and through His bounty He multiplies blessings.

Two groups of people have gone astray on this matter:

One group believed in predestination and supposed that this alone was sufficient to attain their goal. They therefore disregarded the divinely prescribed means and righteous deeds. These people ultimately come to disbelieve in Allah’s Books, His messengers, and His religion.

Another group began demanding recompense from Allah as a hired worker demands it from his employer, relying on their own ability, strength, and deeds, and as slaves demand it from their masters. These people are ignorant and misguided. Allah did not command His servants to do what He commanded out of any need for it, nor did He forbid them what He forbade out of stinginess. Rather, He commanded what benefits them and forbade what harms them. As He, glorified be He, said:

“O My servants, you can never harm Me, nor can you ever benefit Me.”

When a king commands his slaves to do something, he does so because he needs their service. They carry it out with strength that he did not create for them, and so they demand recompense for it. Allah Most High, however, has no need of any of His creation. If they do good, they do so for themselves; if they do evil, its consequences fall upon them. The good they earn is theirs, and the evil they earn counts against them.

“Whoever does righteousness—it is for his own soul; and whoever does evil—it is against it. And your Lord is not ever unjust to His servants.”

In an authentic hadith, Allah Most High is reported to have said:

“O My servants, I have forbidden injustice for Myself and made it forbidden among you, so do not wrong one another. O My servants, you sin by night

and day, and I forgive all sins, and I do not mind. So seek My forgiveness, and I will forgive you. O My servants, all of you are astray except those whom I guide, so seek My guidance, and I will guide you. O My servants, all of you are hungry except those whom I feed, so ask Me for food, and I will feed you. O My servants, you can never harm Me, nor can you ever benefit Me. O My servants, if all of you, from the first to the last, humans and jinn alike, had hearts as devout as the most devout heart among you, that would add nothing to My dominion. O My servants, if all of you, from the first to the last, humans and jinn alike, had hearts as wicked as the most wicked heart among you, that would diminish My dominion in no way. O My servants, if all of you, from the first to the last, humans and jinn alike, gathered on a single plain and asked of Me, and I gave each person what they requested, that would diminish My dominion no more than the sea is diminished by dipping a needle into it once. O My servants, it is only your deeds that I record for you and then recompense you for in full. Whoever finds good should praise Allah, and whoever finds otherwise should blame no one but himself.”

Although He, glorified be He, has no need of any of His creation, He created them and sent them a messenger to explain what brings them happiness and what brings them misery. Then, by His permission, He guided His believing servants to the truth concerning which they differed, graciously bestowing faith and righteous deeds upon them. Thus, His creation is by His bounty, His sending the Messenger is by His bounty, and His guiding them is by His bounty. Everything through which they attain good, whether their own abilities or anything else, is by His bounty. Likewise, reward and recompense are by His bounty, even though He has made this binding upon Himself, just as He has forbidden injustice for Himself, and has promised it. As He said:

“Your Lord has decreed mercy upon Himself.”

And He Most High said:

“And it is incumbent upon Us to help the believers.”

It will therefore assuredly come to pass, being binding by virtue of His own decree and promise

, for created beings cannot impose any obligation upon Allah or forbid Him anything. They are far too powerless and insignificant for that. Every blessing from Him is a bounty, and every punishment from Him is just, as stated in the preceding hadith:

“It is only your deeds that I record for you and then recompense you for in full. Whoever finds good should praise Allah, and whoever finds otherwise should blame no one but himself.”

An authentic hadith states:

“The finest supplication for forgiveness is for the servant to say: ‘O Allah, You are my Lord; none has the right to be worshipped but You. You created me, and I am Your servant. I remain faithful to Your covenant and promise as best I can. I seek refuge in You from the evil of what I have done. I acknowledge Your favor upon me, and I acknowledge my sin. So forgive me, for none forgives sins but You.’ Whoever says this in the morning, firmly believing in it, then dies that night, will enter Paradise.”

The words, “I acknowledge Your favor upon me, and I acknowledge my sin,” acknowledge both the Lord’s favors and the servant’s sin. As one of the early generations said:

“Each morning, I find myself between a blessing descending upon me from Allah and a sin ascending from me to Allah. So I wish to respond to the blessing with gratitude and to the sin by seeking forgiveness.”

Whoever turns away from the commands and prohibitions, the promise of reward and the threat of punishment, looking only to divine decree, has gone astray. Whoever seeks to observe the commands and prohibitions while disregarding divine decree has likewise gone astray. Rather, the believer follows what the Most High has said:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.”

We therefore worship Him in obedience to His command and seek His help out of faith in divine decree. In an authentic hadith, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The strong believer is better and more beloved to Allah than the weak believer, though there is good in both. Strive for what benefits you, seek Allah’s help, and do not give up. If something befalls you, do not say, ‘If only I had done such and such, this and that would have happened.’ Rather, say, ‘Allah decreed it, and He does whatever He wills,’ for ‘if only’ opens the way for Satan’s work.”

Thus the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, instructed him to do two things: to strive for what benefits him—which means complying with the command, worshipping Allah, and obeying Allah and His Messenger—and to seek Allah’s help. This entails believing in divine decree: that there is no might or power except through Allah, and that whatever Allah wills happens, while whatever He does not will does not happen.

Whoever thinks that he can obey Allah without His help, as the Magian Qadariyyah claim, has denied Allah’s perfect power, His unfailingly effective will, and His creation of all things. Whoever thinks that being helped to attain what he wants and having it made easy for him makes him praiseworthy, whether it accords with Allah’s revealed command or contradicts it, has denied Allah’s religion and rejected His Books, His messengers, His promise of reward, and His threat of punishment. He has merited His wrath and punishment in even greater measure than the former.

A servant may desire what Allah approves of, loves, and commands, and what brings him nearer to Him. Or he may desire what Allah hates, detests, is angered by, and forbids, and for which He punishes the one who does it. Either person may have his chosen course made easy for him, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Everyone will find easy that for which he was created. Whoever is among those destined for happiness will find the deeds of those destined for happiness made easy for him; whoever is among those destined for misery will find the deeds of those destined for misery made easy for him.”

The Most High has said:

“Whoever desires this fleeting life, We hasten for him therein whatever We will, for whomever We choose. Then We appoint Hell for him, where he will burn, condemned and banished.”

“But whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it as he should, while being a believer—it is they whose striving will be appreciated.”

“To all—these and those—We extend the gifts of your Lord. The gifts of your Lord are not withheld.”

And the Most High has said: “As for

man, when his Lord tests him by honoring him and granting him ease, he says, ‘My Lord has honored me.’”

“But when He tests him by restricting his provision, he says, ‘My Lord has humiliated me.’”

He, glory be to Him, has explained that His testing someone in this world does not necessarily mean that He has humiliated him. Rather, He tests His servant through both prosperity and adversity. The believer is steadfastly patient and grateful, so both are good for him. As authentically reported, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah decrees nothing for the believer except that it is good for him, and this is true of no one but the believer. If prosperity comes his way, he gives thanks, and that is good for him. If adversity befalls him, he is patient, and that is good for him.”

The hypocrite, however, is anxious and impatient, as the Most High has said:

“Indeed, man was created anxious: fretful when harm touches him, and withholding when good comes his way—except those who pray, who are constant in their prayers, and in whose wealth there is a recognized right for the beggar and the deprived”—up to His words—“honored in Gardens.”

Since a servant may find easy what does not benefit him but instead harms him—disobedience to Allah, arrogance in prosperity, and transgression—while he may intend to worship Allah, obey Him, and do righteous deeds yet be unable to do so, he has been commanded to say in every prayer:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.”

It is authentically reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ‘I have divided the prayer between Myself and My servant into two halves: half is for Me and half is for My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks for.’ When he says, ‘All praise is for Allah, Lord of all worlds,’ He says, ‘My servant has praised Me.’ When he says, ‘The Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful,’ He says, ‘My servant has extolled Me.’ When he says, ‘Master of the Day of Judgment,’ He says, ‘My servant has glorified Me.’ When he says, ‘You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help,’ He says, ‘This verse is between Me and My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks for.’ When he says, ‘Guide us to the path

Some of the early generations said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed one hundred and four books and gathered their knowledge into the four Scriptures: the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and the Criterion. He gathered the knowledge of these four into the Quran, the knowledge of the Quran into the Mufassal section, the knowledge of the Mufassal into al-Fātihah, and the knowledge of al-Fātihah into His words:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.”

Every deed a servant performs that is not obedience to Allah, worship, and righteous action is futile. This world is cursed, and everything in it is cursed except what is for Allah—even if, through such a deed, a person gains leadership and wealth. The utmost that one seeking leadership can attain is to become like Pharaoh, and the utmost that one amassing wealth can attain is to become like Qārūn. In Surah al-Qasas, Allah has related accounts of Pharaoh and Qārūn containing lessons for people of understanding.

Any deed in which Allah does not assist the servant will neither come to pass nor be of benefit. Whatever is not accomplished through Him will not occur, and whatever is not done for Him will neither benefit nor endure. He therefore commanded the servant to say:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.”

The servant has “two states” with regard to what is decreed: a state before the decree takes effect, and “a state” afterward. Before the decreed event, he must seek Allah’s help, rely upon Him, and supplicate to Him. When the decreed event occurs independently of his own action, he must bear it patiently or be content with it. If it results from his own action and is a blessing, he praises Allah for it; if it is a sin, he seeks His forgiveness for it.

He also has “two states” with regard to what he is commanded to do: a state before the action, consisting of the resolve to comply

and seeking Allah’s help in doing so. The other state comes after the action: seeking forgiveness for one’s shortcomings and thanking Allah for the good He has graciously enabled one to do. Allah Most High says:

“So be patient; indeed, Allah’s promise is true. And seek forgiveness for your sin.”

He commanded him to bear decreed calamities patiently and to seek forgiveness for sin, although each servant seeks forgiveness according to his own state, for the good deeds of the righteous count as sins for those brought near to Allah.

Allah Most High says:

“But if you are patient and mindful of Allah, that is indeed a matter requiring firm resolve.”

Joseph said:

“Indeed, whoever is mindful of Allah and patient—Allah does not allow the reward of those who do good to be lost.”

He thus mentioned patience in the face of calamities and mindfulness of Allah through avoiding blameworthy deeds. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Strive for what benefits you, seek Allah’s help, and do not give up. If something befalls you, do not say, ‘If only I had done such and such, this and that would have happened.’ Rather, say, ‘Allah has decreed, and He does whatever He wills,’ for ‘if only’ opens the way for Satan’s work.”

He thus commanded a person, when calamities befall him, to consider the divine decree rather than lament the past. Instead, he should know that whatever befell him could never have missed him, and whatever missed him could never have befallen him. Thus, one should look to the divine decree in the face of calamities and seek forgiveness for one’s faults. Allah Most High says:

“No calamity befalls the earth or yourselves without being written in a Record before We bring it into being. That is certainly easy for Allah.”

“So that you may neither grieve over what you have missed nor exult in what He has given you.”

Allah Most High also says:

“No calamity befalls except by Allah’s permission. Whoever believes in Allah, He guides his heart.”

‘Alqamah and others said: This is a man who is struck by a calamity and knows that it is from Allah, so he is content and submits.

And Allah, Glorified and Most High, knows best.

He was asked about the Creator—glory be to Him:

“Does He lead astray and guide?”

He replied:

Everything in existence is created by Him; He created it through His will and power. Whatever He wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass. He is the One who gives and withholds, lowers and raises, honours and humiliates, enriches and impoverishes, leads astray and guides, and grants happiness and brings misery. He grants sovereignty to whomever He wills and takes it away from whomever He wills. He opens the heart of whomever He wills to Islam, and makes the heart of whomever He wills constricted, as though he were climbing into the sky.

He turns hearts: every heart of His servants is between two fingers of the Most Merciful. If He wills to set it straight, He sets it straight; and if He wills to make it deviate, He makes it deviate. He is the One who has endeared faith to the believers and made it beautiful in their hearts, and has made disbelief, wickedness and disobedience hateful to them. Those are the rightly guided. He is the One who makes the Muslim a Muslim and the worshipper one who prays.

Abraham, the intimate friend of Allah, said:

“Our Lord, make us both submissive to You, and from our descendants a community submissive to You.”

He also said:

“My Lord, make me one who establishes prayer, and make some of my descendants so as well.”

Allah Most High says:

“And We made from among them leaders guiding by Our command when they were patient.”

He says of Pharaoh’s people:

“And We made them leaders inviting to the Fire.”

Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, man was created

anxious: fretful when evil touches him, and withholding when good touches him.”

He says:

“Build the Ark under Our watchful eyes and according to Our revelation.”

And He says:

“And he was building the Ark.”

Ships are made by human beings, yet Allah, Blessed and Exalted, has stated that He created them, saying:

“And We created for them other vessels like it, which they ride.”

He says:

“And Allah has made your homes a place of rest for you, and made for you tents from the hides of livestock, which you find light to carry when you travel and when you camp; and from their wool and fur…”

—and the subsequent verses. All these things are made by human beings.

Allah Most High says:

“Do you worship what you carve, when Allah created you and what you make?”

Here, mā (“what”) means “that which.” Whoever interprets it as a nominalizing particle is mistaken. Nevertheless, if He created the carved object, just as He created manufactured goods, clothing and buildings, this shows that He is the Creator of every maker and what he makes.

Allah Most High says:

“Whoever Allah guides is rightly guided, but whoever He leads astray—you will never find for him a protecting guide.”

And He says:

“Whoever Allah wills to guide, He opens his heart to Islam; and whoever He wills to lead astray, He makes his heart tight and constricted.”

He—glory be to Him—is the Creator, Lord and Sovereign of everything. In what He has created there is consummate wisdom, abundant blessing, and mercy both general and particular. He is not questioned about what He does, whereas they will be questioned—not merely because of His power and irresistible might, but because of the perfection of His knowledge, power, mercy and wisdom. For He, Glorified and Exalted, is the wisest of judges and the most merciful of those who show mercy. He is more merciful to His servants than a mother is to her child, and He has made everything He created good.

Allah Most High says:

“And you see the mountains

which you think are motionless, while they pass like clouds—the handiwork of Allah, who has perfected everything.”

He has created things through causes, as Allah Most High says:

“And the water Allah sends down from the sky, reviving the earth thereby after its death.”

And He says:

“Then We sent down water through it, and brought forth with it fruits of every kind.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Through it Allah guides those who seek His pleasure to the ways of peace.”

translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked about the goodness of Allah Most High’s will to create His creatures and bring beings into existence, and whether He creates for a reason or without one:

If it is said that He creates without a reason, this would be purposeless—exalted is Allah above that. If it is said that He creates for a reason, then if you say that this reason has always existed, it follows that its effect must also have always existed. If you say that it came into existence, it follows that it must itself have a cause, yet an infinite regress is impossible.

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds. This is a weighty question, among the greatest questions people have discussed, among the most extensive in its ramifications and subsidiary issues, and among those occasioning the most doubts and perplexities.

It concerns Allah Most High’s attributes, names, actions, and rulings, including His commands, prohibitions, promises, and threats. It pertains to both His creation and His command, so everything in existence is connected to this question: all created things are connected to it, and it concerns the Creator, glorified is He. Likewise, all revealed laws—their commands, prohibitions, promises, and threats—are connected to it. It also concerns questions of divine decree and command, and questions of divine attributes and actions. These encompass the principal fields of human knowledge. Thus, jurisprudence, which concerns commands and prohibitions, is connected to this question.

translated_text:
People have also discussed “the reasons underlying religious rulings, commands, and prohibitions,” such as the commands to affirm Allah’s oneness, be truthful and just, establish prayer, pay zakah, fast, and perform Hajj, and the prohibitions against associating partners with Allah, lying, wrongdoing, and indecencies. Did He prescribe these things for a wise purpose, a benefit, and a reason that called for them? Or was this solely a matter of His will and sheer volition? Are the reasons assigned by revealed law to be understood as motives and impetuses, or as indicators and signs? Is it compatible with wisdom for Allah to forbid affirming His oneness, truthfulness, and justice, and to command associating partners with Him, lying, and wrongdoing, or not?

People have also discussed Allah Most High’s freedom from injustice: is He free from it despite having the power to commit it, or is injustice intrinsically impossible and therefore incapable of occurring? They have discussed Allah’s love, pleasure, anger, and displeasure: do these mean His will, or are they the created reward and punishment, or are they attributes more specific than will?

They have disagreed concerning the disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience that occur on earth: does He will, love, and approve of them just as He wills and loves everything else that happens? Or do they occur independently of His power and will, while He is unable to guide someone who is astray or lead astray someone who is rightly guided? Or do they occur by His power and will, such that nothing occurs in His dominion that He does not will, and He has consummate wisdom in all that He creates, while He hates and abhors these things and detests those who commit them, neither loves corruption nor approves of disbelief for His servants, and does not will it by His religious will, which entails His love and pleasure, even if He wills it by His universal will, which encompasses whatever He has ordained and decreed?

The subsidiary questions arising from this fundamental issue are numerous; this is not the place to examine them exhaustively.

Because of the conflicting considerations and ambiguities surrounding this fundamental issue, people have adopted the three possibilities mentioned in the question. Each has been upheld by groups of people, both Muslims and non-Muslims.

The first possibility:

This is the position of those who say that He created His creatures and prescribed His commands for no reason, motive, or impetus, but solely by His will and sheer volition. This is the position of many speculative theologians, jurists, and others who affirm divine decree and profess adherence to the Sunnah. Groups among the followers of Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad, and others have held this view. It is also the position of al-Ash‘arī and his followers, and of many Zāhirī “opponents of analogical reasoning in jurisprudence,” such as Ibn Hazm and others like him.

One of their arguments is that if He created creation for a reason, He would be deficient without it and acquire perfection through it. For, with respect to Him, either the existence and nonexistence of that reason are equal, or its existence is preferable. If the former is true, He cannot act for its sake. If the latter is true, then its existence is established as preferable for Him; He would therefore acquire perfection through it and would consequently have been deficient before it.

Another of their arguments is what the questioner mentioned: if the cause were eternal, the effect would necessarily have to be prior as well. For although the final cause precedes the effect in knowledge and intention—as it is said, “What comes first in thought comes last in execution, and what comes first as a goal comes last in attainment,” and it is said that the final cause is what makes the agent an agent—there is no doubt that, in actual existence, it comes after the effect. Thus, if it were said that He acts for an eternal reason, this would entail that nothing ever comes into being, contrary to what is observed. If, however, it were said that He acts for a temporally originated reason, two untenable consequences would follow.

The first is that He would be a locus of temporal occurrences. For if the reason is separate from Him and produces no effect upon Him, its existence cannot be preferable to its nonexistence with respect to Him. If it is assumed to produce an effect upon Him, that effect would be temporally originated, and temporal occurrences would therefore subsist in Him.

The second untenable consequence is that this entails an infinite regress in two respects.

First, that temporally originated reason sought through the act is itself something Allah Most High brings into being through His power and will. If He brings it into being for no reason, this entails purposelessness, as explained above. If He does so for a reason, the same alternatives arise again. Thus, if everything He brings into being is brought into being for a reason, and that reason is itself something He brings into being, an infinite regress of temporal occurrences necessarily follows.

Second, that reason must be intended either for its own sake or for another reason. If it is intended for its own sake, it cannot have a temporal beginning, because Allah Most High does not delay bringing into being something He wills for its own sake and has the power to bring about. If it is intended for the sake of something else, the same argument applies to that other thing, and an infinite regress necessarily follows. These and similar arguments are advanced by those who deny that Allah Most High’s actions and rulings are based on reasons.

The fundamental premise of their position is that the Originator of the world is a complete cause that necessarily entails its effect, such that its effect cannot come after it.

Their strongest argument is as follows:

“If everything required for Him to act existed from eternity, then the effect must also have existed from eternity, because the effect of a complete cause cannot come after it. If it did, not all the conditions for the act would have existed from eternity. By a complete cause, we mean nothing other than that which necessarily entails its effect. Thus, if the effect is assumed not to accompany it, the cause would not be complete.

“If, however, the complete cause—that is, everything required for the act, constituting the fully sufficient cause of its existence and comprising all the conditions whose existence necessarily entails the existence of the act—did not exist in its entirety from eternity, then, if the effect subsequently came into existence, a new cause must have arisen. Otherwise, one of the two alternatives for a contingent thing would have been favored without a determining factor. If there is a newly arisen cause, the same argument applies to its coming into existence as applies to the first temporal occurrence, and an infinite regress necessarily follows.”

They say: “Denying the existence of a complete cause that necessarily entails its effect therefore entails either an infinite regress or a preference without a determining factor.”

Most of these philosophers also affirm a final cause for the act, identifying it with the efficient cause itself. Yet they contradict themselves: they affirm a final cause for Him and a final cause for His act, while also saying that He has no will, but rather produces effects by the necessity of His essence, not as an agent acting by choice. Their position is false on many grounds.

One is as follows:

This position entails that nothing comes into being, and that whatever does come into being does so without being brought into being by an originator. Clearly, the falsity of this is more evident than the falsity of an infinite regress or of a preference without a determining factor. For a complete cause that necessarily entails its effect is accompanied by that effect, and no part of its effect can come after it. Thus, no temporal occurrence can arise from this complete cause. Yet there is nothing from which contingent things can proceed other than the intrinsically necessary being, whom these philosophers call a complete cause. If temporal occurrences cannot proceed from Him, and there is nothing else to bring them into being, it follows that they come into being without an originator.

(Moreover, suppose that something other than Him brought them into being. If it were intrinsically necessary, the same argument would apply to it as to the first necessary being. Their fundamental premise is that the intrinsically necessary being is a complete cause whose effect must accompany it. According to their position, therefore, no temporal occurrence can proceed from a complete cause, either through an intermediary or without one. For if that intermediary were a necessary concomitant of His existence, it would be eternal along with Him, making it impossible for temporal occurrences to proceed from it. If it came into being, the same argument would apply to it as to any other temporal occurrence.

If, on the other hand, the originator of temporal occurrences were assumed not to be intrinsically necessary, it would be contingent and dependent upon a necessitating cause to bring it into existence. Then, if it were said to have been brought into being, it would itself be one of the temporal occurrences. If it were said to be eternal, it would have a complete cause that necessarily entailed it, and temporal occurrences could not then arise from it. For neither a contingent being nor any of its attributes or acts can exist except through the intrinsically necessary being.

Thus, if temporal occurrences are assumed to arise from an eternal contingent being that is the effect of an eternal cause, the question is: has a cause arisen within it

(The second argument demonstrating the falsity of their position is as follows:

The substance of the argument is that, unless there is an eternal cause, either an infinite regress or a preference without a determining factor must follow. Yet you consider an infinite regress possible. Indeed, their fundamental position is that these temporal occurrences form an infinite succession, one after another, and that the movements of the celestial sphere prepare receptive substrates for newly arising forms to emanate upon them from the eternal cause—whether you say that this cause is the active intellect or the Necessary Being, from whom they proceed through the intellects or other intermediaries. Since you consider an infinite regress possible, temporal occurrences could arise from something other than a cause that necessarily entails its effect, even if this involves an infinite regress. Indeed, this is better, in light of both revelation and reason, than your position.

For revelation states that Allah created the heavens and the earth in six days. This is agreed upon by the adherents of the religious communities: Muslims, Jews, and Christians.

If it is said that He created them through a cause that had come into being before that, this would be better, in light of revelation, than your claim that they are eternal and have existed with Him from all eternity. It may then be said:

Either you affirm that the Originator of the world acts with wisdom and for an intended end, or you do not. If you do not, your affirmation of a final cause is invalidated, as is what you say about the wisdom of the Creator Most High in creating animals and other creatures. For example, He—glory be to Him—brings forth His blessings and mercy when His creatures need them: He brings rain in winter in the measure needed, and provides human beings with the faculties and organs they require in proportion to their needs. There are other such examples, which this is not the place to discuss at length.

If, however, you affirm that He acts for an intended wise purpose—which, in your terminology, is the final cause—you must necessarily affirm that He possesses will and volition. For to say that an agent performed a particular act for a particular wise purpose without intending that purpose is to affirm two contradictories together. These philosophers are among the most self-contradictory of people. Thus, they identify knowledge with the knower, knowledge with will, and will with power, and make similar assertions. Their views have been discussed at length elsewhere.
