You explained His acts in terms of purposes to avoid purposelessness, yet you fell into purposelessness yourselves. For a purposeless act is one that brings its doer no advantage, benefit, or gain. For this reason, neither Allah Most High, nor His Messenger (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), nor any rational person has enjoined anyone to do good to others, benefit them, or the like, except because of the benefit and advantage this brings to the doer. Otherwise, enjoining someone to perform an act that brings him no pleasure, happiness, benefit, or joy whatsoever, either immediately or in the future, is not commendable on the part of the one issuing the command.

This discussion gave rise to a dispute among the Mu‘tazilah, others, and those who agreed with them over “the rational discernment of moral goodness and badness.” The Mu‘tazilah and others affirmed this, as did those who agreed with them among the followers of Abū Hanīfah, Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, and Ahmad, as well as scholars of hadith and others. They also attributed this position to Abū Hanīfah himself. The Ash‘arīs denied it, as did those who agreed with them among the followers of Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad, and others.

Both sides agreed that, when goodness is understood as an act’s being beneficial and congenial to its doer, and badness as its being harmful and uncongenial to him, these can be known through reason as well as through revealed law. Some among them supposed that the goodness and badness known through revealed law fall outside this meaning. This is not so. Rather, all the acts that Allah Most High has made obligatory or recommended are beneficial to those who perform them and serve their welfare. All the acts that Allah has forbidden are harmful to those who perform them and detrimental to their welfare. The praise and reward resulting from obedience to the Lawgiver benefit the doer and serve his welfare, while the blame and punishment resulting from disobedience to Him harm the doer and are detrimental to his welfare.

translated_text:
The Mu‘tazilah affirmed goodness in the acts of Allah Most High, but not in the sense that any consequence of His acts accrues to Him. Their opponents, believing that an act can be good or bad only insofar as it has some consequence for its doer, denied this and said: “With regard to Allah Most High, what is bad is what is intrinsically impossible; every act conceived as possible is good.” For, according to them, there is no distinction between one thing He brings about and another with respect to Him.

The Mu‘tazilah, by contrast, affirmed goodness and badness without any consequence accruing to the doer that subsists in His essence. For, according to them, neither an attribute, nor an act, nor anything else subsists in His essence, although they may contradict themselves. They then began drawing analogies with what is good or bad on the part of a servant. Thus, they imposed upon Allah, glorified be He, the obligations they imposed upon the servant, and forbade Him things of the same kind as those they forbade the servant. They called this justice and wisdom, despite their reason’s inability to comprehend His wisdom and justice.

They affirm neither an all-encompassing will nor perfect power for Him. Thus, they do not acknowledge that He has power over all things, nor do they say, “Whatever Allah wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass.” Nor do they acknowledge that He is the Creator of all things. They ascribe to Him forms of injustice from which He, glorified be He, has declared Himself free. For He said:

“Whoever does righteous deeds while being a believer need fear neither injustice nor loss.”

That is, he need not fear being wronged by being made to bear the sins of others, nor having his good deeds diminished. And He Most High said:

“My word cannot be changed, and I am never unjust to My servants.”

The Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said in the hadith of the card, narrated by Imam Ahmad, al-Tirmidhī, and others:

“A man from my nation will be brought forward on the Day of Resurrection, and ninety-nine scrolls will be unrolled before him, each extending as far as the eye can see. He will be asked, ‘Do you deny any of this?’ He will reply, ‘No, my Lord.’ He will be asked, ‘Do you have any excuse? Do you have any good deed?’ He will reply, ‘No, my Lord.’ Then He will say, ‘Indeed you do!

You have a good deed credited with Us, and you will not be wronged today.’ He said: A card will then be brought out for him bearing the words, ‘I bear witness that there is no god but Allah.’ The card will be placed in one pan of the balance and the scrolls in the other. The scrolls will rise, outweighed by the card.”

The Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) thus stated that this man would not be wronged, but would instead be rewarded for the monotheism he had professed, as Allah Most High says:

“Whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it,
and whoever does an atom’s weight of evil will see it.”

Yet most of those who call themselves “upholders of justice” say that whoever commits a single major sin thereby nullifies all his good deeds and will remain in the Fire of Hell forever. Thus, they attribute to Allah what Allah and His Messenger have called injustice, despite their claim to declare Him free of injustice. Meanwhile, they call it injustice when He singles out whomever He wills for His mercy and bounty, and when He creates what He creates for the consummate wisdom inherent in it.

These matters are discussed at length elsewhere. Here, however, we have drawn attention to the main principles underlying people’s positions on this subject.

These Mu‘tazilah, together with those among the Shia who agree with them, hold that Allah, glorified be He, is obliged to do what is best for every servant in matters of religion. They disagree over whether He is obliged to do what is best for him in worldly matters. Their position is that He cannot do anything for a creature’s religious welfare other than what He has already done, and that He cannot guide someone who is astray, nor lead someone rightly guided astray.

As for the other groups who affirm that His acts have purposes—among the jurists, scholars of hadith, Sufis, and theologians such as the Karrāmiyyah and others, as well as the philosophers—they do not agree with them on

this; rather, they say that He, glorified be He, does what He does for a wise purpose known to Him, glorified and exalted be He. His servants, or some of them, may know whatever He discloses to them of His wisdom, or they may not know it. His acts of general scope serve a general wisdom and mercy, such as His sending Muhammad (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), concerning whom He Most High says:

“We have sent you only as a mercy to the worlds.”

His sending him was among the greatest blessings bestowed upon creation, embodying the Creator’s supreme wisdom and His mercy towards His servants. As He Most High says:

“Allah has certainly bestowed a great favour upon the believers by raising among them a Messenger from their own midst, reciting His verses to them, purifying them, and teaching them the Book and wisdom.”

He Most High also says:

“Thus We have tested some of them through others, so that they may say, ‘Are these the ones Allah has favoured from among us?’ Does Allah not know best those who are grateful?”

And He says:

“Muhammad is no more than a messenger; messengers have passed away before him. If he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels? Whoever turns back on his heels will not harm Allah in the least, and Allah will reward the grateful.”

He Most High also says:

“Have you not seen those who exchanged Allah’s favour for disbelief?”

They said: “This refers to Muhammad (may Allah bless him and grant him peace).”

If someone says, “Yet some people were harmed by his message, such as those among the polytheists and the People of the Book who rejected him,” there are two answers to this.

The first is that he benefited them as far as possible. He reduced the evil they would have committed had it not been for the message, by presenting the proofs and signs that shook what was in their hearts, and through jihad and the jizyah tax, which frightened and humbled them until their evil diminished. Those of them whom he killed died before they could live longer in disbelief and thereby increase in it. This therefore diminished their evil. The messengers—may Allah’s blessings be upon them—

were sent to secure and perfect benefits, and to prevent and reduce harms as far as possible.

The second answer is that any harm that occurred was negligible beside the benefit achieved. This is like rain whose benefits are widespread, even if it destroys some houses or hinders some travellers and people pursuing their livelihoods, such as cloth-bleachers and the like. Whatever brings widespread benefit and welfare is an intended good and a cherished mercy, even if some people suffer harm from it. This answer has been given by various groups of Muslims: speculative theologians, jurists and others among the Hanafīs, Hanbalīs and others, as well as the Karrāmiyyah and Sufis. It is also the answer given by many who engage in philosophy.

They say:

All the harm He brings into existence must involve a wise purpose. Allah Most High says:

“The work of Allah, who has perfected all things.”

And He says:

“Who has made good everything He created.”

Harm through which a desired wise purpose is achieved is not absolute evil, even if it is evil in relation to those harmed by it. Hence, neither the words of Allah Most High nor the words of His Messenger (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) attribute evil alone to Allah. Rather, evil is mentioned only in one of three ways: it is included within the generality of created things; it is attributed to the cause that produces it; or its agent is left unmentioned. When it is included within that generality, this conveys the all-encompassing nature of His power, will and creation, and encompasses the wisdom pertaining to the whole.

The first is exemplified by His saying, Most High:

“Allah is the Creator of all things,”

and similar passages. This category also includes Allah’s names that occur in pairs, such as the Giver and the Withholder, the Bringer of Harm and the Giver of Benefit, the Bestower of Honour and the Abaser, the Lowerer and the Raiser.

so the name “the Withholder” is not used apart from its counterpart, nor “the Bringer of Harm” apart from its counterpart, because pairing them conveys an all-encompassing meaning. Every instance of mercy, benefit and welfare in existence comes from His bounty, Most High, while everything else comes from His justice. Every blessing from Him is bounty, and every affliction from Him is justice. As reported in the two Sahīh collections, the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said:

“Allah’s right hand is full, undiminished by expenditure, pouring forth night and day. Have you considered what He has spent since He created the heavens and the earth? It has not diminished what is in His right hand. In His other hand is justice; He lowers and raises.”

He thus explained that His right hand holds kindness towards creation, while His other hand holds justice and the balance by which He lowers and raises. His lowering and raising proceed from His justice, and His kindness towards His creation proceeds from His bounty.

As for leaving the agent unmentioned, an example is the statement of the jinn:

“And we do not know whether evil is intended for those on earth, or whether their Lord intends right guidance for them.”

Another is His saying, Most High, in Sūrat al-Fātihah:

“The path of those You have blessed, not of those who have incurred wrath, nor of those who have gone astray.”

There are other similar examples.

As for attributing evil to its cause, an example is His saying:

“From the evil of what He has created.”

Another is His saying:

“So I intended to damage it,”

in contrast with His saying:

“So your Lord intended that they should reach maturity and bring forth their treasure.”

And His saying, Most High:

“Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself.”

And His saying:

“Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves.”

And His saying, Most High:

“Why, when a calamity befell you, although you had inflicted twice as much, did you say, ‘Where has this come from?’ Say, ‘It is from yourselves.’”

There are many similar examples.

For this reason, none of Allah’s most beautiful names entails evil. Evil is mentioned only in what He brings about, as in His saying:

“Tell My servants that I am indeed the All-Forgiving, the Most Merciful, and that My punishment is indeed the painful punishment.”

And His saying:

“Indeed, your Lord is swift in punishment, and indeed, He is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

And His saying:

“Know that Allah is severe in punishment, and that Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

And His saying:

“Indeed, your Lord’s onslaught is severe. Indeed, it is He who originates creation and restores it. And He is the All-Forgiving, the Most Loving.”

He thus makes clear—glory be to Him—that His onslaught is severe, and that He is the All-Forgiving, the Most Loving.

“The Avenger” is not among Allah’s most beautiful names established in reports from the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace). Rather, it occurs in the Quran only with qualifications, as in His saying, Most High:

“We shall indeed exact retribution from the criminals.”

And His saying:

“Indeed, Allah is Almighty, Possessor of Retribution.”

As for the hadith enumerating the most beautiful names, which includes “the Avenger” in the sequence “the Beneficent, the Accepter of Repentance, the Avenger, the Pardoner, the Most Compassionate,” those versed in hadith do not regard this enumeration as the words of the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace). Rather, al-Walīd ibn Muslim related it from Sa‘īd ibn ‘Abd al-‘Azīz or from one of his other teachers.

For this reason, none of the compilers of the well-known collections transmitted it except al-Tirmidhī, who narrated it through al-Walīd ibn Muslim with one wording. Others narrated it with differences in the names and their order, showing that it is not the words of the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace). All the other narrators who transmitted this hadith from Abū Hurayrah, then through al-A‘raj, then through Abū al-Zinād, did not specify the individual names. Rather, they related his saying (may Allah bless him and grant him peace):

“Allah has ninety-nine names, one hundred less one. Whoever enumerates them will enter Paradise.”

This is how the compilers of authentic collections, such as al-Bukhārī, Muslim and others, recorded it. However, an enumeration of the names was also transmitted through

another chain of transmission, in the report of Muhammad ibn Sīrīn from Abū Hurayrah. Ibn Mājah narrated it, but its chain is weak. Hadith scholars know that it is not the words of the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace). These are the only two reports attributed to the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) that enumerate the most beautiful names, and both are transmitted through Abū Hurayrah. This is discussed at length in its proper place.

The purpose here is to draw attention to principles that help one understand this question, for it continues to weigh heavily upon human souls. If a servant knows, in general, that Allah has great wisdom in what He creates and commands, that suffices him. Then, as his knowledge and faith increase, aspects of Allah’s wisdom and mercy become apparent to him that astound his mind and demonstrate the truth of what Allah has declared in His Book, where He says:

“We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth.”

For the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said in an authentic hadith:

“Allah is more merciful to His servants than a mother is to her child.”

It is also reported from him in the two Sahīh collections that he said:

“When Allah created mercy, He created it in one hundred parts. He sent down one part, through which creatures show mercy to one another; even an animal lifts its hoof away from its young because of that mercy. He kept ninety-nine parts with Himself. On the Day of Resurrection, He will join this one to those and show mercy to His servants through them.”

Or words to that effect, as spoken by the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and grant him peace).

Furthermore, these people—the majority of Muslims and others, such as the imams of the four schools and other early authorities and scholars—affirm His wisdom and do not deny it—as the Ash‘arīs and others like them have denied it

, who affirm only a will without wisdom and a volition without mercy, love, or pleasure. They regard all created things as equal in relation to Him, making no distinction between will, love, and pleasure. Rather, concerning whatever disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience occurs, they say that He loves and approves of it just as He wills it. When they say that He does not love or approve of it as religion, they also say that He does not will it as religion. As for faith and piety that do not come to pass, in their view He neither loves nor approves of them, just as He does not will them. Yet Allah Most High says:

“When they plot by night words that displease Him.”

Thus, He declares that He does not approve of it, although He has ordained and decreed it. The majority mentioned above do not agree with the Mu‘tazilah in denying Allah Most High’s power and the all-encompassing scope of His creation, will, and power. Nor do they liken Him to His creatures in what He makes obligatory and forbids, as these others have done. Nor do they strip Him of the attributes and acts with which He has described Himself. Rather, they affirm for Him the attributes and acts He has affirmed for Himself, and declare Him free of the attributes and acts from which He has declared Himself free.

They say that Allah is the Creator and Sovereign of all things; whatever He wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass; and He has power over all things. He loves those who do good, those who are mindful of Him, and those who act justly. He is pleased with the foremost pioneers among the Emigrants and the Helpers, and those who follow them in goodness. He does not love corruption, does not approve of disbelief for His servants, and does not approve of speech that contravenes the command of Allah and His Messenger.

They also say:

Although He is the Creator, Lord, and Sovereign of all things, He has nevertheless made distinctions among created beings, both in themselves and in their deeds. As Allah Most High says:

“Shall We then treat Muslims like criminals?”

And as He says:

“Or do those who commit evil deeds think that We will make them like those who believe and do righteous deeds—equal in their life and their death? How evil is their judgment!”

Allah Most High also says:

“Or shall We treat those who believe and do righteous deeds like those who spread corruption on earth? Or shall We treat the righteous like the wicked?”

And Allah Most High says:

“The blind and the seeing are not equal.”

“Nor are darkness and light.”

“Nor shade and scorching heat.”

“Nor are the living and the dead equal.”

There are other such passages that make clear the differences between created beings and their division into the wretched and the blessed. As Allah Most High says:

“He is the One who created you, yet some of you are disbelievers and some are believers.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Some He has guided, while others have deserved to go astray.”

And Allah Most High says:

“He admits whom He wills into His mercy; but for the wrongdoers He has prepared a painful punishment.”

And Allah Most High says:

“On the Day the Hour comes, they will be divided.”

“As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, they will rejoice in a garden.”

“But those who disbelieved and denied Our signs and the meeting of the Hereafter will be brought into punishment.”

There are many similar passages in the Quran. It should be understood that various groups among the practitioners of speculative theology and Sufism have stumbled over this matter, arriving at positions worse than those of the Mu‘tazilah and other Qadariyyah like them. For the latter hold in high regard the divine commands and prohibitions, the promise of reward and threat of punishment, and obedience to Allah and His Messenger. They enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong. Yet they went astray concerning divine decree, believing that affirming an all-encompassing will, comprehensive power, and creation extending to everything would necessarily impugn the Lord’s justice and wisdom. In this they were mistaken.

Opposing them were people among the scholars, devout worshippers, and practitioners of speculative theology and Sufism. They affirmed divine decree and believed that Allah is the Lord and Sovereign of all things; that whatever He wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass; and that He is the Creator, Lord, and Sovereign of all things. This is good and correct. Yet they fell short regarding the divine commands and prohibitions, the promise of reward and threat of punishment. They went to such excess that their extremists fell into heresy, becoming like the polytheists who said:

“Had Allah willed, neither we nor our forefathers would have associated partners with Him, nor would we have forbidden

anything.”

Although those Qadariyyah resemble the Magians in affirming an agent other than Allah—glorified is He—for what they consider evil, these others resemble the polytheists who said:

“Had Allah willed, neither we nor our forefathers would have associated partners with Him, nor would we have forbidden anything.”

The polytheists are worse than the Magians. Muslims unanimously agree that the Magians may retain their religion upon payment of the jizyah, and some scholars have held that marrying their women and eating their food are lawful. As for the polytheists, the Muslim community unanimously agrees that marrying their women and eating their food are forbidden. The position of al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad—according to the well-known report from him—and others is that they may not retain their religion upon payment of the jizyah. The majority of scholars hold that the Arab polytheists may not do so, even though the Magians may. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not accept the jizyah from any of the polytheists. Rather, he said:

“I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that none is worthy of worship but Allah and that I am the Messenger of Allah. If they say this, their lives and property are protected from me, except when its requirements warrant otherwise, and their reckoning rests with Allah, Mighty and Majestic.”

The point here is that whoever affirms divine decree and invokes it to invalidate the divine commands and prohibitions is worse than someone who affirms the divine commands and prohibitions but does not affirm divine decree. This is agreed upon by Muslims and adherents of other religions—indeed, by all creation. For whoever invokes divine decree and the witnessing of Allah’s universal lordship over all created beings, without distinguishing between what is commanded and what is forbidden, between believers and disbelievers, and between the obedient and the disobedient, believes in none of the messengers and none of the scriptures. To him, Adam and Iblīs are alike; Noah and his people are alike; Moses and Pharaoh are alike; and the first and foremost believers and the disbelievers of Mecca are alike. This error has become widespread among many practitioners of Sufism, asceticism, and worship, especially

when they combine this with the conception of divine oneness held by speculative theologians who affirm divine decree and will without affirming love and hatred, pleasure and displeasure. They say that “divine oneness” means oneness in lordship, and that “divinity” means the power to create. They do not understand Allah’s exclusive right to worship, nor do they know that a deity is an object of worship and devotion, and that merely acknowledging Allah as the Lord of everything does not constitute affirmation of His oneness until one testifies that none is worthy of worship but Allah. As Allah Most High says:

“Most of them do not believe in Allah without associating others with Him.”

Ikrimah said: “You ask them who created the heavens and the earth, and they say, ‘Allah,’ yet they worship others besides Him.”

These people claim spiritual realization and annihilation in divine oneness. They say that this is the pinnacle of knowledge, and that when someone possessing spiritual knowledge reaches this station, he no longer regards a good deed as good or an evil deed as evil, because he witnesses Allah’s universal lordship and His all-encompassing sustaining of creation. As many of the great shaykhs as Allah willed have fallen into this error. There is no might or power except through Allah.

The utmost these people attain in affirming divine oneness is the same affirmation made by the idol-worshipping polytheists, of whom Allah said:

“Say, ‘To whom belong the earth and whoever is in it, if you know?’”

“They will say, ‘To Allah.’ Say, ‘Then will you not take heed?’”

“Say, ‘Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the mighty Throne?’”

“They will say, ‘They belong to Allah.’ Say, ‘Then will you not fear Him?’”

“Say, ‘In whose hand is the dominion of all things, who grants protection, while none can grant protection against Him, if you know?’”

“They will say, ‘It belongs to Allah.’ Say, ‘How, then, are you deluded?’”

Allah Most High also says:

“If you ask them who created the heavens and the earth and subjected the sun and the moon, they will surely say, ‘Allah.’ How, then, are they turned away?”

“Allah extends provision for whom He wills of His servants and restricts it for him. Indeed, Allah is, of every

thing, Knowing.”

“If you ask them who sends down water from the sky and thereby revives the earth after its death, they will surely say, ‘Allah.’ Say, ‘All praise belongs to Allah.’ But most of them do not reason.” (1)

Allah Most High also says:

“If you ask them who created the heavens and the earth, they will surely say, ‘Allah.’ Say, ‘All praise belongs to Allah.’ But most of them do not know.”

Allah Most High also says:

“If you ask them who created them, they will surely say, ‘Allah.’ How, then, are they turned away?”

Allah Most High also says:

“Say, ‘Who provides for you from the heaven and the earth? Who controls hearing and sight? Who brings the living out of the dead and the dead out of the living? Who governs all affairs?’ They will say, ‘Allah.’ Say, ‘Then will you not fear Him?’”

“That, then, is Allah, your true Lord. What is there beyond truth except error? How, then, are you turned away?”

“Thus your Lord’s word has been confirmed against those who defiantly disobey: they will not believe.”

“Say, ‘Can any of those you associate with Allah originate creation and then repeat it?’ Say, ‘Allah originates creation and then repeats it.’ How, then, are you deluded?”

“Say, ‘Can any of those you associate with Allah guide to the truth?’ Say, ‘Allah guides to the truth.’ Is He who guides to the truth more worthy of being followed, or one who cannot find the way unless he is guided? What is the matter with you? How do you judge?”

Allah Most High also says:

“Or who created the heavens and the earth and sent down water for you from the sky, with which We caused gardens of beauty to grow? You could never have caused their trees to grow. Is there a god alongside Allah? Rather, they are a people who equate others with Him.”

“Or who made the earth a stable dwelling place, placed rivers through it, set firm mountains upon it, and placed a barrier between the two seas? Is there a god alongside Allah? But most of them do not know.”

“Or who answers the distressed when he calls upon Him, removes hardship, and makes you successors on the earth? Is there a god alongside Allah? How little you take heed!”

“Or who guides you through the darkness of land and sea, and who sends the winds as heralds of His mercy? Is there a god alongside Allah? Exalted is Allah above whatever they associate with Him!”

“Or who originates creation and then repeats it, and who provides for you from the heaven and the earth? Is there a god alongside Allah? Say, ‘Bring your proof, if you are truthful.’”

فَإِنَّ هَؤُلَاءِ الْمُشْرِكِينَ كَانُوا مُقِرِّينَ بِأَنَّ اللَّهَ خَالِقُ السَّمَوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ وَخَالِقُهُمْ وَبِيَدِهِ مَلَكُوتُ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ بَلْ كَانُوا مُقِرِّينَ بِالْقَدَرِ أَيْضًا فَإِنَّ الْعَرَبَ كَانُوا يُثْبِتُونَ الْقَدَرَ فِي الْجَاهِلِيَّةِ وَهُوَ مَعْرُوفٌ عَنْهُمْ فِي النَّظْمِ وَالنَّثْرِ وَمَعَ هَذَا فَلَمَّا لَمْ يَكُونُوا يَعْبُدُونَ اللَّهَ وَحْدَهُ لَا شَرِيكَ لَهُ بَلْ عَبَدُوا غَيْرَهُ كَانُوا مُشْرِكِينَ شَرًّا مِنْ الْيَهُودِ وَالنَّصَارَى. فَمَنْ كَانَ غَايَةُ تَوْحِيدِهِ وَتَحْقِيقِهِ هُوَ هَذَا التَّوْحِيدَ كَانَ غَايَةُ تَوْحِيدِهِ تَوْحِيدَ الْمُشْرِكِينَ. وَهَذَا الْمَقَامُ مَقَامٌ وَأَيُّ مَقَامٍ زَلَّتْ فِيهِ أَقْدَامٌ وَضَلَّتْ فِيهِ أَفْهَامٌ وَبُدِّلَ فِيهِ دِينُ الْمُسْلِمِينَ وَالْتَبَسَ فِيهِ أَهْلُ التَّوْحِيدِ بِعُبَّادِ الْأَصْنَامِ عَلَى كَثِيرٍ مِمَّنْ يَدَّعُونَ نِهَايَةَ التَّوْحِيدِ وَالتَّحْقِيقِ وَالْمَعْرِفَةِ وَالْكَلَامِ. وَمَعْلُومٌ عِنْدَ كُلِّ مَنْ يُؤْمِنُ بِاَللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ أَنَّ الْمُعْتَزِلَةَ وَالشِّيعَةَ الْقَدَرِيَّةَ الْمُثْبِتِينَ لِلْأَمْرِ وَالنَّهْيِ وَالْوَعْدِ وَالْوَعِيدِ خَيْرٌ مِمَّنْ يُسَوِّي بَيْنَ الْمُؤْمِنِ وَالْكَافِرِ وَالْبَرِّ وَالْفَاجِرِ وَالنَّبِيِّ الصَّادِقِ وَالْمُتَنَبِّئِ الْكَاذِبِ وَأَوْلِيَاءِ اللَّهِ وَأَعْدَائِهِ وَيَجْعَلُ هَذَا غَايَةَ التَّحْقِيقِ وَنِهَايَةَ التَّوْحِيدِ وَهَؤُلَاءِ يَدْخُلُونَ فِي مُسَمَّى 
" الْقَدَرِيَّةِ "
 الَّذِينَ ذَمَّهُمْ السَّلَفُ بَلْ هُمْ أَحَقُّ بِالذَّمِّ مِنْ الْمُعْتَزِلَةِ وَنَحْوِهِمْ كَمَا قَالَ أَبُو بَكْرٍ الْخَلَّالُ فِي 
" كِتَابِ السُّنَّةِ "
: الرَّدُّ عَلَى الْقَدَرِيَّةِ وَقَوْلُهُمْ إنَّ اللَّهَ أَجْبَرَ الْعِبَادَ عَلَى الْمَعَاصِي وَذَكَرَ عَنْ المروذي قَالَ قُلْت لِأَبِي عَبْدِ اللَّهِ: رَجُلٌ يَقُولُ إنَّ اللَّهَ أَجْبَرَ الْعِبَادَ فَقَالَ: هَكَذَا لَا تَقُولُ وَأَنْكَرَ ذَلِكَ وَقَالَ 
{يُضِلُّ اللَّهُ مَنْ يَشَاءُ وَيَهْدِي مَنْ يَشَاءُ}
 وَذَكَرَ عَنْ المروذي أَنَّ رَجُلًا قَالَ إنَّ اللَّهَ لَمْ يُجْبِرْ الْعِبَادَ عَلَى الْمَعَاصِي
translated_text:
For these polytheists acknowledged that Allah created the heavens and the earth and created them, and that dominion over all things rests in His hand. Indeed, they also acknowledged divine decree: the Arabs affirmed it in the pre-Islamic age, as is well known from their poetry and prose. Nevertheless, because they did not worship Allah alone, without partners, but worshipped others besides Him, they were polytheists worse than the Jews and Christians. Thus, anyone whose utmost attainment in monotheism and its realization amounts to this has attained nothing beyond the monotheism of the polytheists.

This is a matter of tremendous consequence: here feet have slipped, understandings have gone astray, and the religion of the Muslims has been altered. Here, too, many who claim the highest attainment in monotheism, realization, knowledge, and theological discourse have confused those who worship Allah alone with idolaters.

Everyone who believes in Allah and His Messenger knows that the Mu‘tazilah and the Qadarī Shiites, who affirm divine commands and prohibitions, promises of reward and threats of punishment, are better than those who make no distinction between the believer and the unbeliever, the righteous and the wicked, the truthful prophet and the lying pretender to prophethood, or Allah’s allies and His enemies, and who regard this as the utmost realization and the highest attainment in monotheism. These people fall under the designation “Qadariyyah” whom the early generations condemned. Indeed, they deserve condemnation more than the Mu‘tazilah and others like them.

As Abū Bakr al-Khallāl wrote in Kitāb al-Sunnah (The Book of the Sunnah): “Refutation of the Qadariyyah and their assertion that Allah compelled His servants to commit sins.” He related that al-Marwadhī said: “I said to Abū ‘Abd Allāh, ‘A man says that Allah compelled His servants.’ He replied, ‘Do not put it that way.’ He rejected this and said:

‘Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills.’”

He also related from al-Marwadhī that a man said, “Allah did not compel His servants to commit sins.”

فَرَدَّ عَلَيْهِ آخَرُ فَقَالَ إنَّ اللَّهَ جَبَرَ الْعِبَادَ أَرَادَ بِذَلِكَ إثْبَاتَ الْقَدَرِ فَسَأَلُوا عَنْ ذَلِكَ أَحْمَدَ بْنَ حَنْبَلٍ فَأَنْكَرَ عَلَيْهِمَا جَمِيعًا عَلَى الَّذِي قَالَ جَبَرَ وَعَلَى الَّذِي قَالَ لَمْ يُجْبِرْ حَتَّى تَابَ وَأَمَرَ أَنْ يُقَالَ:
 - 
{يُضِلُّ اللَّهُ مَنْ يَشَاءُ وَيَهْدِي مَنْ يَشَاءُ}
 . وَذَكَرَ عَنْ عَبْدِ الرَّحْمَنِ بْنِ مَهْدِيٍّ قَالَ أَنْكَرَ سُفْيَانُ الثَّوْرِيُّ

 يَعْنِي قَوْلَهُ 
{إنَّ فِيك لَخُلُقَيْنِ يُحِبُّهُمَا اللَّهُ: الْحِلْمُ وَالْأَنَاةُ فَقَالَ: أَخُلُقَيْنِ تَخَلَّقْت بِهِمَا أَمْ خُلُقَيْنِ جُبِلْت عَلَيْهِمَا؟
 فَقَالَ بَلْ خُلُقَيْنِ جُبِلْت عَلَيْهِمَا فَقَالَ:
 الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي جَبَلَنِي عَلَى خُلُقَيْنِ يُحِبُّهُمَا}
 .
 وَذَكَرَ عَنْ أَبِي إسْحَاقَ الفزاري قَالَ قَالَ الأوزاعي:
 أَتَانِي رَجُلَانِ فَسَأَلَانِي عَنْ الْقَدَرِ فَأَحْبَبْت أَنْ آتِيَك بِهِمَا تَسْمَعُ كَلَامَهُمَا وَتُجِيبُهُمَا: قُلْت رَحِمَك اللَّهُ أَنْتَ أَوْلَى بِالْجَوَابِ قَالَ: فَأَتَانِي الأوزاعي وَمَعَهُ الرَّجُلَانِ فَقَالَ تَكَلَّمَا فَقَالَا: قَدِمَ عَلَيْنَا نَاسٌ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْقَدَرِ فَنَازَعُونَا فِي الْقَدَرِ وَنَازَعْنَاهُمْ فِيهِ حَتَّى بَلَغَ بِنَا وَبِهِمْ إلَى أَنْ قُلْنَا: إنَّ اللَّهَ جَبَرَنَا عَلَى مَا نَهَانَا عَنْهُ وَحَالَ بَيْنَنَا وَبَيْنَ مَا أَمَرَنَا بِهِ وَرَزَقَنَا مَا حَرَّمَ عَلَيْنَا فَقُلْت: يَا هَؤُلَاءِ إنَّ الَّذِينَ أَتَوْكُمْ بِمَا أَتَوْكُمْ بِهِ قَدْ ابْتَدَعُوا بِدْعَةً وَأَحْدَثُوا حَدَثًا وَإِنِّي أَرَاكُمْ قَدْ خَرَجْتُمْ مِنْ الْبِدْعَةِ إلَى مِثْلِ مَا خَرَجُوا إلَيْهِ.
 فَقَالَ:
 أَصَبْت وَأَحْسَنْت يَا أَبَا إسْحَاقَ. وَذَكَرَ عَنْ بَقِيَّةَ بْنِ الْوَلِيدِ قَالَ سَأَلْت الزُّبَيْدِيَّ وَالْأَوْزَاعِي عَنْ 
" الْجَبْرِ "
translated_text:
whereupon another man replied to him, “Allah did compel His servants,” intending thereby to affirm divine decree. They asked Ahmad ibn Hanbal about this, and he rebuked them both—the one who said, “He compelled,” and the one who said, “He did not compel”—until he repented. He instructed them to say:

“Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills.”

He also related from ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn Mahdī, who said: “Sufyān al-Thawrī rejected the expression ‘He compelled’ and said, ‘Allah endowed His servants with their innate natures.’”

Al-Marwadhī said that he meant the Prophet’s words—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—to al-Ashajj of ‘Abd al-Qays:

“You have two qualities that Allah loves: forbearance and deliberation.”

He asked, “Are these two qualities that I have acquired, or two qualities that are innate to me?”

He replied, “Rather, they are two qualities innate to you.”

He said, “Praise be to Allah, who endowed me with two innate qualities that He loves.”

He also related from Abū Ishāq al-Fazārī, who said: “Al-Awzā‘ī said to me, ‘Two men came to me and asked me about divine decree. I wished to bring them to you so that you could hear what they have to say and answer them.’

“I replied, ‘May Allah have mercy on you; you are better qualified to answer.’

“Then al-Awzā‘ī came to me with the two men and said, ‘Speak.’

“They said, ‘Some adherents of the Qadariyyah came to us and disputed with us about divine decree. We disputed with them until our argument reached the point where we said: “Allah compelled us to do what He forbade us, prevented us from doing what He commanded us, and provided us with what He prohibited to us.”’

“I said, ‘You two! Those people who came to you with such claims have introduced an innovation and brought something new into the religion. Yet I see that, in departing from their innovation, you have gone to something like that to which they went.’

“Al-Awzā‘ī said, ‘You are right and have spoken well, Abū Ishāq.’”

He also related from Baqiyyah ibn al-Walīd, who said: “I asked al-Zubaydī and al-Awzā‘ī about ‘compulsion’

original_text:
فَقَالَ الزُّبَيْدِيُّ أَمْرُ اللَّهِ أَعْظَمُ وَقُدْرَتُهُ أَعْظَمُ مِنْ أَنْ يُجْبِرَ أَوْ يُعْضِلَ وَلَكِنْ يَقْضِيَ وَيُقَدِّرَ وَيَخْلُقَ وَيُجْبِلَ عَبْدَهُ عَلَى مَا أَحَبَّ.
 وَقَالَ الأوزاعي:
 مَا أَعْرِفُ لِلْجَبْرِ أَصْلًا مِنْ الْقُرْآنِ وَالسُّنَّةِ فَأَهَابُ أَنْ أَقُولَ ذَلِكَ وَلَكِنَّ الْقَضَاءَ وَالْقَدَرَ وَالْخَلْقَ وَالْجَبْلَ فَهَذَا يُعْرَفُ فِي الْقُرْآنِ وَالْحَدِيثِ عَنْ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ.
 وَقَدْ قَالَ مُطَرِّفُ بْنُ الشخير:
 لَمْ نُوكَلْ إلَى الْقَدَرِ وَإِلَيْهِ نَصِيرُ.
 وَقَالَ ضَمْرَةُ بْنُ رَبِيعَةَ:
 لَمْ نُؤْمَرْ أَنْ نَتَّكِلَ عَلَى الْقَدَرِ وَإِلَيْهِ نَصِيرُ.
 وَقَدْ ثَبَتَ فِي الصَّحِيحِ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ قَالَ:
 
{مَا مِنْكُمْ مِنْ أَحَدٍ إلَّا وَقَدْ عَلِمَ مَقْعَدَهُ مِنْ الْجَنَّةِ وَمَقْعَدَهُ مِنْ النَّارِ قَالُوا يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ أَفَلَا نَدَعُ الْعَمَلَ وَنَتَّكِلُ عَلَى الْكِتَابِ؟
 فَقَالَ:
 لَا اعْمَلُوا فَكُلٌّ مُيَسَّرٌ لِمَا خُلِقَ لَهُ}
 . وَهَذَا بَابٌ وَاسِعٌ. وَالْمَقْصُودُ هُنَا أَنَّ الْخَلَّالَ وَغَيْرَهُ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْعِلْمِ أَدْخَلُوا الْقَائِلِينَ بِالْجَبْرِ فِي مُسَمَّى 
" الْقَدَرِيَّةِ "
 وَإِنْ كَانُوا لَا يَحْتَجُّونَ بِالْقَدَرِ عَلَى الْمَعَاصِي فَكَيْفَ بِمَنْ يَحْتَجُّ بِهِ عَلَى الْمَعَاصِي؟ وَمَعْلُومٌ أَنَّهُ يَدْخُلُ فِي ذَمِّ مَنْ ذَمَّ اللَّهُ مِنْ الْقَدَرِيَّةِ مَنْ يَحْتَجُّ بِهِ عَلَى إسْقَاطِ الْأَمْرِ وَالنَّهْيِ أَعْظَمُ مِمَّا يَدْخُلُ فِيهِ الْمُنْكِرُ لَهُ؛ فَإِنَّ ضَلَالَ هَذَا أَعْظَمُ وَلِهَذَا قُرِنَتْ الْقَدَرِيَّةُ بِالْمُرْجِئَةِ فِي كَلَامِ غَيْرِ وَاحِدٍ مِنْ السَّلَفِ وَرُوِيَ فِي ذَلِكَ حَدِيثٌ مَرْفُوعٌ؛ لِأَنَّ كُلًّا مِنْ هَاتَيْنِ الْبِدْعَتَيْنِ تُفْسِدُ الْأَمْرَ وَالنَّهْيَ وَالْوَعْدَ وَالْوَعِيدَ؛ فَالْإِرْجَاءُ يُضْعِفُ الْإِيمَانَ بِالْوَعِيدِ وَيُهَوِّنُ أَمْرَ الْفَرَائِضِ وَالْمَحَارِمِ
translated_text:
and al-Zubaydī replied, ‘Allah’s command is too great, and His power too great, for Him to compel or obstruct. Rather, He decrees, ordains, creates, and endows His servant with whatever innate disposition He wills.’

Al-Awzā‘ī said, ‘I know of no basis for “compulsion” in the Quran and Sunnah, so I hesitate to use that expression. But decree, ordainment, creation, and the bestowal of innate dispositions—these are recognized in the Quran and in the hadiths of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.’”

Mutarrif ibn al-Shikhkhīr said:

“We have not been left to divine decree, yet we arrive at what it ordains.”

Damrah ibn Rabī‘ah said:

“We were not commanded to rely on divine decree, yet we arrive at what it ordains.”

It is established in the Sahīh that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“There is not one of you whose place in Paradise and whose place in Hell are not already known.”

They asked, “O Messenger of Allah, should we not then abandon deeds and rely on what has been written?”

He replied, “No. Act, for everyone will find it made easy to do that for which he was created.”

This is a vast subject. The point here is that al-Khallāl and other scholars included those who affirm compulsion under the designation “Qadariyyah,” even when they did not invoke divine decree to justify sins. What, then, of those who do invoke it to justify sins?

Clearly, those who invoke divine decree to set aside commands and prohibitions fall more fully under Allah’s condemnation of the Qadariyyah than those who deny it, for the former’s misguidance is greater. This is why the Qadariyyah were associated with the Murji’ah in the statements of several of the early generations, and a hadith traced back to the Prophet has been narrated to this effect. Each of these two innovations undermines commands and prohibitions, promises of reward and threats of punishment. Thus, irjā’ weakens belief in the threats of punishment and makes light of obligatory duties and prohibitions

and if a Qadarī invokes divine decree as an excuse, he supports the Murji’ah; but if he denies it, he and the Murji’ah stand at opposite extremes. The former goes to extremes in severity, leaving no room for the servant to seek Allah’s help in doing what he has been commanded and refraining from what he has been forbidden, while the latter goes to the opposite extreme.

It is well known that Allah Most High sent the messengers and revealed the scriptures so that the messengers would be believed in what they reported and obeyed in what they commanded. As He Most High says:

“We did not send any messenger except to be obeyed by Allah’s permission.”

And He Most High says:

“Whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah.”

Belief in divine decree completes this. Whoever affirms divine decree but sets it against the divine command has thereby destroyed the very foundation. It is well known that anyone who sets aside the commands and prohibitions with which Allah sent His messengers is an unbeliever, as Muslims, Jews, and Christians all agree. Indeed, these people’s position is self-contradictory: none of them can live by it, no creature’s welfare can be maintained on its basis, and no two people can live together according to it. For if divine decree is a valid excuse, it is a valid excuse for everyone; otherwise, it is a valid excuse for no one.

Suppose someone wrongs a man, insults him, takes his wealth, corrupts his family, or does something else of this kind. Whenever that man blames or condemns the offender, or seeks his punishment, he invalidates the use of divine decree as an excuse.

Whoever claims that a gnostic, upon witnessing divine decree, is no longer bound by the divine command has uttered words of unbelief that neither Jews nor Christians would accept. Indeed, this is rationally impossible and inconceivable under divine law. A hungry person distinguishes bread from dust, and a thirsty person distinguishes water from a mirage. He desires what satisfies his hunger and quenches his thirst, rather than what does him no good, although all of these things are created by Allah Most High. Thus a living being—even if

it be what it may—must distinguish between what benefits it, brings it comfort and joy, and what harms it, brings it misery and pain. This is the essence of divine commands and prohibitions: Allah Most High has commanded His servants to do what benefits them and forbidden them from what harms them.

People fall into “four categories” with respect to divine law and decree. The worst of creation are those who invoke divine decree as an excuse for themselves but do not accept it as an excuse for others. They appeal to it to justify sins and faults, yet find no reassurance in it when calamities strike. As one scholar said: “When obedient, you are a Qadarī; when disobedient, a Jabrī. You adopt whichever doctrine suits your desires.”

At the opposite extreme are the best of creation: those who patiently endure calamities and seek forgiveness for their faults. As Allah Most High says:

“So be patient. Indeed, Allah’s promise is true. And seek forgiveness for your sin.”

And He Most High says:

“No calamity befalls the earth or yourselves without being recorded in a Book before We bring it into being. That is surely easy for Allah.”

“So that you may neither grieve over what you have missed nor exult over what He has given you.”

And He Most High says:

“No calamity befalls except by Allah’s permission. And whoever believes in Allah, He guides his heart.”

One of the early generations said: “This is a man who is struck by a calamity and knows that it is from Allah, so he is content and submits.”

He Most High says:

“And those who, when they commit an indecency or wrong themselves, remember Allah and seek forgiveness for their sins—and who forgives sins except Allah?—and do not knowingly persist in what they have done.”

Allah Most High relates that when Adam, peace be upon him, had done what he did, he said:

“Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves. If You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will surely be among the losers.”

And He relates that Iblīs said:

“Because You have led me astray, I will surely make evil appealing to them on earth, and I will lead them all astray.”

Thus, whoever repents resembles

his father Adam, while whoever persists in sin and invokes divine decree as an excuse resembles Iblīs.

In the hadith recorded in the two Sahīhs concerning the debate between Adam and Moses, peace be upon them, Moses said to Adam:

“You are Adam, the father of humankind. Allah created you with His hand, breathed into you of His spirit, and taught you the names of all things. Why did you cause us and yourself to be expelled from Paradise?”

Adam replied:

“You are Moses, whom Allah chose for His message and to whom He spoke, and for whom He inscribed the Torah with His hand. How many years before I was created did you find it written concerning me: ‘Adam disobeyed his Lord and went astray’?”

He replied: “So many years.” The narration states: “Thus Adam prevailed over Moses in argument.”

This hadith is recorded in the two Sahīhs on the authority of Abū Hurayrah. It has also been narrated with a good chain of transmission on the authority of ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him.

Adam, peace be upon him, prevailed over Moses only because Moses blamed him for what he had done on account of the calamity that had befallen them through his eating from the tree. He was not blaming him on account of Allah’s right that had been violated by the sin. Adam had already repented of that sin, as Allah Most High says:

“Then Adam received words from his Lord, and He accepted his repentance.”

And He Most High says:

“Then his Lord chose him, accepted his repentance, and guided him.”

Moses, peace be upon him—and even those below Moses in rank—knows that after repentance and forgiveness, no blame for the sin remains. Adam knew Allah too well to invoke divine decree as an excuse for sin, and Moses, peace be upon him, knew Allah Most High too well to accept such an argument. If it were a valid argument for sin, it would also have been a valid argument for Iblīs, Adam’s enemy; for Pharaoh, Moses’ enemy; and for every disbeliever and evildoer. Allah’s commands and prohibitions would thereby have been rendered void.

Rather, divine decree was a valid argument for Adam against Moses only because Moses blamed another for a calamity that had befallen him through that person’s action, when that calamity had already been decreed for him.

Allah Most High has said:

“No calamity befalls except by Allah’s permission. And whoever believes in Allah, He guides his heart.”

Anas said:

“I served the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, for ten years. He never uttered a word of irritation to me, nor did he ever say about something I had done, ‘Why did you do that?’ or about something I had not done, ‘Why did you not do it?’ When any of his family reproached me for something, he would say, ‘Leave him alone. Had something been decreed, it would have happened.’”

In the two Sahīhs, ‘Ā’ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, never struck a servant, a woman, an animal, or anything else with his hand, except when fighting in Allah’s cause. He never avenged himself for any harm done to him, unless Allah’s sacred limits were violated. When Allah’s sacred limits were violated, nothing could withstand his anger until he had exacted retribution for Allah’s sake.”

He also said, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“If Fātimah, the daughter of Muhammad, were to steal, I would cut off her hand.”

Thus, in matters of Allah’s commands and prohibitions, he would hasten to obey and enforce the prescribed punishments upon those who transgressed Allah’s limits, undeterred by anyone’s blame in fulfilling his duty to Allah. But when someone harmed him or fell short in fulfilling his rights, he would pardon that person and not hold him accountable, mindful of divine decree.

This is the path of those whom Allah has blessed: the prophets, the steadfastly truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous. What excellent companions they are!

This is obligatory regarding decreed calamities that occur without human agency, such as natural disasters, or through an act for which punishment is no longer possible, such as Adam’s action, peace be upon him. There is no basis for blaming him under revealed law—because of his repentance—or in terms of divine decree, because the matter had been foreordained and decreed.

But when one person wrongs another, the wronged person may obtain just redress. If he pardons the offender, however, that is better for him, as Allah Most High says:

“And for wounds there is equal retribution. But whoever waives it as an act of charity, it will be an expiation for him.”

As for the “third category,” they are those who take no account of divine decree, either in misdeeds or in calamities caused by human actions. Rather, they attribute all of this to the person concerned. When they do wrong, they seek forgiveness, and this is good. But when a calamity befalls them through someone’s actions, they do not consider the divine decree by which it was ordained for them. Nor do they say of someone who has fallen short in fulfilling their rights, “Leave him alone. Had something been decreed, it would have happened.” Moreover, that calamity may have come about because of their own sins, yet they take no account of those sins. Allah Most High has said:

“When a calamity befell you, although you had inflicted twice as much, did you say, ‘How has this happened?’ Say, ‘It is from yourselves.’”

And Allah Most High has said:

“Whatever calamity befalls you is because of what your own hands have earned.”

And Allah Most High has said:

“But if evil befalls them because of what their own hands have sent ahead, then man is indeed ungrateful.”

Also relevant are His words, Most High:

“Wherever you may be, death will overtake you, even if you are in lofty towers. If good befalls them, they say, ‘This is from Allah’; but if evil befalls them, they say, ‘This is from you.’ Say, ‘All is from Allah.’ What is the matter with these people that they can hardly understand any words?”

“Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself.”

Many who affirm divine decree and many who deny it have disputed over this verse. The former say that all actions are from Allah, citing His words, Most High:

“Say, ‘All is from Allah.’”

The latter say that good is from Allah and evil is from yourself, citing His words:

“Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself.”

The former may answer them by citing a fabricated reading of “from yourself,” with an a-vowel, giving it an interrogative meaning. Some of them instead supply an implied interrogative, yielding the meaning: “Is it, then, from yourself?” Others posit an implicit “they say” in the passage beginning with His words, Most High, “Whatever befalls you.” Thus they say that the verse is to be understood as: “What is the matter with these people that they can hardly

understand any words?”—with “they say” supplied after it. They thereby distort both the wording and the meaning of the Quran, making what is Allah’s speech—His truthful speech—into the words of the hypocrites whose statements Allah condemned. They posit unexpressed words in the Quran for which there is no evidence; indeed, the context rules them out. Thus, both groups are ignorant of the meaning of the Quran and of the true implications of the position they defend.

As for the Quran, what is meant here by good and evil is blessings and calamities, not acts of obedience and disobedience. This is like His words, Most High:

“If good befalls you, it distresses them; but if evil befalls you, they rejoice in it. Yet if you are patient and mindful of Allah, their scheming will not harm you at all.”

And His words:

“If good befalls you, it distresses them; but if a calamity befalls you, they say, ‘We took our precautions beforehand,’ and turn away rejoicing. Say, ‘Nothing will ever befall us except what Allah has decreed for us. He is our Protector’”—to the end of the verse.

Another example is His saying, Most High:

“We tested them with good and bad things so that they might return.”

As He, Most High, also said:

“We test you with evil and good as a trial, and to Us you will be returned.”

That is, with blessings and calamities. This differs from His saying:

“Whoever comes with a good deed will have ten times its like, and whoever comes with an evil deed will be repaid only with its like.”

In this and similar passages, what is meant is obedience and disobedience. In each passage, there is something that clarifies the intended meaning of the expression. Thus, praise be to Allah Most High, there is no obscurity in the mighty Quran; rather, it is clear.

This is because, when He says “whatever befalls you,” “whatever touches you,” or similar expressions, it refers to something done to you by someone other than yourself. As He said:

“Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself.”

And as He, Most High, said:

“If good befalls you, it distresses them.”

And He, Most High, said:

“But if evil befalls them because of what their own hands have sent ahead.”

And when He says, “Whoever comes with a good deed,” the deed is something that person has done, since he is the one who brings it. This therefore concerns what the servant does, not what is done to him.

The context of the verse makes this clear, for He mentions this while urging jihad and condemning those who stay behind. He, Most High, says:

“O you who believe, take your precautions, then advance in groups or advance all together. Among you is one who will surely hang back. If a calamity befalls you, he says, ‘Allah has blessed me, for I was not there with them.’ But if a bounty from Allah comes to you, he will surely say—as though there had never been any affection between you and him—‘If only I had been with them, I would have achieved a great triumph.’”

Thus He, glorified be He, commands jihad, condemns those who discourage others from it, and mentions how the believers sometimes suffer calamity in it and sometimes receive Allah’s bounty. A calamity befell them on the day of Uhud, concerning which He said:

“When a calamity befell you, although you had inflicted twice as much, did you say, ‘How did this happen?’ Say, ‘It is from your own selves.’”

On the day of Badr, they received Allah’s bounty through His granting them victory and support, as He, Most High, said:

“Allah certainly granted you victory at Badr when you were weak.”

Then He, glorified be He, said:

“Let those who trade the life of this world for the Hereafter fight in Allah’s cause. Whoever fights in Allah’s cause, whether he is killed or victorious, We will grant him a great reward. And why should you not fight in Allah’s cause and for the oppressed among men, women and children?”

—up to His words:

“Wherever you may be, death will overtake you, even if you are in lofty, fortified towers. If good befalls them, they say, ‘This is from Allah’; but if evil befalls them, they say, ‘This is from you.’”

These are the words of the disbelievers and hypocrites. When victory or other blessings come to them, they say, “This is from Allah.” But when humiliation, fear or other calamities befall them, they say:

“This is from Muhammad, because of the religion he has brought.” For the disbelievers attribute the calamities that befall them to the actions of the believers.

He mentions something similar in the account of Moses and Pharaoh. He, Most High, says:

“We afflicted Pharaoh’s people with years of drought and shortages of crops, so that they might take heed. When good came to them, they said, ‘This is our due.’ But when misfortune befell them, they regarded Moses and those with him as an evil omen. Surely their fate is with Allah.”

Similarly, He, Most High, says in Surah Yā Sīn:

“They said, ‘Our Lord knows that we have indeed been sent to you, and our duty is only to convey the message clearly.’ They said, ‘We regard you as an evil omen. If you do not desist, we will surely stone you, and you will suffer a painful punishment at our hands.’”

Thus Allah, Most High, tells us that the disbelievers regarded the believers as an evil omen: whenever affliction befell them, they blamed the believers for it, while whatever good came to them they regarded as theirs from Allah, Mighty and Majestic. He, Most High, therefore said:

“What is the matter with these people that they can hardly understand what they are told?”

Allah, Most High, has sent down the finest discourse. Had they understood the Quran, they would have known that Allah commanded them to do what is right and forbade them to do what is wrong: He commanded good and forbade evil. Nothing in the message with which Allah sent His messengers is therefore a cause of evil. Rather, evil results from people’s sins. He, Most High, said:

“Whatever good befalls you is from Allah.”

That is, whatever victory, provision or well-being comes to you is from Allah, as a blessing He has bestowed upon you. Even if it comes through your righteous deeds, He is the One who guided you, helped you, eased your way to ease, bestowed faith upon you, made it pleasing to your heart, and made disbelief, wickedness and disobedience hateful to you.

At the end of the authentic hadith narrated by Abū Dharr from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who relates it from his Lord, Blessed and Most High, He says: “O My servants, these are but your deeds, which I record for you

then recompense you for them in full. Whoever finds good should praise Allah, and whoever finds otherwise should blame no one but himself.”

Another authentic hadith states:

“The best supplication for forgiveness is for a servant to say: ‘O Allah, You are my Lord; none has the right to be worshipped but You. You created me, and I am Your servant. I hold to Your covenant and promise as best I can. I seek refuge in You from the evil of what I have done. I acknowledge Your blessings upon me, and I confess my sin. So forgive me, for none forgives sins but You.’ Whoever says this in the morning with firm conviction and dies that day will enter Paradise. Whoever says it in the evening with firm conviction and dies that night will enter Paradise.”

Then He, Most High, says:

“Whatever evil befalls you”—such as humiliation, fear and defeat, as befell them on the day of Uhud—“is from yourself.”

That is, it is because of your sins and transgressions, even though it was written and decreed for you. For no one may invoke divine decree as an argument against either Allah or His creation. If anyone were permitted to invoke divine decree to excuse the evil he commits, no wrongdoer would be punished, no polytheist would be fought, no prescribed punishment would be carried out, and no one would refrain from wronging anyone else. The corruption this would cause in religious and worldly affairs is self-evident to sound reason, which accords with what the Messenger brought.

Divine decree must therefore be believed in, not invoked as an excuse. Whoever does not believe in divine decree resembles the Magians; whoever invokes it as an excuse resembles the polytheists. Whoever acknowledges both Allah’s command and His decree, yet impugns His justice and wisdom, resembles Iblīs. For Allah relates that he challenged His wisdom and opposed Him with his own opinion and desire, saying:

“Because You have led me astray, I will surely make evil alluring to them on earth and mislead them all.”

Yet this debate between Iblīs and the angels, which al-Shahrastānī mentions at the beginning of his work on religious doctrines and transmits from some of the People of the Book, has no reliable chain of transmission. Even if we found it in the books of the People of the Book, that alone would not justify accepting it as true. For it is reliably reported in the authentic collection that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When the People of the Book tell you something, neither affirm nor deny it, for they may tell you something true and you reject it, or tell you something false and you accept it.”

It appears—and Allah knows best—that this debate was fabricated by some who deny divine decree, whether from the People of the Book or from the Muslims. Al-Shahrastānī transmitted it from works on religious doctrines. Writers on religious doctrines draw many of their accounts from Muʿtazilite books, just as al-Ashʿarī and others drew the accounts they presented in their works on religious doctrines from Muʿtazilite books. For the Muʿtazilah were among the earliest and most prolific groups to write on this subject. Hence these doctrines are found transmitted in their wording.

They thus fabricated this debate, putting its words into the mouth of Iblīs, just as we have seen many of them compose a book or a poem in the voice of a Jew or someone else. Their purpose is to refute those who affirm divine decree. They say that Allah’s case against His creation can only be established by denying divine decree. Likewise, among the accusations they fabricated to disparage Ibn Kullāb was that he was a Christian, because he affirmed the divine attributes; in their view, whoever affirms the attributes resembles the Christians. Such stories are accepted by some who profess adherence to the Sunnah but do not know their true nature.

It is also evidence against those who deny divine decree, for He, glory be to Him, states that good comes from Allah and that evil comes from the servant himself. The Qadariyyah agree that the servant brings his disobedience into being just as he brings his obedience into being. In their view, Allah brings neither into being; rather, He commands obedience and forbids disobedience.

According to them, Allah has bestowed no religious blessing upon His believing servants without bestowing its like upon the disbelievers. Thus, in their view, ʿAlī ibn Abī Tālib, may Allah be pleased with him, and Abū Lahab received equal religious blessings from Allah: the Messenger was sent to each, each was given the ability to act, and any impediment had been removed for each. Yet the former came to faith by himself, without Allah singling him out for a blessing through which he believed, while the latter disbelieved by himself, without Allah favoring that believer over him or granting the believer a special blessing on account of which he believed.

In their view, Allah made faith as beloved to disbelievers such as Abū Lahab and his like as He did to believers such as ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, and his like. He adorned it in the hearts of both groups and equally made disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience hateful to both. Yet the believers hated what Allah had made hateful to them without receiving any blessing peculiar to them, while the disbelievers did not hate what Allah had made hateful to them.

Anyone who imagines that they hold, or reports them as holding, that obedience comes from Allah while disobedience comes from the servant is ignorant of their doctrine. None of the scholars of the Qadariyyah has said this, nor could he do so, for their fundamental position is that the servant’s performance of obedience is like his performance of disobedience: he performs both through a capacity he possesses, without Allah singling him out by creating in him a will or placing in him a power specific to either one. Thus, if they invoke this verse as evidence for their doctrine, they would be ignorant of their own doctrine, and the verse would be evidence against them

not in their favor; for Allah Most High says:

“Say, ‘All is from Allah.’”

Yet according to them, neither good deeds nor evil deeds come from Allah; rather, both come from the servant. His words, Most High,

“Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself,”

contradict their position, since they hold that good deeds and evil deeds come from the servant, not from Allah, glory be to Him.

Likewise, anyone who affirms divine decree but seeks to establish it by citing His words, Most High, “Say, ‘All is from Allah,’” is mistaken. Allah stated this verse to refute those who say that good comes from Allah and evil comes from the servant. Yet no group has said that good deeds come from Allah while evil deeds come from the servant.

Furthermore, although those who affirm divine decree say that Allah created the servant’s act itself, and that it is His creation and something He has brought about, they do not deny that it is the servant who moves and acts, that these acts take place in him and originate from him, even though Allah created them.

Moreover, His subsequent words,

“Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself,”

cannot be interpreted as referring to obedience and disobedience. Those who affirm divine decree do not say that Allah creates one but not the other. Rather, they say that Allah creates all acts and everything that occurs.

It should also be understood that the position of the early generations of the Muslim community—while they affirm that Allah is the Creator of all things

and their Lord and Sovereign; that whatever He wills happens and whatever He does not will does not happen; that He has power over all things; that it is He who created the servant anxious—fretful when evil touches him and withholding when good comes to him—and other such truths—is that the servant truly acts and possesses will and power. Allah Most High says:

“For whoever among you wills to take a straight path.”
“But you do not will unless Allah, Lord of the worlds, wills.”

And He Most High says:

“Indeed, this is a reminder, so whoever wills may take a path to his Lord.”
“But you do not will unless Allah wills.”

And He Most High says:

“No! Indeed, it is a reminder.”
“So whoever wills may heed it.”
“But they will not heed it unless Allah wills. He is worthy of being feared, and He is the One who grants forgiveness.”

Those who have delved into divine decree have fallen into confusion over this point. The Muʿtazilah and others like them who deny divine decree said: “Disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience are evil acts. Muslims unanimously agree that Allah is exalted above doing evil, so these cannot be His acts.”

Those inclined toward the doctrine of compulsion replied: “Rather, they are His acts, not the servants’ acts; they are instead acquisitions on the servant’s part.”

They said that the servant’s power has no effect on bringing about the act within its scope, nor on any of its attributes. Rather, Allah has established the customary pattern of creating that act concurrently with the servant’s power. Thus, the act is a creation on Allah’s part, through His originating it and bringing it into being, and an acquisition on the servant’s part, because it occurs concurrently with his power. They also said that the servant neither originates his acts nor brings them into existence. Yet despite this, they may say: “We do not uphold absolute compulsion. Rather, we affirm that the servant possesses a created power. An absolute proponent of compulsion is someone who affirms no power for the servant.”

Furthermore, if influence is explained as mere concurrence, it makes no difference whether the distinguishing factor is within the locus or outside it.

They said:

“This parallels what you and all others who affirm the divine attributes have said: it is firmly rooted in human nature that whoever has knowledge subsisting in him is knowledgeable; whoever has power subsisting in him is capable; whoever has motion subsisting in him is moving; whoever has speech subsisting in him is speaking; and whoever has will subsisting in him is willing. You have also said that if speech were created, it would be the speech of the locus in which He created it, just as with the other attributes. This consistent principle concerning those in whom attributes subsist has its counterpart in those who perform actions.”

They also said:

“The Quran abounds in passages attributing these actions to the servants, such as His words, Exalted is He:

‘As a reward for what they used to do,’

and His words:

‘Do whatever you will,’

and His words:

‘And say, “Work, for Allah will see your deeds,”’

and His words:

‘Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds,’

and other such passages.”

They also said:

“Revelation and reason agree that the servant is praised or blamed for his own action, which counts as a good or evil deed on his part. If it were nothing but someone else’s action, that other would be the one praised or blamed for it.”

This is not the place for a full discussion of this question. We shall, however, draw attention to some useful points concerning this difficult issue. Thus we say:

translated_text:
The statement, “This person did this and did that,” is ambiguous, for “act” sometimes means the action itself and sometimes what the verbal noun denotes. Thus one says, “I did this; I do it; a doing,” and “I performed this work; I perform it; a working.” When “work” means the action itself, which is what the verbal noun denotes—as with a person’s prayer, fasting, and the like—the work here is the very thing done: the verbal noun and the act denote the same thing. But when what is intended is the result of one’s work—as with weaving cloth, building a house, and the like—the work here differs from the thing produced. Allah, Exalted is He, says:

“They made for him whatever he wished: sanctuaries, statues, basins as large as reservoirs, and firmly set cauldrons.”

He thus describes these manufactured objects as things made by the jinn. The same applies to His words, Exalted is He:

“Allah created you and what you make.”

According to the more correct of the two interpretations, mā means “that which,” referring to the idols they carve. As Allah, Exalted is He, says:

“Do you worship what you carve, when Allah created you and what you make?”

That is, Allah created you and created the idols you carve. The hadith narrated by Hudhayfah from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is another example:

“Allah is the Creator of every craftsman and his handiwork.”

Nevertheless, the verse may be cited as evidence that Allah created the servants’ actions through another line of reasoning. One may say: If He is the Creator of the carved objects they make, He must also be the Creator of the configuration they produce in them. These objects become idols only through that configuration; without it, they would not be things made by them. If He is the Creator of that configuration, then He is the Creator of their actions.

The point is that the terms “act,” “work,” and “making” have various senses. Like “building,” “sewing,” and “carpentry,” they can denote either the action expressed by the verbal noun or the thing produced. Likewise, the terms “recitation,” “reading,” “speech,” and “utterance” can denote the very referent of

translated_text:
the verbal noun or the actual utterance and speech produced by that action. Thus, “recitation” and “reading” may refer to the Quran itself that is read and recited, just as they may refer to the action denoted by the verbal noun.

The point here is that when someone says, “These actions are Allah’s act,” or “They are the servant’s act,” if he means that they are Allah’s act in the sense denoted by the verbal noun, this is false by the consensus of the Muslims and according to clear reason. But if someone says that they are Allah’s act, meaning that they are produced and created by Allah, like all other created things, this is true.

Some who hold this view say that Allah has no act subsisting in Him. They therefore make no distinction between His act and what He produces, or between His act of creation and what He creates. The majority, however, who distinguish between these things, say: These actions are created and produced by Allah; they are not His act itself. As for the servant, they are his act, subsisting in him. They are also something he produces, if “act” is used to mean the thing produced.

Thus, when someone who does not distinguish, with respect to the Lord, Exalted is He, between the act and the thing produced says that these actions are Allah’s act, the expression “Allah’s act” has no two distinct meanings for him. Consequently, they cannot be the servant’s act, still less something produced by him. Some of these people say that they are an act of both the Lord and the servant, thereby affirming one effect produced by two agents.

Most of the Muʿtazilah agree with these people that the act of the Lord, Exalted is He, can mean only what He produces, although they distinguish, in the servant’s case, between the act and the thing produced. For this reason, the dispute became intense

translated_text:
and the issue became obscure to both groups, leaving them bewildered.

Those, however, who hold that the Lord’s creation of His creatures is not identical with the creatures themselves maintain that the servants’ acts are created like all other created things and are produced by the Lord like everything else He produces. They do not say that these acts are the Lord’s own act and act of creation; rather, they say that they are the servant’s own acts. On this understanding, the difficulty disappears. For lying, wrongdoing, and other such evils characterize the one whose acts they are—as when the servant performs them and they subsist in him. They do not characterize the One who created them, when He has made them attributes of another. Likewise, glorified is He, He is not characterized by the tastes, colors, smells, shapes, dimensions, movements, and other things He creates in others. When He creates a person’s color, He Himself does not take on that color. When He creates a foul smell, a bitter taste, an ugly form, or anything else that is loathsome, blameworthy, and repugnant, He is not characterized by these ugly, blameworthy, and loathsome created things, nor by evil acts. The evil of these acts means that they harm their doer, give cause for his blame and punishment, and bring him pain and torment. This affects the doer in whom they subsist, not the Creator who created them as the acts of another.

Furthermore, the majority, who affirm that He has wisdom in creating whatever is repugnant, harmful, and hurtful in the world, say that He has great wisdom in creating these evil acts that harm their doers, just as He has great wisdom in creating illnesses and sorrows.

As for those who say that His acts are not explained by underlying reasons, neither of these is so explained on their view.

This is clarified by the fact that when Allah Most High creates blindness, illness, hunger, thirst, pain, weariness, and the like in a person, it is the servant who is ill, hungry, thirsty, and in pain. The harm, suffering, and unpleasantness inherent in these created things affect him; none of this affects Allah Most High. Likewise, the lying, wrongdoing, unbelief, and similar things He creates in him are harmful, repugnant, and hurtful. This is what it means to call them evil and reprehensible: they distress and harm the person who commits them. They may also distress and harm others, just as his illness, foul smell, and the like may distress and harm others.

This is further clarified by the fact that the Qadariyyah concede that Allah may create unbelief and wickedness in the servant as recompense, as in His words, Most High:

“We turn their hearts and eyes away, just as they did not believe in it the first time.”

And His words:

“In their hearts is a disease, so Allah has increased their disease.”

And His words:

“When they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate.”

Now, it is well known that these created things are acts performed and acquired by the servant, for which he is recompensed and deserves blame and punishment, while they are created by Allah Most High. Thus, according to those who affirm divine decree, what He creates of the servants’ deeds in the first instance is, in this respect, no different from what He creates as recompense, even though the two differ in another respect. The Qadariyyah cannot distinguish between them on the grounds that one, but not the other, is Allah’s act, and that one, but not the other, is the servant’s act. Rather, they say that creation as recompense is fitting for Allah Most High because it is recompense for the servant, whereas initial creation is not fitting for Him because it is an initial action toward the servant

Sound reason plainly establishes that when Allah Most High creates an attribute in a subject, it is an attribute of that subject. Thus, when He creates motion in a subject, that subject is what moves by it. When He creates a colour or an odour in a body, that body is what bears the colour or odour. When He creates knowledge, power, or life in a subject, that subject is what knows, possesses power, or lives. Likewise, when He creates will, love, or hatred in a subject, that subject is what wills, loves, or hates. When He creates an act for a servant, the servant is the one who performs it. Thus, if He creates lying, wrongdoing, or disbelief for him, the servant is the liar, wrongdoer, or disbeliever. If He creates prayer, fasting, or pilgrimage for him, the servant is the one who prays, fasts, or performs pilgrimage.

Allah Most High is not described by any of His created things; rather, His attributes subsist in His own Essence. This is consistent with the principles of the early generations and the majority of Muslims, both Ahl al-Sunnah and others. They maintain that Allah’s creation of the heavens and the earth is not the heavens and the earth themselves; rather, the act of creation is distinct from what is created. This is especially true of the position of the early generations, the leading scholars, and those of Ahl al-Sunnah who agreed with them in affirming Allah’s attributes and acts. For the Mu'tazilah and those Jahmiyyah and Qadariyyah who agreed with them challenged the consistency of this principle as upheld by those who did not maintain that the act of creation is distinct from what is created, such as al-Ash'arī and those who agreed with him.
