“If you say that when an attribute subsists in a subject, that subject alone is described by it—as you have stated regarding motion, knowledge, power, and all other accidents—then your principle is contradicted by justice, beneficence, and other acts of Allah Most High. For He is called just on account of justice He creates in another, and beneficent on account of beneficence He creates in another. Likewise, He may be called a speaker on account of speech He creates in another.”

The majority of Ahl al-Sunnah and others respond by consistently upholding this principle. They say that He is just only by virtue of the justice that subsists in His own Essence, and beneficent by virtue of the beneficence that subsists in His own Essence. As for the created benefit received by the servant, it is the effect of that beneficence. Likewise, He is the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy, by virtue of the mercy that is His attribute; whatever mercy He creates is an effect of that mercy.

A term denoting an attribute sometimes refers to the attribute itself, as denoted by the verbal noun, and sometimes to its object, as denoted by the passive participle. Thus, “creation” sometimes refers to the act of creating and sometimes to what is created. “Mercy” likewise refers to either. Similarly, “command” may refer to His commanding—the verbal noun in the sequence “he commanded, he commands, commanding”—and sometimes to what is brought about by it, as in His saying, Most High:

“Allah’s command is a decree determined.”

Likewise, the word “knowledge” may refer to what is known, and “power” to the object of power. There are numerous similar examples.

Among the proofs Imām Ahmad and other leading scholars of the Sunnah cited to establish that Allah’s speech is uncreated was the Prophet’s saying, peace be upon him:

“I seek refuge in the perfect words of Allah,”

and similar expressions. They said that refuge is not attained through anything created. Comparable to this is the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

translated_text:
Whoever reflects on this subject and others like it will find that the people of innovation and misguidance gain the upper hand over a group professing adherence to the Sunnah and guidance only because that group has itself adopted some other innovation or error—especially when it has agreed with its opponents on that point. They then argue against it on the basis of those concessions and press their implications until, if they can, they draw its members out of the religion as easily as a hair is drawn from dough. This is what the esoteric Qarmatians, the philosophers, and others like them have done to certain groups of Muslims.

The “Muʿtazilah” gained the upper hand over the “Ashʿarīs” and others who affirm the divine attributes and decree through their agreement with them in denying acts subsisting in Allah Most High. They thereby undermined the very principle their opponents had used against them to establish that Allah’s speech is uncreated: namely, that when speech or anything similar is created in a subject, the corresponding description applies to that subject.

They also gained the upper hand over them through this concession on the “question of divine decree,” forcing them into holding that the very evil deeds committed by the servant are acts of Allah, the Lord of the worlds, rather than of the servant. They then affirmed an acquisition that has no reality, for no intelligible distinction exists between acquisition and action in terms of the relation of power to its object. Hence people began to ridicule those who held this view, saying:

“Three things have no reality: al-Nazzām’s leap, Abū Hāshim’s states, and al-Ashʿarī’s acquisition.”

They also forced them to explain the efficacy of power upon its object as mere customary conjunction. Yet customary conjunction occurs between anything and its necessary concomitant, and between the object of power and power itself. There is therefore no more reason to regard one as exerting an effect upon the other than the reverse. It also occurs between an effect and its cause

Thus, when they saw the contradictions inherent in this position, Qādī Abū Bakr resorted to one view, Abū Ishāq al-Isfarāyīnī to another, and Abū al-Maʿālī al-Juwaynī to yet another. This is discussed at length in its proper place; the purpose here is merely to draw attention to it.

Among the subtle points in this discussion is that expressions such as “causal efficacy,” “compulsion,” and “provision” are general terms. If someone asks, “Does the servant’s power have an effect upon its object or not?” he should first be told that the term “power” encompasses two kinds:

The first is the capacity recognized by the Law, which enables action and forms the basis for commands and prohibitions. (The second is the capacity determined by the divine decree, which necessarily brings about the act and is simultaneous with it: the act does not lag behind this capacity.

The first is what is mentioned in the words of Allah Most High:

“Pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to Allah by those who are able to make their way to it.”

If this ability were the capacity simultaneous with the act, pilgrimage to the House would be obligatory only upon those who actually performed it. Someone who did not perform pilgrimage would therefore not be disobedient for abandoning it, whether he had provisions and a mount and was capable of performing pilgrimage or not.

The same applies to the Prophet’s words—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—to ʿImrān ibn Husayn:

“Pray standing; if you cannot, then sitting; and if you cannot, then on your side.”

Likewise, Allah Most High says:

“So fear Allah as much as you are able.”

And the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“When I command you to do something, do as much of it as you are able.”

Had he meant an ability that exists only alongside the act, he would effectively have said, “Do as much of it as you actually do.” Thus, someone who did nothing would not be disobedient

translated_text:
to him. This is the ability referred to in works of jurisprudence and in common usage.

People disagree over what the terms “ability” and “power” denote. Some recognize only this ability and maintain that ability must precede the act. Others recognize only an ability that accompanies the act. You will find many jurists contradicting themselves: when discussing the matter with speculative theologians who affirm divine decree and maintain that ability exists only alongside the act, they agree with them. Yet when discussing jurisprudence, they affirm the prior ability that forms the basis for commands and prohibitions.

From this distinction arises “the question of imposing duties beyond one’s capacity.” Capacity means ability, and the term admits of more than one meaning. Allah has never imposed any duty upon anyone without the ability recognized by the Law, which forms the basis for commands and prohibitions. Thus, according to this interpretation, He does not impose duties beyond one’s capacity. As for the capacity that exists only alongside the act, all commands and prohibitions impose duties beyond one’s capacity in this sense, for Muslims agree that this capacity is not a prerequisite for any command or prohibition.

The same applies to their disagreement over whether the servant has the power to act contrary to what Allah knows will occur. If “power” means the power recognized by the Law, which forms the basis for commands and prohibitions—like the ability mentioned in the words of Allah Most High:

“So fear Allah as much as you are able”—

then everyone whom Allah commands and forbids possesses ability in this sense, even if Allah knows that he will not obey Him. If, however, power is understood as “determined by the divine decree,” existing only alongside the act, then anyone whom Allah knows will not perform the act does not possess this power.

Another example is people’s disagreement over “command and will”: does Allah command what He does not will, or does He command only what He wills? The term “will” admits of more than one meaning. It may refer to His universal will, which encompasses all events, as in the Muslims’ saying, “Whatever Allah wills happens, and whatever He does not will does not happen.” Likewise, Allah Most High says:

“Whoever Allah wills to guide, He opens his breast to Islam; and whoever He wills to lead astray, He makes his breast tight and constricted, as though he were ascending into the sky.”

And Noah, peace be upon him, said:

“My advice will not benefit you, even if I wish to advise you, if Allah wills to lead you astray.”

There is no doubt that Allah commands His servants to do things He does not will in this sense. As Allah Most High says:

“Had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance.”

This indicates that He has not given every soul its guidance, although He has commanded every soul to follow its guidance. Similarly, the scholars agree that if someone swears by Allah that he will repay his creditor tomorrow, if Allah wills; or return property entrusted to him or property he has wrongfully seized; or perform the noon or afternoon prayer, if Allah wills; or fast Ramadan, if Allah wills—or do some other thing Allah has commanded—then he does not break his oath if he fails to do what he swore to do, even though Allah commanded him to do it. This is because he said, “If Allah wills.” Thus, it is known that Allah did not will it, although He commanded it.

As for His legislative will, it means love and approval and is inseparable from His command. As Allah Most High says:

“Allah wills to make things clear to you, guide you to the ways of those before you, and turn to you in forgiveness.”

This is also the meaning intended when Muslims say of someone committing an indecency, “This person is doing something Allah does not will.” That is, He neither loves nor approves of it; rather, He forbids and dislikes it.

Likewise, the term “compulsion” admits of more than one meaning. It may mean forcing someone to act without

their consent, as when it is said that a father compels a woman to marry. Allah Most High is far too exalted and great to compel in this sense, for He creates in the servant willingness and choice concerning what he does. In this respect, that is not compulsion.

“Compulsion” may also mean creating the beliefs and intentions within souls, as in the statement of Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazī: “Al-Jabbār (the Compeller) is He who compels His servants to what He wills.” Likewise, in the supplication transmitted from ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him:

“Compeller of hearts according to their innate dispositions, whether wretched or blessed.”

Compulsion in this sense is affirmed. Since the term “compulsion” admits of more than one meaning, the eminent imams prohibited affirming or denying it without qualification.

Likewise, the term “provision” admits of more than one meaning. It may refer to what Allah has made lawful or granted someone ownership of. Unlawful things are therefore not included in provision in this sense, as in His words, Most High:

“And they spend out of what We have provided for them.”

And His words, Most High:

“And spend out of what We have provided for you before death comes to one of you.”

And His words:

“And one whom We have provided with good provision from Us, from which he spends secretly and openly.”

There are other similar passages. “Provision” may also refer to whatever a living creature benefits from, even where neither lawful permission nor ownership has been granted. In this sense, it includes unlawful things, as in His words, Most High:

“There is no creature on earth whose provision is not upon Allah.”

And in his words, peace be upon him, in an authentic hadith:

“Then his provision, deeds and lifespan are recorded, and whether he will be wretched or blessed.”

Since the terms “compulsion,” “provision” and others like them admit of more than one meaning, the imams prohibited affirming or denying them without qualification, as previously reported from al-Awzāʿī, Abū Ishāq al-Fazārī and other imams.

Likewise, the term “causal efficacy” admits of more than one meaning. Capacity stands in relation to what it enables as a causal means does to its effect, a cause to what it causes, and a condition to what is conditional upon it. If “capacity” means the capacity recognized by the revealed law, which makes the act possible and precedes it, then it is a condition for the act, one of its causal means, and an incomplete cause of it. If, however, “capacity” means the capacity that accompanies the act and necessarily entails it, then it is a cause of the act and a sufficient causal means.

It is well known that nothing among created things is, by itself, a complete cause and sufficient causal means for events, in the sense that its existence necessarily entails their occurrence. This belongs exclusively to the will of Allah Most High: whatever Allah wills occurs, and whatever He does not will does not occur. As for created causal means—such as fire in burning, the sun in illumination, and food and drink in satisfying hunger and quenching thirst—none of these produces the event by itself. Rather, another causal means must join it. Even then, there are impediments that prevent the two from producing their effect. Thus, every causal means depends upon the presence of the requisite conditions and the absence of impediments. Nothing among created things produces anything entirely by itself.

This makes clear to you the error of the philosophizers who said:

“From one, only one proceeds.”

They drew an analogy with natural effects, such as things that are heated or cooled, and the like. This is mistaken, for heating requires two things: first, an agent, such as fire; and second, a recipient, such as a body capable of receiving heat and being burned. Otherwise, when fire comes into contact with a salamander or a ruby, it does not burn it. Likewise, the sun’s rays depend upon a body facing the sun, onto which the rays are reflected; and they are obstructed by clouds, roofs, and other

such things. Thus, this “one” that they have conceived in their minds has no existence in external reality. This has been explained at length elsewhere. The conceptual “one” affirmed by the philosophers—such as existence stripped of attributes, immaterial intellects, the universals from which they claim species are composed, conceptual matter and form, and similar things—has no existence in external reality. Such things exist only in minds, not as concrete entities. They are even further removed from existence than the indivisible atom affirmed by some speculative theologians. This “one” has no reality outside the mind, and neither does that atom, as has been explained in its proper place.

The point here is that if “causal efficacy” means the presence of a condition for an event, or of a causal means whose production of the event depends upon another causal means and the absence of impediments—all of which Allah Most High creates—then this is true. In this sense, the servant’s capacity does indeed have causal efficacy in bringing about what it enables. But if “causal efficacy” means that the agent independently produces the effect, with neither a helper sharing in its production nor an obstacle preventing it, then nothing created has causal efficacy. Rather, Allah alone is the Creator of everything, without partner or equal. Whatever Allah wills occurs, and whatever He does not will does not occur.

Once the ambiguity and multiple meanings of “causal efficacy” are understood, the misconception is dispelled and the balanced position between the two groups becomes clear.

Whoever says that the believer and the unbeliever are equal in the causes conducive to faith that Allah has bestowed upon them; that Allah has not specially granted the believer any capacity or volition through which he came to believe; and that, when the servant acts, he gains no assistance from Allah or volition that he did not have before the act—his position is plainly false.

These people may be told: The servant’s action is itself one of the contingent things that come into being. Thus, every argument establishing that Allah Most High brought something else into being also establishes that Allah brought this action into being. If this contingent occurrence could arise without a necessarily existent originator to bring it into being and give precedence to its existence over its nonexistence, the same would be possible for other things, thereby invalidating the proof establishing the Creator’s existence.

 وَالْقَائِلِينَ بِقِدَمِ الْعَالَمِ قَالُوا:
 هَذَا الَّذِي قُلْتُمُوهُ مَعْلُومُ الْفَسَادِ بِالضَّرُورَةِ وَتَجْوِيزُ هَذَا يَقْتَضِي حُدُوثَ الْحَوَادِثِ بِلَا سَبَبٍ وَالتَّرْجِيحُ بِلَا مُرَجِّحٍ وَذَلِكَ يَسُدُّ بَابَ إثْبَاتِ الصَّانِعِ.
 ثُمَّ إنَّ هَؤُلَاءِ الْمُثْبِتِينَ لِلْقَدَرِ احْتَجُّوا بِهَذِهِ الْحُجَّةِ عَلَى نفاة الْقَدَرِ وَقَالُوا:
 حُدُوثُ فِعْلِ الْعَبْدِ بَعْدَ أَنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ لَا بُدَّ لَهُ مِنْ مُحْدِثٍ مُرَجِّحٍ تَامٍّ غَيْرِ الْعَبْدِ فَإِنَّ مَا كَانَ مِنْ الْعَبْدِ فَهُوَ مُحْدَثٌ أَيْضًا وَعِنْدَ وُجُودِ ذَلِكَ الْمُحْدَثِ الْمُرَجِّحِ التَّامِّ يَجِبُ وُجُودُ فِعْلِ الْعَبْدِ وَهَذَا الَّذِي قَالُوهُ حَقٌّ وَهُوَ حُجَّةٌ قَاطِعَةٌ عَلَى الْقَدَرِيَّةِ وَالْمُعْتَزِلَةِ؛ لَكِنَّهُمْ نَقَضُوهُ وَتَنَاقَضُوا فِيهِ فِي فِعْلِ الرَّبِّ تَبَارَكَ وَتَعَالَى وَادَّعَوْا هُنَاكَ أَنَّ الْبَدِيهَةَ فَرَّقَتْ بَيْنَ فِعْلِ الْقَادِرِ وَبَيْنَ الْمُوجِبِ بِالذَّاتِ فَإِنْ كَانَ هَذَا الْفَرْقُ صَحِيحًا بَطَلَتْ حُجَّتُهُمْ عَلَى الْمُعْتَزِلَةِ وَلَمْ يَبْطُلْ قَوْلُ الْقَدَرِيَّةِ وَإِنْ كَانَ بَاطِلًا بَطَلَ قَوْلُهُمْ فِي إحْدَاثِ اللَّهِ وَفِعْلِهِ لِلْعَالَمِ وَهَذَا هُوَ الْبَاطِلُ فِي نَفْسِ الْأَمْرِ فَإِنَّ الْقَوْلَ بِأَنَّ الْمُمْكِنَ لَا يَتَرَجَّحُ وُجُودُهُ عَلَى عَدَمِهِ إلَّا بِمُرَجِّحِ تَامٍّ أَمْرٌ مَعْلُومٌ بِالْفِطْرَةِ الضَّرُورِيَّةِ لَا يُمْكِنُ الْقَدْحُ فِيهِ وَهُوَ عَامٌّ لَا تَخْصِيصَ فِيهِ فَالْفَرْقُ الْمَذْكُورُ بَاطِلٌ وَذَلِكَ يُبْطِلُ قَوْلَهُمْ بِأَنَّ خَلْقَ الْعَالَمِ هُوَ الْعَالِمُ وَأَنَّهُ حَدَثَ بَعْدَ أَنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ بِغَيْرِ سَبَبٍ حَادِثٍ. وَمَنْ قَالَ إنَّ قُدْرَةَ الْعَبْدِ وَغَيْرَهَا مِنْ الْأَسْبَابِ الَّتِي خَلَقَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى بِهَا الْمَخْلُوقَاتِ لَيْسَتْ أَسْبَابًا أَوْ أَنَّ وُجُودَهَا كَعَدَمِهَا وَلَيْسَ هُنَاكَ إلَّا مُجَرَّدُ اقْتِرَانٍ

through acts subsisting in Himself and that Allah created the heavens and the earth and all that is between them in six days, as well as by those who maintain the eternity of the world. They said:

“What you have said is self-evidently false. To admit this possibility entails that events can arise without a cause and that one alternative can prevail without a determining factor. This closes the door to establishing the Creator’s existence.”

Then these affirmers of divine decree used this argument against those who deny divine decree, saying:

“For the servant’s action to come into being after not existing, there must be an originating and fully determining cause other than the servant, since whatever proceeds from the servant is itself also brought into being. When that originating and fully determining cause exists, the servant’s action must necessarily exist.”

What they have said is true and constitutes a decisive argument against the Qadariyyah and the Muʿtazilah. Yet they undermined it and contradicted themselves concerning the acts of the Lord, blessed and exalted is He. There they claimed that self-evident reason distinguishes between the action of an agent possessed of power and the operation of a cause that necessitates its effect by its very essence. If this distinction is valid, their argument against the Muʿtazilah fails, and the Qadariyyah’s position has not been refuted. If it is invalid, their account of Allah’s bringing the world into being and creating it is false. And this account is indeed false.

For the principle that the existence of a contingent thing cannot prevail over its nonexistence without a fully determining factor is known through the innate disposition as a self-evident necessity and cannot be challenged. It is universal, admitting no exceptions. The distinction mentioned is therefore invalid. This invalidates their claim that the creation of the world is the world itself, and that it came into being after not existing without any newly arising cause.

Whoever says that the servant’s power and the other causes through which Allah Most High has created things are not causes, or that their existence is no different from their nonexistence, and that there is nothing beyond a mere conjunction

based on habit, like the association of evidence with what it indicates, has denied the causes, wise purposes, and underlying reasons present in Allah’s creation and His revealed law. Such a person recognizes no power of sight in the eye distinguishing it from the cheek, no power of understanding in the heart distinguishing it from the leg, and no power of burning in fire distinguishing it from earth. These people deny the inherent natures and dispositions of physical bodies.

One learned man said:

“Some people argued against the existence of causes, powers, and inherent natures, making themselves a laughingstock among people of sound reason.”

Moreover, these people say that one should not say that one’s hunger was satisfied by bread or one’s thirst quenched by water. Rather, one should say, “My hunger was satisfied upon eating it, and my thirst was quenched upon drinking it.” For, according to them, Allah creates satiety, the quenching of thirst, and other such occurrences when the things habitually associated with them are present—not through those things.

This contradicts the Quran and the Sunnah, for Allah Most High says:

“It is He who sends the winds bearing glad tidings before His mercy, until, when they carry heavy clouds, We drive them to a lifeless land, then send down water thereby and bring forth thereby every kind of fruit”—to the end of the verse.

Allah Most High also says:

“And the water Allah sends down from the sky, thereby giving life to the earth after its death and spreading throughout it every kind of creature.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Fight them; Allah will punish them by your hands.”

He also says:

“Say, ‘Are you awaiting anything for us but one of the two best outcomes? We, however, await for you that Allah should afflict you with punishment from Himself or at our hands.’”

He also says:

“And We sent down blessed water from the sky, thereby causing gardens and grain for harvest to grow.”

Allah Most High also says:

“It is He who sends down water from the sky, and thereby We bring forth vegetation of every kind.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Do you not see that Allah sends down water from the sky, and thereby We bring forth fruits of varying colours?”

Allah Most High also says:

“It is He who sends down water from the sky; from it you drink, and from it grows vegetation among which

you pasture your livestock.”

“Through it He causes crops, olives, date palms, grapes, and every kind of fruit to grow for you.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to set forth a parable”—up to His words—“Through it He leads many astray and guides many.”

He also says:

“There has come to you from Allah a light and a clear Book.”

“Through it Allah guides those who seek His pleasure to the ways of peace.”

There are many such passages in the Quran. The same is true of the hadiths of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, such as his saying:

“Whenever any of you dies, be sure to inform me so that I may offer the funeral prayer for him, for through my prayer for him Allah will bring blessing and mercy.”

He also said, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“These graves are filled with darkness for their occupants, and through my prayer for them Allah will bring light.”

There are many such examples.

Comparable to those who deny the causes decreed in Allah’s creation are those who deny the means prescribed in His commands. Such are those who suppose that if the good things attained through supplication, righteous deeds, and other such means are decreed, they will occur without those means; and if they are not decreed, those means will not bring them about.

These people are like those who said to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, “Should we not then give up deeds and rely on what has been written?” He replied, “No. Act, for everyone will be enabled to do that for which he was created.”

It is also reported in the Sunan collections that he was asked, “O Messenger of Allah, what do you say about medicines we use to treat ourselves, healing recitations we ask others to recite over us, and precautions we take? Can they ward off anything of Allah’s decree?” He replied, “They are part of Allah’s decree.”

Hence some scholars have said: Reliance on causes compromises monotheism by associating partners with Allah

and denying the causal role of causes distorts reason; disregarding causes altogether undermines the revealed Law. Allah, glorified be He, created causes and their effects and made one thing a cause of another. If someone says, “If this is decreed, it will happen without the cause; otherwise, it will not happen,” the answer is that it is decreed to occur through the cause, not without it. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah created people for Paradise; He created them for it while they were still in their fathers’ loins. And He created people for the Fire; He created them for it while they were still in their fathers’ loins.”

He also said, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Act, for everyone will be enabled to do that for which he was created. Those destined for bliss will be enabled to do the deeds of those destined for bliss, while those destined for misery will be enabled to do the deeds of those destined for misery.”

In the two Sahīh collections, Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace—the truthful one whose truthfulness is confirmed—told us:

“The creation of each of you is brought together in his mother’s womb for forty days as a drop of fluid. Then he becomes a clot for a similar period, then a lump of flesh for a similar period. Then the angel is sent to him and commanded to record four things. He is told, ‘Write down his provision, his deeds, his lifespan, and whether he will be wretched or blessed.’ Then the soul is breathed into him.”

He said:

“By Him in whose hand is my soul, one of you may do the deeds of the people of Paradise until only a cubit stands between him and it; then the written decree overtakes him, and he does the deeds of the people of the Fire and enters it. And one of you may do the deeds of the people of the Fire until only a cubit stands between him and it; then the written decree overtakes him, and he does the deeds of the people of Paradise and enters it.”

Thus the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained that one person enters Paradise through the deeds he performs and with which his life ends, while another enters the Fire through the deeds he performs and with which his life ends. As he said, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Deeds are judged by their endings.”

This is because all good deeds are nullified by apostasy, and all sins are forgiven through repentance. Similarly, if someone fasts but breaks his fast before sunset, or prays but deliberately breaks his state of ritual purity before completing the prayer, his act of worship is invalidated.

In sum, the position of the early generations of this community and its leading scholars is what Allah sent His messengers with and revealed His Books to convey. They believe in Allah’s creation and His command, His decree and His revealed Law, His decrees governing creation and His religious rulings, and His universal and legislative will. As He said in the first verse:

“Whoever Allah wills to guide, He opens his heart to Islam; and whoever He wills to lead astray, He makes his heart tight and constricted, as though he were ascending into the sky.”

Noah, peace be upon him, said:

“My advice will not benefit you, even if I wish to advise you, if Allah wills to lead you astray.”

Concerning His legislative will, Allah Most High said:

“Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you.”

He also said:

“Allah wishes to make things clear to you, guide you to the ways of those before you, and accept your repentance. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.”

And He said:

“Allah does not intend to impose hardship upon you, but He intends to purify you and complete His favor upon you.”

While acknowledging that Allah is the Creator, Lord, and Sovereign of everything, and that He created all things through His power and will, they also acknowledge that there is no deity worthy of worship except Him and that none other deserves worship. They obey Him and His messengers, love Him, place their hope in Him, fear Him, rely upon Him, and turn to Him in repentance. They ally themselves with His allies and oppose His enemies. They acknowledge His love for what He has commanded and for His believing servants

and His pleasure in them, His hatred of what He has forbidden and of the disbelievers, and His wrath and loathing toward them. They also acknowledge what has been widely reported from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Allah rejoices more at the repentance of His repentant servant than a man who lost his mount, carrying his food and drink, in a desolate, deadly wilderness. He searched for it but could not find it, then took a midday nap beneath a tree. When he awoke, there was his mount with his food and drink upon it! Allah rejoices more at His servant’s repentance than this man rejoices at recovering his mount.”

He is their God whom they worship and their Lord whom they ask, as Allah Most High says:

“All praise is for Allah, Lord of all worlds,”

through to His words:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.”

Thus, He is the One worshipped and the One whose help is sought. Worship combines perfect love with perfect humility.

They love Him more deeply than any lover loves their beloved, as Allah Most High says:

“Yet among people are those who take others as equals to Allah, loving them as they should love Allah. But those who believe are stronger in their love for Allah.”

Whatever else they love, they love only for His sake. As reported in the two Sahīh collections, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever possesses three qualities will taste the sweetness of faith: that Allah and His Messenger are dearer to him than everything else; that he loves someone only for Allah’s sake; and that he hates returning to disbelief, after Allah has saved him from it, as much as he hates being thrown into the Fire.”

In al-Tirmidhī and elsewhere, it is reported:

“The firmest bonds of faith are love for Allah’s sake and hatred for Allah’s sake. Whoever loves for Allah’s sake, hates for Allah’s sake, gives for Allah’s sake, and withholds for Allah’s sake has perfected his faith.”

He, glorified be He, loves His believing servants. The perfection of love is intimate friendship, which Allah bestowed upon Abraham and Muhammad, may Allah bless them both and grant them peace. For Allah took Abraham as an intimate friend. And it has been widely reported

from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, through several authentic chains of transmission, that he said:

“Allah has taken me as an intimate friend, just as He took Abraham as an intimate friend.”

He also said:

“If I were to take an intimate friend from among the people of the earth, I would take Abū Bakr as an intimate friend. But your companion is Allah’s intimate friend.”

He meant himself. Thus, the early generations of this community, its leading scholars, and all the people of the Sunnah and those with knowledge of Allah agreed that Allah Himself is loved and loves. The Jahmiyyah and their followers denied this love.

The first to deny it was al-Ja'd ibn Dirham, the teacher of al-Jahm ibn Safwān. Khālid ibn ‘Abd Allāh al-Qasrī offered him as a sacrifice at Wāsit, saying:

“O people, offer your sacrifices! May Allah accept your sacrifices, for I am sacrificing al-Ja'd ibn Dirham. He claims that Allah did not take Abraham as an intimate friend and did not truly speak to Moses. Exalted is Allah, far above what al-Ja'd says!”

Then he descended and slaughtered him. This is the foundation of the faith of Abraham, whom Allah made a leader for mankind. Allah Most High says:

“And when Abraham was tested by his Lord with certain commands, which he fulfilled, He said, ‘I will make you a leader for the people.’”

He also says:

“Who is better in religion than one who submits himself to Allah, does good, and follows the faith of Abraham, devoted to Allah alone? And Allah took Abraham as an intimate friend.”

Whoever says that loving Allah means loving to draw near to Him contradicts himself, for loving to draw near to Him follows from loving Him. Whoever loves Allah Himself loves to draw near to Him, while someone who does not love Him Himself cannot love to draw near to Him. As for someone who obeys Him and complies with His command only for some other end, in reality he loves only the end for which he acts, and has

made obedience to Allah a means to that end. It is established in an authentic hadith that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, a caller will announce: ‘People of Paradise, Allah has a promise for you that He wishes to fulfil.’ They will ask: ‘What is it? Has He not brightened our faces, made our scales heavy, admitted us to Paradise, and saved us from the Fire?’ Then the veil will be lifted, and they will look upon Him. Nothing He has given them will be dearer to them than looking upon Him. This is the additional reward.”

He thus explained that looking upon Him is dearer to them than all the pleasures they enjoy. Their love of looking upon Him follows from their love for Him: they love to look upon Him only because they love Him. Every believer finds in his heart love for Allah, tranquillity in remembering Him, delight in knowing Him, and pleasure and joy in remembering Him and speaking intimately to Him. This grows stronger or weaker, increases or decreases, according to people’s faith. The more complete a person’s faith, the more complete his delight in these things.

For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in the hadith narrated by Ahmad and others:

“Of the things of your world, women and perfume have been made dear to me.” Then he said: “And my greatest delight has been placed in prayer.”

He would also say:

“Bring us comfort through prayer, Bilāl.”

This is discussed at length elsewhere. The point here is that His believing servants love Him, and He, glorified and exalted, loves them. Their love for Him is in proportion to their doing what He loves. Thus, in Sahīh al-Bukhārī, Abū Hurayrah narrates that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah Most High says: ‘Whoever shows enmity towards a close servant of Mine has openly challenged Me to war. Nothing by which My servant draws near to Me compares to fulfilling what I have made obligatory upon him. My servant continues to draw near to Me through voluntary acts of worship until I love him. When I love him, I am his hearing with which he hears, and his sight with which he sees

and his hand with which he grasps, and his foot with which he walks. Through Me he hears, through Me he sees, through Me he grasps, and through Me he walks. If he asks Me, I will surely give him, and if he seeks My protection, I will surely protect him. I have never hesitated over anything I am going to do as I hesitate over taking the soul of My believing servant: he dislikes death, and I dislike causing him distress, yet death is inevitable for him.’”

He has thus made clear that when a servant draws near to Allah through the voluntary acts He loves, after fulfilling the obligatory duties, Allah loves him. Allah’s love for His servant is therefore proportionate to the servant’s doing what Allah loves. His love for the worship and obedience offered to Him follows from His love for Himself. His love for that worship and obedience is the reason He loves His believing servants; thus, His love for the believers follows from His love for Himself.

Although the believers praise and extol their Lord, they cannot fully praise Him. Rather, He is as He has praised Himself. As related in an authentic hadith, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to say:

“O Allah, I seek refuge in Your pleasure from Your wrath, in Your pardon from Your punishment, and in You from You. I cannot praise You as You deserve; You are as You have praised Yourself.”

It is also authentically established that he said:

“No one loves praise more than Allah; for that reason, He has praised Himself.”

Al-Aswad ibn Sarīʿ said to him, “I have praised my Lord with words of praise.” He replied, “Your Lord loves praise.”

He loves His servants’ praise of Him, yet His praise of Himself is greater than their praise of Him. He loves their extolling Him, yet His extolling Himself is greater than their extolling Him. The same holds for His love for Himself and His exaltation of Himself. He, glorified be He, knows Himself better than anyone else does, and He possesses attributes of perfection beyond the grasp of created minds. Majesty is His lower garment, and grandeur is His cloak. It is also authentically reported from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace,

that he recited from the pulpit:

“They have not esteemed Allah as He deserves. On the Day of Resurrection, the whole earth will be in His grasp, and the heavens will be folded in His right hand. Glory be to Him!”

He said: “Allah grasps the earth and folds up the heavens in His right hand, then shakes them and says: ‘I am the King! I am the Most Holy! I am the Source of Peace! I am the Giver of Security! I am the Guardian! I am the One who originated the world when it was nothing! I am the One who will bring it back!’” Another narration states: “The Lord glorifies Himself—glorified be He.”

Thus He praises, extols, and glorifies Himself, glorified and exalted be He. He is self-sufficient, needing no one else; rather, everything besides Him is in need of Him:

“All who are in the heavens and the earth ask of Him; every day He is engaged in some affair.”

He is the One, the Eternal Refuge, who neither begets nor is born, and to whom none is equal.

When He rejoices at the repentance of one who repents, loves those who draw near to Him through voluntary acts of worship, is pleased with the earliest forerunners, and so forth, it is not permissible to say that He thereby needs another or is made perfect by anything besides Himself. For He is the One who created these people, guided them, and helped them until they did what He loves, is pleased with, and rejoices in. These things He loves came about only through His power, His will, and His creation. His is the sovereignty, with no partner; to Him belongs all praise in this world and the Hereafter; His is the judgment, and to Him you will be returned.

This and similar evidence is cited by the majority, who affirm that His actions have a wisdom relating to Himself, which He loves and is pleased with, and for the sake of which He acts.

قَالُوا:
 وَقَوْلُ الْقَائِلِ: إنَّ هَذَا يَقْتَضِي أَنَّهُ مُسْتَكْمَلٌ بِغَيْرِهِ فَيَكُونُ نَاقِصًا قَبْلَ ذَلِكَ عَنْهُ أَجْوِبَةٌ.
أَحَدُهَا:
 أَنَّ هَذَا مَنْقُوضٌ بِنَفْسِ مَا يَفْعَلُهُ مِنْ الْمَفْعُولَاتِ فَمَا كَانَ جَوَابًا فِي الْمَفْعُولَاتِ كَانَ جَوَابًا عَنْ هَذَا وَنَحْنُ لَا نَعْقِلُ فِي الشَّاهِدِ فَاعِلًا إلَّا مُسْتَكْمَلًا بِفِعْلِهِ.
 الثَّانِي أَنَّهُمْ قَالُوا:
 كَمَا لَهُ أَنْ يَكُونَ لَا يَزَالُ قَادِرًا عَلَى الْفِعْلِ بِحِكْمَةِ فَلَوْ قُدِّرَ كَوْنُهُ غَيْرَ قَادِرٍ عَلَى ذَلِكَ لَكَانَ نَاقِصًا.
 الثَّالِثُ قَوْلُ الْقَائِلِ:
 إنَّهُ مُسْتَكْمَلٌ بِغَيْرِهِ بَاطِلٌ؛ فَإِنَّ ذَلِكَ إنَّمَا حَصَلَ بِقُدْرَتِهِ وَمَشِيئَتِهِ لَا شَرِيكَ لَهُ فِي ذَلِكَ فَلَمْ يَكُنْ فِي ذَلِكَ مُحْتَاجًا إلَى غَيْرِهِ وَإِذَا قِيلَ كَمُلَ بِفِعْلِهِ الَّذِي لَا يُحْتَاجُ فِيهِ إلَى غَيْرِهِ كَانَ كَمَا لَوْ قِيلَ كَمُلَ بِصِفَاتِهِ أَوْ كَمُلَ بِذَاتِهِ.

translated_text:
They said:

There are several answers to the claim, “This entails that He is made perfect by something other than Himself, and thus was deficient beforehand.”

First: this objection is countered by the very effects He produces. Whatever answer is given concerning those effects also answers this objection. In the observable world, we know of no agent who is not perfected through his action.

Second: they said that His perfection consists in His always being able to act with wisdom. Were He supposed to be incapable of that, He would be deficient.

Third: the claim that He is made perfect by something other than Himself is false. For that comes about only through His power and will, with no partner sharing in it; thus, He has no need of another in this regard. To say that He is perfect by virtue of His action, in which He needs no other, is like saying that He is perfect by virtue of His attributes or His very essence.

Fourth: regarding the claim that He was deficient beforehand, if this means the absence of what has newly come about, we do not concede that its absence before the time at which wisdom required its existence constitutes a deficiency. If His being deficient is intended to mean something else, that is denied. Rather, the absence of something at a time when wisdom does not require its existence is an aspect of perfection, just as its existence at the time when wisdom requires it is perfection. Not everything’s absence, then, is a deficiency; rather, the absence of what ought to exist

is deficiency, just as the existence of what ought not to exist is deficiency. Thus, it is clear that the existence of these things when wisdom requires their absence is the deficiency—not their absence.

For this reason, the Lord, exalted is He, is described by affirmative attributes that embody His perfection, and by negative attributes that likewise necessarily imply His perfection. The absence of whatever is negated of Him is therefore an aspect of perfection, just as the presence of whatever is rightly affirmed of Him is an aspect of perfection. Once this is understood concerning attributes, the same applies to actions and the like. Not every addition the mind conceives is an aspect of perfection; rather, many additions detract from the perfection of that to which they are added, as can be understood in the case of many existing things. For a human being, the presence of certain things at one time may constitute a deficiency and a fault, while at another time it constitutes perfection and is praiseworthy, just as something may harm him at one time and benefit him at another.

(Fifth: If we suppose one who is able to bring about temporal events for a wise purpose and another who is unable to do so, it is self-evident to reason that the one who is able is more perfect. Yet temporal events can exist only as things that come into being; they cannot be beginningless. If the ability to bring this about is more perfect, and what this ability produces can only be something that comes into being, then its existence is perfection, while its absence beforehand contributes to complete perfection. For the absence of what is impossible, which is a prerequisite for the existence of perfection, is itself an aspect of perfection.

as disbelievers, as is held by some among the Kullābiyyah, the scholars of hadith, the jurists, and the Sufis. Their position therefore does not entail an infinite regress on account of temporal events inhering in Him. However, the majority oppose them concerning the wise purpose He loves, just as they oppose them concerning His will.

They say to them: “If His will is beginningless and has always existed, and its relation to all times and temporal events is the same, then singling out one time rather than another for something to come into being, and one effect rather than another, is a selection without a determining factor.”

The former reply: “It is the nature of will to select.”

Their opponents say to them: “Selection in general belongs to its nature. But selecting this particular thing over that particular thing is not something necessarily entailed by will. Rather, there must be a cause that necessitates one of the two being willed rather than the other. A person finds within himself that he selects through his will, but he knows that he wills this rather than that only because of a reason that calls for this selection. Otherwise, if all the possible objects of will were equal in every respect, it would be impossible for the will to single out one rather than its counterparts, for that would be preference without a deciding factor. Once this is admitted as possible, the way to establishing the existence of the Maker is closed.”

They say: “Anyone who reflects on this and examines it thoroughly will recognize its truth. Only someone who blindly follows another’s statement without considering its reality disputes it.”

Likewise, the majority say to them: “If Allah Most High, in His beginningless eternity, is pleased with, loves, and rejoices in what He brings into being, even before He brings it into being, then, when He does bring it into being, does doing so realize a wise purpose that He loves, is pleased with, and rejoices in? (The second group say: “The wise purpose relating to Him is realized through His will and power, just as the act occurs through His will and power.” They say: “Even if this inheres in His Essence, it is like all the other attributes and acts of which He has informed us inhering in His Essence.”

The Muʿtazilah deny that attributes and acts inhere in Him. They call attributes “accidents” and acts “temporal events,” and say: “Neither accidents nor temporal events inhere in Him.” Those who do not understand the true nature of their position therefore imagine that they are declaring Allah Most High free of imperfections, defects, and deficiencies.

There is no doubt that Allah must be declared free of every defect, imperfection, and deficiency. For He is the Most Holy, the Flawless, the Self-Sufficient, the Master who is perfect in every attribute of perfection, with a perfection whose reality creation can comprehend. He is free of every imperfection, and creation cannot comprehend the fullness of this transcendence. Every perfection established for an existent being that entails no imperfection belongs more rightfully to the Creator Most High, who possesses it more perfectly. Every imperfection from which a created being is declared free is something from which the Creator has a greater right to be declared free, and from which He is more fittingly held to be exempt.

Yet when the Muʿtazilah said that He is free of accidents and temporal events, their sole intention was to deny His attributes and acts. The vast majority of Muslims disagree with them on this. Some groups dispute their position regarding the attributes but not the acts; others dispute it regarding some attributes but not others. Some dispute their position regarding the beginningless act, saying that His act is beginningless even though what it produces comes into existence, analogous to the position held by some concerning the will. These positions, their proponents, and their arguments are discussed at length elsewhere.

the things within His power, and other matters discussed in detail in their proper place. Circular dependence is of “two kinds”: circular dependence involving priority is impossible. This means that one thing cannot exist until after another, while the other cannot exist until after the first. This is circular dependence among causes. As for circular dependence involving coexistence and concomitance—where one thing exists only together with another, and the other exists only together with the first—this concerns conditions and similar things that are mutually relative or mutually entailing. Circular dependence of this kind is possible.

These are the main outlines of the answers people have given to this question. They comprise several positions:

The first is the position of those who hold that neither His acts nor His rulings are based on reasons.

The second is the position of those who explain them by reference to things distinct and separate from Him, among the effects He brings into being.

The third is the position of those who explain them by reference to beginningless things subsisting in Him.

The fourth is the position of those who explain them by reference to things subsisting in Him and connected with His power and will, but who hold that their kind has a beginning.

The fifth is the position of those who explain them by reference to things connected with His will and power. If the act that gives rise to wisdom belongs to a kind that has a beginning, then the wisdom is likewise. If, however, it is supposed that speech or action connected with His will subsists in Him, and that this has always been so, then the wisdom is likewise. Thus, the kind is beginningless, even though its individual instances come into being.

Thus, if someone says, “If He acted for a reason that came into being, the explanation of how that reason came into being would be the same as the explanation of how its effect came into being, necessitating an infinite regress,” the answer, on this assumption, is that events must have a beginning. If He performs an act for a wisdom that comes into being, both the act and its wisdom come into being. A reason that comes into being need not itself have another reason that comes into being, unless it is possible for events to have no beginning. If events may have a beginning, this objection falls away; how much more so if both must have a beginning.

If, on the other hand, it is said:

“Events may extend infinitely into the past, just as they extend infinitely into the future according to Muslims, the other religious communities, and the vast majority of humanity. Only certain adherents of innovation have disputed the latter: those who maintain that Paradise and Hell will cease to exist, as al-Jahm ibn Safwān maintains, or that the movements of the people of Paradise will cease, as Abū al-Hudhayl maintains. These two held that events, as a kind, must have an end, just as, in their view, they must have a beginning. Most of those who agreed with them that events must have a beginning disagreed with them about their having an end, saying that they have a beginning but no end. A third group said that they have neither a beginning nor an end. These three positions are well known among Muslim groups.”

The point here is that an answer is available on either assumption. Whoever allows that events may extend infinitely into the past allows an infinite regress of events and says: “This is an infinite regress of effects and conditions, not an infinite regress of causes and agents that produce effects. It is only the latter that is impossible, not the former.”

Whoever holds that events must have a beginning says of the coming into being of the reason what he says of the coming into being of the effect, since there is no difference between them in this respect.

Among the answers that exhaust the possibilities is the following:

Allah’s act of creation either may or may not be explained in terms of a reason. If it may not, this is the first formulation. On this assumption, it is not called pointless. If someone does call it pointless, that designation does not undermine what has been established. For our discussion assumes that explaining it in terms of a reason is impossible. If that is impossible, this conclusion must be affirmed, whatever anyone may call it.

If, however, it may be explained in terms of a reason, then either it may be explained by a reason that comes into being, or it may not. If it is said that this is not possible, it follows that the reason is eternal, while on this assumption the effect cannot be eternal. For we are discussing the supposition that an effect which comes into being may be explained by an eternal reason. If it is said that it may be explained by a reason that comes into being, that position can be maintained.

Then it may be said that events may be explained by a finite reason belonging to the agent, so that it does not follow that something which comes into being subsists in Him—something that must subsist in Him for a wise purpose, even though that purpose is within His power and intended by Him. If the former is maintained, it follows that the reason which comes into being is separate from Him. On this basis, it also follows that the agent brings events into being after they did not exist, for a reason that comes into being in something other than Him, without any cause coming into being that necessitates the first event, and without anything that comes into being subsisting in the originator.

It must then be said either that this entails an infinite regress or that it does not. If it is said that it does not, then no infinite regress follows, and the objectionable consequence is avoided. If it is said that an infinite regress necessarily follows, then, on this supposition, an infinite regress is not objectionable. For the supposition is that His acts may be explained by a reason that comes into being, and that this entails an infinite regress. It is well known that what is possible cannot entail something impossible. If it did, it would be impossible on account of something else, even if possible in itself. Yet the supposition is that it is possible without qualification, with no impossibility involved. Whatever is possible without qualification, with no impossibility involved, cannot entail something whose existence is impossible. Thus, on this supposition, an infinite regress is not impossible.

This answers the objection without committing to any particular position. Rather, we show that no objectionable consequence actually arises. The objection, however, rests on six premises: that pointlessness necessarily follows, and that it is ruled out; that the effect must be eternal, and that this is ruled out; and that an infinite regress necessarily follows, and that it is ruled out.

The proponent of the first position says: “I do not concede that pointlessness necessarily follows.” The proponent of the second position says: “I do not concede that the effect must be eternal.” The proponent of the third position says:

Among their answers is the following:

This objection does not apply exclusively to the world’s coming into being. Rather, it applies to every event that comes into being in existence. That things come into being is witnessed, perceived by the senses, and agreed upon by rational people. Thus, whatever objection someone raises against the heavens and the earth having been created with a beginning, an equivalent objection can be raised against him concerning events that are directly witnessed. We have indicated the kinds of arguments advanced by each group in this discussion. However, an exhaustive treatment would exceed the scope of these pages and would not be appropriate here.

Whoever understands what has been written will find this subject opened up to him and will be able to attain a full understanding of questions of this kind. For it is by discussing them gradually, stage by stage, that the intended aim is achieved. Otherwise, if firm assent to positions is thrust upon the heart before one has mastered their proofs, the reasoning behind them, and the answers to objections against them, one will be more inclined to reject and disbelieve them than to affirm them.

For this reason, difficult questions must be discussed by presenting the evidence for each position and the objections raised against it by the opposing side, until the truth becomes clear through the reasoning that establishes it, for those whom Allah wills to guide.

“Whoever Allah does not grant light has no light.” “Allah speaks the truth, and He guides to the way.” Allah, glorified is He, knows best and is most wise. All praise belongs to Allah, Lord of all worlds. May Allah’s blessings and peace be upon Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

translated_text:
He was also asked:
“Did Allah Most High will disobedience from His creation or not?”

He replied:
The term “will” has two possible meanings: it may refer to His willing what He creates, or to His love and approval of what He commands.

If the questioner means that He loves acts of disobedience, approves of them, and commands them, then He does not will them in this sense. Allah does not love corruption, does not approve of disbelief for His servants, and does not command indecency. Rather, He said concerning what He has forbidden:

“All the evil in that is hateful to your Lord.”

But if he means that these acts are among the things Allah has willed and created, then Allah is the Creator of all things. Whatever He wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass. Nothing exists except what He wills.

Allah has mentioned in one passage that He wills them, and in another that He does not will them. The former means that He willed their creation; the latter means that, in terms of His commands, He neither loves nor approves of them. As He Most High said:

“Whoever Allah wills to guide, He opens his heart to Islam; and whoever He wills to lead astray, He makes his heart tight and constricted.”

Noah said:

“My advice will not benefit you, even if I wish to advise you, if Allah wills to lead you astray. He is your Lord.”

Concerning the second meaning, He said:

“Allah intends ease for you and does not intend for you

hardship.” And He Most High said:

“Allah intends to make things clear to you, guide you to the ways of those before you, and accept your repentance. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.”

“Allah intends to accept your repentance, but those who follow their desires want you to stray far from the right path.”

“Allah intends to lighten your burden, for mankind was created weak.”

And He said:

“Allah does not intend to place any hardship upon you, but He intends to purify you and complete His favour upon you.”

And He said:

“Allah intends only to remove impurity from you, O people of the household, and to purify you thoroughly.”

The shaykh, imam and eminent scholar Abū al-'Abbās Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah be pleased with him—was asked:

“What is the meaning of the saying of 'Alī—may Allah be pleased with him—‘No servant should place his hope in anyone but his Lord, nor fear anything but his sin’?”

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. This saying is reported from the Commander of the Faithful, 'Alī ibn Abī Tālib—may Allah be pleased with him. It is among the finest, most eloquent and most comprehensive sayings.

Hope concerns good, whereas fear concerns evil. Evil only befalls a servant because of his sins, as Allah Most High said:

“Whatever misfortune befalls you is because of what your own hands have earned, and He pardons much.”

And He Most High said:

“Wherever you may be, death will overtake you, even if you are in lofty, fortified towers. If good befalls them, they say, ‘This is from Allah’; but if evil befalls them, they say, ‘This is from you.’ Say, ‘All is from Allah.’ What is the matter with these people that they can hardly understand what they are told?”

“Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself.”

Many people think that the good and evil mentioned in this verse refer to acts of obedience and disobedience.

Then “those who affirm divine decree” cite His saying, “All is from Allah,” as evidence, but their argument is countered by His saying:

“Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself.”

“Those who deny divine decree” cite this second verse as evidence, although they are mistaken in doing so, for their doctrine is that the servant creates all his own deeds. Their argument is countered by His saying, “All is from Allah.”

Both groups have erred because, as mentioned above, they assume that good and evil here mean acts of obedience and disobedience. Rather, good and evil in this verse mean blessings and calamities, as in His saying, Most High:

“We tested them with good and evil, so that they might return.”

And His saying, Most High:

“When good came their way, they said, ‘This is our due.’ But if evil befell them, they regarded Moses and those with him as an evil omen.”

And His saying, Most High:

“If good comes your way, it grieves them; but if evil befalls you, they rejoice in it.”

And His saying, Most High:

“And protect them from evils.”

There are many other such examples.

In this verse, Allah censures the hypocrites who shrink from what He has commanded, whether fighting in His cause or anything else. When they receive provision, victory and well-being, they say, “This is from Allah.” But when poverty, humiliation and illness befall them, they say, “This is from you”—O Muhammad—because of the religion you have commanded us to follow. This is like what Pharaoh’s people said to Moses, as Allah Most High relates:

“When good came their way, they said, ‘This is our due.’ But if evil befell them, they regarded Moses and those with him as an evil omen.”

Likewise, the disbelievers said to the messengers of Jesus:

“We regard you as an evil omen.”

Thus, when calamities befall the disbelievers and hypocrites because of their sins, they regard the believers as an evil omen. It was therefore made clear

by Allah, Glorified is He, that good comes from Allah, who bestows it upon them, and that evil befalls them only because of their sins. Hence He, Most High, says:

“But Allah would not punish them while you are among them, nor would Allah punish them while they seek forgiveness.”

He thus states that He does not punish anyone who seeks forgiveness, because seeking forgiveness erases the sin that causes punishment, thereby averting the punishment. Thus, in the Sunan of Abū Dāwūd and Ibn Mājah, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever frequently seeks forgiveness, Allah will grant him relief from every worry, a way out of every hardship, and provision from where he does not expect.”

He, Most High, also says:

“Worship none but Allah. Indeed, I am to you from Him a warner and a bearer of good tidings.”

“And seek your Lord’s forgiveness, then repent to Him. He will grant you good enjoyment for an appointed term and bestow His bounty upon everyone deserving of it.”

He thus makes clear that whoever worships Him alone and seeks His forgiveness will be granted good enjoyment for an appointed term; and whoever thereafter does good, He will grant him more of His bounty. A hadith states:

“Satan says, ‘I destroyed people through sins, but they destroyed me by saying “There is no god but Allah” and seeking forgiveness. When I saw this, I spread vain desires among them, so they sin without repenting, because they think they are doing good.’”

Hence He, Most High, says:

“So We afflicted them with poverty and hardship, that they might humble themselves.”

“Why, then, did they not humble themselves when Our punishment came upon them?”

That is: why did they not humble themselves when Our punishment came upon them? When punishment comes, it is incumbent upon them to humble themselves. He, Most High, also says:

“We certainly seized them with punishment, yet they neither submitted to their Lord nor humbled themselves in supplication.”

ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said: “No affliction descends except because of a sin, nor is it lifted except through repentance.” Hence He, Most High, says:

“Those to whom people said, ‘The people have gathered against you

so fear them.’ But this increased them in faith, and they said, ‘Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.’”

“So they returned with blessings and bounty from Allah, untouched by harm. They pursued Allah’s pleasure, and Allah is the Possessor of great bounty.”

“It is only Satan who makes you fear his allies. So do not fear them, but fear Me, if you are believers.”

He thus forbade the believers to fear Satan’s allies and commanded them to fear Him. Fearing Him requires doing what He has commanded, refraining from what He has forbidden, and seeking forgiveness for sins. Affliction is then averted, and victory is gained over enemies. Hence ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, said: “Let no servant fear anything but his own sin.” If a creature is given power over him, it is only because of his sins. Let him therefore fear Allah and repent of the sins through which he has suffered what has befallen him. As a report states:

“Allah says: ‘I am Allah, Sovereign of kings. The hearts of kings and their forelocks are in My hand. Whoever obeys Me, I make them a mercy to him; whoever disobeys Me, I make them a punishment for him. So do not occupy yourselves with reviling kings. Obey Me, and I will incline their hearts toward you.’”

As for his saying, “Let no servant place his hope in anyone but his Lord,” one who hopes seeks to obtain good and avert evil. None but Allah brings good things, and none but Allah removes evils:

“If Allah afflicts you with harm, none can remove it but Him; and if He intends good for you, none can repel His bounty.”

“Whatever mercy Allah grants to people, none can withhold; and whatever He withholds, none can release thereafter.”

Hope is coupled with reliance, for one who relies seeks what he hopes for: obtaining benefit and averting harm. Reliance may be placed only in Allah, as He, Most High, says:

“And put your trust in Allah, if you are believers.”

He also says:

“And in Allah let those who would rely put their trust.”

He, Most High, also says: “If

Allah helps you, none can overcome you. But if He forsakes you, who can help you after Him? And in Allah let the believers put their trust.” He, Most High, also says:

“If only they had been content with what Allah and His Messenger gave them and had said, ‘Allah is sufficient for us. Allah will give us from His bounty, and so will His Messenger. To Allah alone we turn in hope.’”

He, Most High, also says:

“Those to whom people said, ‘The people have gathered against you, so fear them.’ But this increased them in faith, and they said, ‘Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.’”

These said, “Allah is sufficient for us,” meaning that Allah suffices them in warding off affliction; the others were instructed to say, “He is sufficient for us,” in obtaining blessings. Thus He, glorified be He, suffices His servant both in removing evil and in granting good. “Is Allah not sufficient for His servant?” Whoever relies on someone other than Allah and places his hope in him will be let down by that very one and deprived.

“The example of those who take protectors besides Allah is that of the spider that makes itself a home. Indeed, the frailest of homes is the spider’s home.”

“They have taken gods besides Allah to be a source of strength for them.”

“No! They will disown their worship and turn against them.”

“Whoever associates partners with Allah is like one who falls from the sky and is snatched away by birds or swept by the wind to a distant place.”

“Do not set up another god alongside Allah, lest you be left condemned and forsaken.”

Allah’s intimate friend said:

“So seek provision from Allah, worship Him, and give thanks to Him. To Him you will be returned.”

Whoever acts for someone other than Allah, hoping to benefit from the one for whom he acts, has made a losing bargain. Allah, Most High, says:

“As for those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage on a level plain, which a thirsty person mistakes for water, until, when he reaches it, he finds nothing there. But he finds Allah there, who pays him his account in full. And Allah is swift in reckoning.”

He, Most High, also says: “The example of those who disbelieve in their Lord is that their deeds are like ashes blown fiercely by the wind on a stormy day. They have no power

over anything they have earned.” He, Most High, also says:

“And We will turn to whatever deeds they have done and make them scattered dust.”

He, Most High, also says:

“Everything will perish except His Face.”

As has been said in explanation of this verse, every deed is worthless except what is done seeking His Face. Whoever acts for someone other than Allah and places his hope in him will find his efforts fruitless. A person may express his hope by performing deeds for the one in whom he places his hope, or by relying upon him in his heart, turning to him for refuge, and asking of him. The former is a kind of worship of him, while the latter is a kind of seeking his help. He, Most High, has said:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.”

He also says:

“So worship Him and put your trust in Him.”

And He says:

“Say, ‘He is my Lord; there is no god but Him. In Him I put my trust, and to Him I turn in repentance.’”

This is further clarified by the fact that every good thing and blessing that reaches the servant comes only from Allah. Every evil and calamity that is warded off from him or lifted from him is prevented only by Allah and removed only by Allah. Even when the means by which these things come about operate through His creatures, Allah, glorified be He, is the Creator of all those means. This applies whether the means consist of the movement of a living being acting by its own choice and intention—as with what He, Most High, brings about through the movements of angels, jinn, human beings, and animals—or the movement of an inanimate thing through the natural properties Allah has placed within it or through an external force that compels it to move, as with the movement of winds, waters, and the like. Allah is the Creator of all of this. There is no might or power except through Him. Whatever He wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass.

All hope must therefore be placed in the Lord, all trust in Him, and all supplication directed to Him. If He wills something and facilitates it, it will come about and be made easy, even if people do not will it. If He does not will it and does not facilitate it, it will not come about, even if people will it.

place one’s hope in none but Allah, put one’s trust in Him alone, ask of Him alone, seek help from Him alone, and appeal to Him alone for deliverance. To Him belongs all praise, to Him all complaints are addressed, and He alone is sought for help and deliverance. There is no might or power except through Him. How much more so, then, when no cause can independently produce the desired outcome! Rather, other causes must join it, and obstacles and counteracting factors must also be removed before the intended result can be achieved.

Every cause has something that assists it and something that opposes it. Unless its assisting factor supports it and its opposing factor is averted, it will not produce its result. Rain alone does not make plants grow without the air, soil, and other things that work alongside it. Then the crop cannot fully develop unless destructive blights are kept away from it. Food and drink provide nourishment only through the organs and faculties placed within the body, and all of these together are of no benefit unless harmful factors are averted.

As for a created being who gives to you or supports you—notwithstanding that Allah creates within him the will, power, and action—what he does cannot be accomplished without many causes beyond his control that assist him in achieving his aim, even if he is a king whose commands are obeyed. Whatever opposes or obstructs these assisting causes must also be averted. Thus, the desired outcome can be achieved only when the causal basis is present and impediments are absent. Every particular cause is merely one component of that causal basis; no single thing in existence constitutes it on its own. Even if one calls a particular cause the “causal basis” and calls everything else that assists it “conditions,” this is merely a disagreement over terminology.

In that case, one would say:

The causal basis and the conditions must be present, and impediments must be absent. As for there being among created things a complete cause that necessarily entails its effect, this is false.

And whoever truly understands this will find the door to understanding Allah’s oneness opened to him. He will know that none but Allah deserves to be invoked, let alone worshipped, and that trust and hope must be placed in Him alone. This is established by both revelation and reason. In this respect, there is no difference between heavenly and earthly causes, the deeds and intercession of angels, prophets, and believers, or any other causes. Whoever places his trust in an angel, a prophet, a righteous man, or anyone similar for intercession or supplication should be told:

This too is merely one cause among others. The one who intercedes or supplicates does so only by Allah’s will and power. Moreover, those who obey Him intercede only for someone with whom He is pleased. As the Exalted says:

“They intercede only for those with whom He is pleased.”

No one intercedes with Him except by His permission—permission pertaining to His universal decree. For intercession, being an act performed by His servants, occurs only by His will and power. He is not like a created being approached by an intercessor whose intercession takes place independently of the might and power of the one being approached. Rather, He, glorified be He, creates the intercessor’s intercession, just as He creates all other changes. There is no might or power except through Him.

The word hawl (might) encompasses a change from one state to another, whether through movement, volition, or something else. Thus, the intercessor has no power to bring about any change, in intercession or anything else, except through Him. Furthermore, those who obey Him and whose intercession is accepted intercede only for those with whom He is pleased. They do not ask Him for anything that He does not love to be asked for. Indeed, even the angels—His own angels—are as He says of them:

“They say, ‘The Most Merciful has taken a son.’ Glory be to Him! Rather, they are honored servants.

“They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command.

“He knows what is before them and what is behind them. They intercede only for those with whom He is pleased, and they stand in awe of Him.”

We must likewise conduct ourselves toward Him and His messengers: we must not speak about religion until He has spoken, nor put ourselves ahead of Allah and His Messenger, nor worship Him except as He has commanded. A higher degree still is to do nothing except what He has commanded, so that all our actions are either obligatory or recommended.

If this is the case with causes such as these, what of someone who places his trust or hope in other causes—heavenly bodies, for example—or in the actions of human beings, such as kings, leaders, companions, friends, slaves, followers, and others?

Among the things that should be understood is the statement made by a group of scholars:

“Placing one’s reliance in causes is a form of associating partners with Allah that violates His oneness. Denying that causes are causes is a deficiency in reason, while disregarding causes altogether undermines the revealed law. True trust and hope combine what is required by belief in Allah’s oneness, reason, and the revealed law.”

The explanation is this: looking to a cause means that the heart depends on it, places hope in it, and relies upon it. Nothing in creation deserves this, for nothing acts independently: it necessarily has cooperating causes and opposing forces. Moreover, despite all this, unless the One who ordains causes makes it operate, it will not operate.

One of the greatest examples of this is the “starless ninth sphere.” Many metaphysical philosophers, astrologers, and others suppose that its motion causes all events, and their knowledge of the causes of events goes no further than this motion. They either regard it as known to the Necessary Existent through the mediation of an intellect or a soul, or without such mediation; or else they deny that it is an effect and regard it as necessarily existent in itself. This claim of theirs is among the most utterly unsound, although, despite their intelligence, they fail to recognize this, and many people do not know how to refute them on this point.

Anyone who looks at the sky knows that its motion is not the cause of all celestial motions. It is often said that, through its easterly motion, all the spheres within it move from east to west. Yet each sphere also has another motion peculiar to it, contrary to this motion: the sphere of the fixed stars, and the spheres of the sun, the moon, and the other celestial bodies that recede, run their courses, and disappear from view. These differing motions do not arise from that motion—they run counter to it—nor are their spheres effects of that ninth sphere.
