translated_text:
different configurations are not effects of the motion of the ninth sphere. Rather, its motion is part of the cause, just as the motion of each sphere is part of the cause. The celestial configuration arises from the combined effect of two motions or several different motions. If we suppose that the nine spheres come into conjunction, they have seven motions—or, according to them, even more, depending on the additional spheres whose existence is inferred from the different motions, such as the badrī spheres and others that account for the direct and retrograde motions of the heavenly bodies and their other movements. Accordingly, anyone who makes the motion of the ninth sphere the cause of all events contradicts what is known to these philosophers and astrologers, and to every rational person.

Even supposing that it causes the motion of all the spheres, it does not independently bring about clouds, thunder, lightning, rain, vegetation, or the conditions of animals and minerals. For the motions of these bodies do not all derive from the motions of the spheres. Rather, they possess powers and causes that produce other motions in them, just as every sphere that initiates motion has a motion that does not derive from another sphere.

All motions are either “natural,” “voluntary,” or “forced.” Forced motion depends on the agent imposing it. Natural motion is motion of which the moving body has no awareness, such as the downward movement of earth. Voluntary motion is motion of which the moving being is aware, such as the movement of an animal. Thus, whatever among these bodies moves by an inherent nature or will has the source of its motion within itself. As for whatever is moved by force, the created agent imposing that force does so only because the body possesses a capacity to receive it; and this is a property that does not derive

from the agent imposing the force. Thus, even when combined, the motions of the spheres do not independently move these bodies, although they may form part of the cause, just as we observe that the sun forms part of the cause of the growth, moisture, dryness, and similar conditions of certain bodies. Moreover, even supposing that they are causes, there are things that impede and counteract them. For every conceivable cause has something that can impede it, whether voluntary, natural, or otherwise. Supplication, charity, and righteous deeds, for example, are among the greatest means of averting calamities descending from heaven. This is why we have been commanded to perform them during eclipses and other heavenly signs that may cause punishment. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The sun and the moon are not eclipsed because of anyone’s death or birth. Rather, they are two of Allah’s signs through which He instils fear in His servants. When you see that, hasten to prayer.”

During an eclipse, he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded prayer, remembrance of Allah, seeking forgiveness, charity, and the emancipation of slaves.

Once it is understood that, when you examine observable beings individually—the ninth sphere and everything else—you find that none independently brings about anything whatsoever, but that events necessarily require other causes, even if the being in question forms part of a cause, and that these causes also face other opposing factors, it becomes clear that none of these things can rightly be said to bring about observable events. Still less can any of them be said to originate bodies whose motion differs from its own and counteracts what its motion would bring about. For a thing does not necessitate what opposes it and runs counter to it. If, among moving bodies, there is something whose effects run counter to what the ninth sphere necessarily produces and entails

and oppose it, neither can be the cause of the other. For an effect cannot oppose its cause, just as it cannot produce its cause. Likewise, a thing cannot be its own opposite or produce itself. Its being opposed to itself would entail its existence depending on its own existence, making it both existent and nonexistent. Its producing itself, given that a cause precedes its effect, would likewise entail its being both existent and nonexistent.

It is known that if the events and motions arising from the powers of bodies do not originate from the “ninth sphere,” and it imparts to them only accidental motion, then there is all the more reason that the bodies themselves and their powers should not originate from it. This establishes that the mover of the spheres and other observable bodies, and the originator of these bodies through another cause, is a Lord distinct from them. He is the One who originated them in their different forms and set them in motion with their different motions. This is what was to be established.

Moreover, even if these heavenly bodies form part of the cause of certain events, they do so only in some circumstances, not others. When they appear above the earth, their light and influence become manifest; when they set, their light and influence cease. They then cease to be either a cause or part of a cause. This is why Allah’s intimate friend, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“I do not love those that set.”

When they set, their influence upon us ceases altogether, leaving no semblance of a justification on which anyone attached to them can rely. The Lord who is invoked and asked, in whom hope and trust are placed, must be the self-subsisting Sustainer who sustains His servant at all times and in every circumstance. As He said:

“And put your trust in the Ever-Living, who does not die.”

And He said:

“Allah—there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all existence.”

Thus this and other forms of

reflection and contemplation establish that the servant should place his hope in Allah alone and rely upon Him alone. As for fearing nothing but his own sin, this follows from the knowledge that no calamity befalls him except because of his sins. This is known through the signs in the world around us and within ourselves, and through what Allah has revealed in His Book, as explained at length elsewhere. We have also explained the underlying reason for this in greater detail than this discussion allows.

This bears out what is established in the authentic hadith narrated by Abū Dharr from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, reporting that his Lord said:

“My servants, it is only your deeds that I record for you and then recompense you for in full. Whoever finds good, let him praise Allah; and whoever finds otherwise, let him blame no one but himself.”

He thus explained that the servant should praise Allah for whatever good he finds, for Allah is the One who bestowed it upon him, and that he should blame no one but himself for whatever evil he finds.

It is also authentically reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The best supplication for forgiveness is for the servant to say: ‘O Allah, You are my Lord; there is no deity except You. You created me, and I am Your servant. I remain true to Your covenant and promise as far as I am able. I seek refuge in You from the evil of what I have done. I acknowledge before You Your blessings upon me, and I acknowledge my sin. So forgive me, for no one forgives sins but You.’”

The words, “I acknowledge before You Your blessings upon me,” express recognition and acknowledgment of His blessings, while the words, “and I acknowledge my sin,” express acknowledgment of sin. Hence one of the early generations said:

“Each morning I find myself between a blessing and a sin, so I wish to respond to the blessing with gratitude and to the sin by seeking forgiveness.”

Gratitude, however, follows the blessing, whereas reliance and hope precede it, as Allah’s intimate friend said:

“So seek from Allah

provision, and worship Him and be grateful to Him.”

In his sermon, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Praise be to Allah. We seek His help and forgiveness, and we seek refuge in Allah from the evils of our souls and from our evil deeds.”

He thus combined praising Allah, seeking His help, and asking His forgiveness. It has therefore become clear that placing one’s reliance on causes constitutes associating partners with Allah, contrary to His oneness, and is wrongdoing and ignorance. This is the condition of someone who invokes another besides Allah and relies upon him.

As for their statement, “To deny that causes are causes is a deficiency in reason,” this is indeed so, and it also undermines the revealed Law. Many speculative theologians have denied causes altogether, treating their existence as no different from their absence. Those naturalists, by contrast, regarded them as causes that necessarily produce their effects, while the Muʿtazilah distinguished between the actions of living creatures and other occurrences. All three views are false, for Allah says:

“He is the One who sends the winds as glad tidings before His mercy. When they bear heavy clouds, We drive them to a lifeless land and send down water through them, bringing forth thereby every kind of fruit.”

And He, Most High, says:

“And the water Allah sends down from the sky, giving life thereby to the earth after its death.”

And He, Most High, says:

“Through it Allah guides those who seek His pleasure to the paths of peace.”

And He, Most High, says:

“Through it He leads many astray and guides many.”

There are many similar passages. Whoever says that effects occur in the presence of causes, but not through them, contradicts the wording of the Quran. Moreover, sensory experience and reason testify that these are causes and recognize the difference between the forehead and the eye, in that one possesses a faculty absent from the other; likewise, between bread and pebbles, in that one provides nourishment while the other does not.

As for their statement, “To disregard causes altogether undermines the revealed Law,” it also undermines reason. The actions of servants are among the strongest causes of the outcomes attached to them. Thus, whoever regards

Rather, the worship, supplications, knowledge and deeds that Allah has commanded are among the greatest causes of the acts of worship linked to them. Likewise, the disbelief, wickedness and disobedience He has forbidden are among the greatest causes of the misery attached to them.

Nevertheless, the best of creation said:

“None of you will enter Paradise by virtue of his deeds.”

They asked, “Not even you, O Messenger of Allah?”

He replied, “Not even me, unless Allah envelops me in His mercy and bounty.”

And when he told them, “There is not one of you whose place in Paradise and whose place in Hell is not already known,” they asked, “O Messenger of Allah, should we not then rely on what has been written and abandon deeds?”

He replied, “No. Act, for everyone will be enabled to do that for which he was created. Whoever is among the people of bliss will be enabled to perform the deeds of the people of bliss, and whoever is among the people of misery will be enabled to perform the deeds of the people of misery.”

Likewise, supplication and reliance upon Allah are among the greatest causes of the outcomes for which Allah has made them causes. Whoever says, “Whatever has been decreed for me will come to me, whether I supplicate or not, and whether I rely upon Allah or not,” is like someone who says, “Whatever bliss or misery has been allotted to me will come to me, whether I believe or not, and whether I obey or disobey.” It is well known that this is misguidance and disbelief, although the former statement is not as misguided as the latter: the connection between attaining one’s aims and supplication and reliance upon Allah is not like the connection between bliss in the Hereafter and faith. Yet there is no doubt that whatever Allah has made supplication a cause of is comparable to that for which action has been made

a cause—namely, righteous action. He, glorified is He, is able to bring about the outcome without this cause, and He may bring it about through another cause.

Likewise, whoever abandons the prescribed means of securing benefits or warding off harm, whether commanded as an obligation or as a recommendation, undermines the revealed Law and departs from sound reason. This is where they went wrong: they abandoned the means they were commanded to take, thinking that this perfected their reliance upon Allah. Yet reliance upon Allah is coupled with worship in His words:

“So worship Him and rely upon Him.”

Worship consists in doing what has been commanded. Whoever abandons the prescribed worship while relying upon Allah is no better off than someone who worships Him without relying upon Him. Rather, both disobey Allah by abandoning part of what they have been commanded to do.

Reliance upon Allah includes relying upon Him to help one do what He has commanded, and relying upon Him to grant what lies beyond one’s own power. Seeking help concerns the performance of deeds, whereas reliance upon Allah is broader than that: it includes relying upon Him to secure benefit and ward off harm. Allah Most High says:

“If only they had been content with what Allah and His Messenger gave them and had said, ‘Allah is sufficient for us. Allah will give us of His bounty, and so will His Messenger. Indeed, to Allah we turn in hope.’”

And Allah Most High says:

“Those to whom people said, ‘The people have gathered against you, so fear them,’ but this only increased them in faith, and they said, ‘Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.’”

Whoever does not do what he has been commanded is not seeking Allah’s help in doing it. Thus, he has abandoned worship and seeking help to perform it, also abandoning reliance upon Allah in this respect. Moreover, Adam invoked divine decree in his argument, yet no one may invoke divine decree to justify sin, as Muslims, adherents of all other religions, and all other rational people agree. If this were acceptable, anyone could commit whatever occurred to him—killing people, seizing their wealth, or perpetrating any other form of corruption on earth—and invoke divine decree as his excuse. Yet the very person who invokes divine decree will not accept this excuse from someone who wrongs him. He thus contradicts himself, and a position’s inconsistency demonstrates its invalidity. The invalidity of invoking divine decree as an excuse is therefore evident even to the most elementary reason.

Whoever supposes that belief in divine decree consists in believing that Allah is the Creator of His servants’ deeds—as supposed by the polytheistic antinomians, who acknowledge divine decree but not divine commands, and the Magian Qadarites, who acknowledge divine commands but not divine decree—or supposes that, given this, imposing religious obligations is unintelligible, but that the Lawgiver is obeyed in this solely because of the divine will, and that Allah acts; and makes this his argument concerning deeds, without including reasons appropriate to commands and prohibitions, but instead denies the benefits, merits, and purposes that the revealed law contains for people in this life and the Hereafter; reduces that law to a mere attribution, without any correspondence or congruity between cause and effect; and denies that deeds have qualities by virtue of which they are good and commanded, or evil and forbidden, invoking divine decree as his argument for this and maintaining that, since the Lord is the Creator, all of this is impossible—

For people generally believe in divine decree and say that aggressors must be punished—even the insane and animals are disciplined to curb their aggression, although their actions are decreed—and that all human beings pardon their aggression, although their actions are decreed.

The servant must therefore be patient and should be content with the afflictions decreed for him. He should seek forgiveness for sins and faults, not invoke divine decree to excuse them, and give thanks for the blessings and gifts Allah has decreed for him. What do the esteemed scholars, the imams of religion—may Allah be pleased with them all—say concerning the words of Allah Most High:

If the one addressed already exists, then bringing into existence what already exists is impossible. But if it does not exist, how can addressing something nonexistent be conceived?

And concerning His words, exalted is He:

 الْفَرْقُ بَيْنَ خِطَابِ التَّكْوِينِ الَّذِي لَا يَطْلُبُ بِهِ سُبْحَانَهُ فِعْلًا مِنْ الْمُخَاطَبِ بَلْ هُوَ الَّذِي يُكَوِّنُ الْمُخَاطَبَ بِهِ وَيَخْلُقُهُ بِدُونِ فِعْلٍ مِنْ الْمُخَاطَبِ أَوْ قُدْرَةٍ أَوْ إرَادَةٍ أَوْ وُجُودٍ لَهُ وَبَيْنَ خِطَابِ التَّكْلِيفِ الَّذِي يَطْلُبُ بِهِ مِنْ الْمَأْمُورِ فِعْلًا أَوْ تَرْكًا يَفْعَلُهُ بِقُدْرَةِ وَإِرَادَةٍ - وَإِنْ كَانَ ذَلِكَ جَمِيعُهُ بِحَوْلِ اللَّهِ وَقُوَّتِهِ إذْ لَا حَوْلَ وَلَا قُوَّةَ إلَّا بِاَللَّهِ - وَهَذَا الْخِطَابُ قَدْ تَنَازَعَ فِيهِ النَّاسُ هَلْ يَصِحُّ أَنْ يُخَاطَبَ بِهِ الْمَعْدُومُ بِشَرْطِ وُجُودِهِ أَمْ لَا يَصِحُّ أَنْ يُخَاطَبَ بِهِ إلَّا بَعْدَ وُجُودِهِ؟ وَلَا نِزَاعَ بَيْنَهُمْ أَنَّهُ لَا يَتَعَلَّقُ بِهِ حُكْمُ الْخِطَابِ إلَّا بَعْدَ وُجُودِهِ. وَكَذَلِكَ تَنَازَعُوا فِي الْأَوَّلِ هَلْ هُوَ خِطَابٌ حَقِيقِيٌّ أَمْ هُوَ عِبَارَةٌ عَنْ الِاقْتِدَارِ وَسُرْعَةِ التَّكْوِينِ بِالْقُدْرَةِ؟ وَالْأَوَّلُ هُوَ الْمَشْهُورُ عِنْدَ الْمُنْتَسِبِينَ إلَى السُّنَّةِ.
وَالْأَصْلُ الثَّانِي:
 أَنَّ الْمَعْدُومَ فِي حَالِ عَدَمِهِ هَلْ هُوَ شَيْءٌ أَمْ لَا؟ فَإِنَّهُ قَدْ ذَهَبَ طَوَائِفُ مِنْ مُتَكَلِّمَةِ الْمُعْتَزِلَةِ وَالشِّيعَةِ إلَى أَنَّهُ شَيْءٌ فِي الْخَارِجِ وَذَاتٌ وَعَيْنٌ. وَزَعَمُوا أَنَّ الْمَاهِيَّاتِ غَيْرُ مَجْعُولَةٍ وَلَا مَخْلُوقَةٍ وَأَنَّ وُجُودَهَا زَائِدٌ عَلَى حَقِيقَتِهَا وَكَذَلِكَ ذَهَبَ إلَى هَذَا طَوَائِفُ مِنْ الْمُتَفَلْسِفَةِ والاتحادية وَغَيْرِهِمْ مِنْ الْمَلَاحِدَةِ.
translated_text:
As for the “first question,” it rests on two principles:

The first is the distinction between the address that brings things into being and the address that imposes obligations. Through the former, He, glorified is He, does not require any action from the addressee. Rather, He Himself brings the addressee into being and creates it through that address, without any action, power, will, or existence on the addressee’s part. Through the latter, He requires the one commanded to perform an act or refrain from it, exercising power and will—although all of this occurs through Allah’s might and power, for there is no might or power except through Allah.

People have disagreed over this latter address: may something nonexistent validly be addressed on condition that it comes into existence, or may it validly be addressed only after it exists? They do not disagree, however, that the ruling conveyed by the address applies to it only after it exists. Likewise, they have disagreed over the former: is it an actual address, or is it an expression of His power and the swiftness with which He brings things into being through that power? The former is the well-known view among those who identify with the Sunnah.

The second principle concerns whether something nonexistent is a thing while it does not exist. Certain groups among the theologians of the Muʿtazilah and the Shīʿah have held that it is a thing outside the mind—an entity and a distinct reality. They have claimed that essences are neither made nor created, and that their existence is something additional to their essential reality. Certain groups among the philosophers, the Ittihādiyyah (advocates of union), and other heretics have likewise adopted this view.

 قَالُوا:
 وَهَذِهِ التَّخْصِيصَاتُ تَمْتَنِعُ أَنْ تَتَعَلَّقَ بِالْعَدَمِ الْمَحْضِ فَإِنْ خُصَّ الْفَرْقُ بَيْنَ الْوُجُودِ الَّذِي هُوَ الثُّبُوتُ الْعَيْنِيُّ وَبَيْنَ الْوُجُودِ الَّذِي هُوَ الثُّبُوتُ الْعِلْمِيُّ زَالَتْ الشُّبْهَةُ فِي هَذَا الْبَابِ.
translated_text:
The view held by the vast majority—and by the affirmationist theologians and those who identify with the Sunnah and the community—is that, before it exists, the nonexistent is nothing at all outside the mind: neither a thing, nor an entity, nor a distinct reality. Nor are there two things outside the mind, one being its essential reality and the other its existence, additional to that reality. Allah brought the entities themselves—that is, their essences—into being. Everything other than Him, glorified and exalted is He, is created, made, brought into being, and originated by Him.

Among those who hold this view, however, some say that the nonexistent is not a thing at all, and that it is called a thing only because it is established in knowledge; the designation is therefore figurative. Others say that it undoubtedly has an established reality and an existence in knowledge, and that, in respect of this reality and existence, it is a thing and an entity.

These people do not distinguish between existence and being established, as those who say that the nonexistent is a thing do. Nor, in holding that the nonexistent is not a thing, do they distinguish between the possible and the impossible, as the latter do. They all agree that the impossible is not a thing; their disagreement concerns only the possible. The principal argument of those who regard it as a thing is simply that it is established in knowledge. In this respect, it can properly be singled out as something intended, created, spoken of, commanded, prohibited, and so forth.

They say that such specific relations cannot pertain to sheer nonexistence. If, then, the distinction is drawn specifically between existence as concrete reality and existence as reality in knowledge, the confusion in this matter disappears.

Concerning His words, exalted is He:

“When We will something, all We say to it is, ‘Be!’ and it is.”

That thing is known before it is brought into being and before this address is directed to it; in this respect, it has already been ordained and decreed. For Allah, glorified and exalted is He, speaks and writes whatever He wills of what He knows. Thus, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in the hadith narrated by Muslim in his Sahīh from Abd Allāh ibn Amr:

“Allah decreed the destinies of all creatures fifty thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth.”

In Sahīh al-Bukhārī, Imrān ibn Husayn relates that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah was, and nothing was with Him. His Throne was upon the water, and He wrote everything in the Record, then created the heavens and the earth.”

In Sunan Abī Dāwūd and elsewhere, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is reported to have said:

“When Allah first created the Pen, He said to it, ‘Write.’ It asked, ‘What shall I write?’ He said, ‘Whatever will happen until the Day of Resurrection.’”

These and similar texts show that, before a created thing is created, it is known, spoken of, and written down. It is therefore a thing in respect of its existence in knowledge, speech, and writing, even though its reality—its concrete existence—is not established outside the mind; rather, it is pure nonexistence and sheer negation. These are the four well-known levels of existence. Allah, glorified and exalted is He, mentioned them in the first surah He revealed to His Prophet, saying:

“Read in the name of your Lord who created—created man from a clinging clot. Read! And your Lord is the Most Generous, who taught by the pen—taught man what he did not know.”

We have discussed this at length elsewhere. Accordingly, the address is directed to that toward which the will is directed and to which is connected

 أَمَّا إذَا قُصِدَ أَنْ يُخَاطَبَ الْمَعْدُومُ فِي الْخِطَابِ بِخِطَابِ يَفْهَمُهُ وَيَمْتَثِلُهُ فَهَذَا مُحَالٌ؛ إذْ مِنْ شَرْطِ الْمُخَاطَبِ أَنْ يَتَمَكَّنَ مِنْ الْفَهْمِ وَالْفِعْلِ وَالْمَعْدُومُ لَا يُتَصَوَّرُ أَنْ يَفْهَمَ وَيَفْعَلَ فَيَمْتَنِعُ خِطَابُ التَّكْلِيفِ لَهُ حَالَ عَدَمِهِ بِمَعْنَى أَنَّهُ يُطْلَبُ مِنْهُ حِينَ عَدَمِهِ أَنْ يَفْهَمَ وَيَفْعَلَ وَكَذَلِكَ أَيْضًا يَمْتَنِعُ أَنْ يُخَاطَبَ الْمَعْدُومُ فِي الْخَارِجِ خِطَابَ تَكْوِينٍ بِمَعْنَى أَنْ يَعْتَقِدَ أَنَّهُ شَيْءٌ ثَابِتٌ فِي الْخَارِجِ وَأَنَّهُ يُخَاطَبُ بِأَنْ يَكُونَ.
translated_text:
His power, and which He creates and brings into being, as He says:

“When We will something, all We say to it is, ‘Be!’ and it is.”

Thus, that to which “Be!” is said is the very thing that is willed. When it is willed, before it is created, it is already established and distinct in knowledge and decree. Otherwise, the thing willed and created would not be distinguished from anything else. This provides the answer to the alternatives posed in the question.

The questioner says: “If that which is addressed exists, then bringing into being what already exists is impossible.”

The reply is: This is so if it already exists in external reality with the very existence in question. Undoubtedly, what is nonexistent does not exist, nor does it have any established reality in itself. But as for what is known and willed, and is a thing in knowledge, will, and decree, its existence in external reality is not impossible. Indeed, no created thing comes into existence until after it exists in knowledge and will.

The questioner also says: “If it is nonexistent, how can addressing the nonexistent be conceivable?”

The reply is: If what is meant is addressing something while it is nonexistent with words that it understands and obeys, this is impossible. For the one addressed must be capable of understanding and acting, whereas it is inconceivable that something nonexistent should understand and act. Thus, it is impossible to address it with a command imposing an obligation while it is nonexistent, in the sense of requiring it to understand and act during its nonexistence. Likewise, it is impossible to address something nonexistent in external reality with a creative command, in the sense of supposing that it is something already established in external reality and is being addressed with the command to be.

فَيُقَالُ:
 هَذِهِ اللَّامُ لَيْسَتْ هِيَ اللَّامَ الَّتِي يُسَمِّيهَا النُّحَاةُ لَامَ الْعَاقِبَةِ وَالصَّيْرُورَةِ وَلَمْ يَقُلْ ذَلِكَ أَحَدٌ هُنَا كَمَا ذَكَرَهُ السَّائِلُ مِنْ أَنَّ ذَلِكَ لَمْ يَصِرْ إلَّا
translated_text:
As for a thing that is known, mentioned, and written down, if addressing it with a creative command is like directing the will toward it, this is not impossible; rather, it is possible. Indeed, a person finds something similar within himself: he conceives of something he wishes to do, then directs his will and desire toward that intended and desired thing he has conceived. Its realization depends on his ability. If he has the power to bring it about, it comes about with resolute will and desire; if he is incapable, it does not. A person may say, “Let such-and-such be,” or use similar expressions of demand, but the realization of what he seeks depends on his power to accomplish it. Allah, glorified is He, has power over all things. Whatever He wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass. Thus, when He wills a thing, His command is only to say to it, “Be!” and it is.

Section

As for the second question, the questioner says:

“In the words of the Exalted,

‘I did not create jinn and mankind except to worship Me,’

if this lām—the particle ‘to’—denotes the eventual outcome, that outcome has not come about. If it denotes purpose, it would follow that none of the created beings could fail to worship Him. Yet this is not the case. How, then, can this difficulty be resolved?”

The reply is:

This lām is not what grammarians call the lām of outcome or eventual result. No one has maintained that it is here, given the questioner’s observation that this outcome did not come about—except

translated_text:
according to those who interpret “worship Me” as “know Me,” meaning the knowledge enjoined upon both believer and unbeliever. But this is a weak view. Some people have made this claim concerning His words near the end of Sūrat Hūd:

“And for that He created them.”

Some of the Qadarīs claimed that this lām denotes outcome or eventual result: that is, their eventual outcome was mercy or disagreement, even though the Creator did not intend it. They likened this to His words:

“Then Pharaoh’s household picked him up, only for him to become an enemy and a source of grief to them,”

and to the poet’s words:

“Bear children for death, and build for ruin.”

This interpretation is also weak here, because the lām of outcome is used only of someone who does not know how matters will ultimately turn out, and who therefore performs an act whose outcome he does not know—as was the case with Pharaoh’s household. But as for one who knows the outcomes and consequences of actions, it is inconceivable that he should perform an act without knowing its outcome. If he knows that his act has a particular outcome, he does not intend by it something he knows will not occur, for that would be wishful thinking, not willing.

Rather, the lām here has its familiar meaning: it is the lām meaning “in order to,” the lām of purpose. When it is omitted, the verbal noun it governs in the genitive takes the accusative as an expression of purpose. This purpose is called the final cause: it precedes the act in knowledge and will, but follows it in existence and realization. This cause is the intended, sought-after objective of the act. However, it should be understood that will in the Book of Allah is of two kinds:

The first is the creational will: the will that necessarily entails the occurrence of what is willed. Of this it is said, “Whatever Allah wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass.” This is the will referred to in such statements as His words:

“Whomever Allah wills to guide, He opens his heart to Islam; and whomever He wills to lead astray, He makes his heart tight and constricted.”

And His words:

“My advice will not benefit you, even if I wish to advise you, if Allah wills to lead you astray.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Had Allah willed, they would not have fought one another, but Allah does whatever He wills.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Why, when you entered your garden, did you not say, ‘What Allah wills! There is no power except through Allah’?”

There are other similar passages.

This will is what the lām signifies in His words:

“They will continue to differ, except those upon whom your Lord has mercy; and for that He created them.”

The early generations said: “He created one group for disagreement and another for mercy.” Since mercy here was the will, and there it was creational, what was willed through it came to pass: some people differed, while others were shown mercy.

As for the second kind, it is the religious, legislative will. It consists in loving and approving what is willed, loving and being pleased with those who fulfill it, and rewarding them with the best. Thus Allah Most High says:

“Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Allah does not intend to place any hardship upon you, but He intends to purify you and complete His favor upon you.”

And He says:

“Allah intends to make things clear to you, guide you to the ways of those before you, and turn to you in forgiveness. Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.”

“Allah intends to turn to you in forgiveness, but those who follow their desires want you to stray far away.”

“Allah intends to lighten your burden, for mankind was created weak.”

This will does not necessarily entail the occurrence of what is willed unless the first kind of will also pertains to it. Thus there are four categories:

translated_text:
The first is that to which both kinds of will pertain: righteous deeds that actually occur. Allah wills them by His religious, legislative will, commanding, loving and approving them; and He wills them by His creational will, so they occur. Otherwise, they would not occur.

The second is that to which only the religious will pertains: righteous deeds that Allah commands, but the disbelievers and the wicked disobey that command. All these deeds are objects of His religious will, and He loves and approves them whether they occur or not.

The third is that to which only the creational will pertains: events that He decrees and wills but has not commanded, such as permissible acts and sins. He has not commanded, approved or loved them, for He does not command indecency, nor does He approve disbelief for His servants. Were it not for His will, His power and His creation of them, they would not occur or come into existence. Whatever Allah wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass.

The fourth is that to which neither kind of will pertains: permissible acts and sins that do not occur.

Accordingly, what the lām signifies in His words:

“I did not create jinn and mankind except to worship Me”

is this religious, legislative will. What is intended by this will may or may not occur. The meaning is that the purpose He loves and approves for them, and which they have been commanded to fulfill, is worship. This is the deed for which He created His servants: it brings about their perfection and well-being, through which they become pleasing and beloved to Him. Whoever does not fulfill this purpose therefore lacks what is loved, approved and intended for him by the religious will, wherein lie his happiness and salvation, and lacks

Section

As for the third question, he asks concerning the reports and verses about contentment with Allah’s decree:

“If sins occur apart from Allah’s decree, that is impossible and undermines belief in His oneness. But if they occur by the decree of Allah Most High, does not disliking and hating them amount to disliking and hating the decree of Allah Most High?”

The answer is that neither the Book of Allah nor the Sunnah of His Messenger contains any verse or hadith commanding people to be content with every decreed and predestined human action, whether good or evil. This is a fundamental principle that requires careful attention. People must, however, be content with what Allah has commanded; no one may resent what He has commanded. Allah Most High says:

“But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge in their disputes, then find within themselves no discomfort at your judgment and submit completely.”

Allah Most High also says:

“That is because they followed what angered Allah and disliked His good pleasure, so He rendered their deeds worthless.”

And He says:

“If only they had been content with what Allah and His Messenger gave them and had said, ‘Allah is sufficient for us. Allah will give us of His bounty, and so will His Messenger. To Allah alone we turn in hope.’”

The mention of the Messenger here makes it clear that this giving is religious and legislative, not creational and decretal. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, also said in

the authentic hadith:

“He has tasted the sweetness of faith who is content with Allah as his Lord, Islam as his religion, and Muhammad as his Prophet.”

A person should be content with the afflictions Allah decrees for him that are not sins, such as being tried with poverty, illness, humiliation, or harm inflicted by others. Patience in the face of affliction is obligatory. Contentment with it is prescribed, but is it obligatory or recommended? The followers of Ahmad and others hold “two views” on this; the sounder view is that it is recommended, not obligatory.

It is well known that the strongest bonds of faith are love for Allah’s sake and hatred for Allah’s sake. Allah has commanded us to enjoin what is right, love it, be pleased with it, and love those who practise it; and to forbid what is wrong, hate it, be displeased with it, hate those who practise it, and strive against them with our hands, tongues, and hearts. How, then, could we imagine that there is nothing among created things that we should hate and dislike? After mentioning various prohibitions, Allah Most High says:

“The evil of all this is hateful in the sight of your Lord.”

If Allah dislikes these things, although He is the One who decreed them, how could those whom He has commanded to dislike and hate them fail to do so? He is the One who says:

“And He has made disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience hateful to you. Those are the rightly guided.”

Allah Most High also says:

“That is because they followed what angered Allah and disliked His good pleasure, so He rendered their deeds worthless.”

Allah Most High says:

“So when they angered Us, We exacted retribution from them.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Allah became angry with them and cursed them.”

Allah Most High also says:

“They hide from people, but they cannot hide from Allah. He is with them when they plot by night to say things that do not please Him.”

He thus states that some of what is actually said does not please Him.

Allah Most High also says:

“Allah has promised those among you who believe and do righteous deeds that He will surely make them successors in the land, as He made those before them successors, and will surely establish for them their religion which He has approved for them.”

He says:

“And I have approved Islam as your religion.”

And He says:

“If you are grateful, He approves it for you.”

He thus makes clear that He approves the religion He has commanded. If He approved everything, that religion would have no special distinction. The two Sahīh collections report that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“No one has greater jealousy than Allah over His male or female servant committing unlawful sexual intercourse.”

He also said:

“Allah is jealous, and the believer is jealous. Allah’s jealousy is over a servant doing what He has forbidden him.”

Jealousy necessarily entails disliking and hating that which occasions it. This is a vast subject.

Section

As for the “fourth question,” it is his statement: “If the Pen has dried after recording all that is to occur, what is the meaning of His saying, ‘Call upon Me; I will answer you’? If supplication is also among the things destined to occur, what is the benefit of commanding it when it must inevitably occur?”

The answer is this: supplication brings about an answer just as other righteous deeds bring about reward, and just as other causes bring about their effects. Whoever says that supplication is merely a sign and indication that what is sought and requested will be obtained, rather than a cause of it; or that it is purely an act of worship with no effect on whether the desired outcome occurs or not—rather, whatever is attained through supplication is attained

without it—has adopted one of two weak views. For Allah has made the answer dependent upon supplication as an effect depends upon its cause, as in His saying:

“Your Lord says, ‘Call upon Me; I will answer you.’”

The two Sahīh collections report that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“No Muslim calls upon Allah with a supplication involving neither sin nor the severing of family ties but that He grants him one of three things through it: either He hastens the fulfilment of his supplication, stores up an equivalent good for him, or averts an equivalent evil from him.” They said, “O Messenger of Allah, then we shall supplicate abundantly!” He replied, “Allah has still more to give.”

Thus, He made these gifts dependent upon supplication, just as the promised reward and recompense depend upon performing the commanded deed. ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb said: “I do not concern myself with the answer; rather, I concern myself with supplication. When I am inspired to supplicate, the answer comes with it.” There are many similar statements.

Moreover, observable reality demonstrates and clarifies this, just as it demonstrates the same relationship in the case of all other causes. Allah, glorified is He, has told us of this in passages such as His saying:

“Noah certainly called upon Us, and how excellent We are at answering!”

And His saying, Most High:

“And the man of the fish, when he went away in anger, thinking that We would not constrain him. Then he called out in the darkness, ‘There is no god but You. Glory be to You! Indeed, I have been among the wrongdoers.’”

“So We answered him and saved him from distress. And thus do We save the believers.”

And His saying:

“Who is it that answers the distressed when he calls upon Him, removes hardship, and makes you successors on the earth?”

And His words, Most High, concerning Zechariah:

“My Lord, do not leave me childless, though You are the best of inheritors.”

“So We answered him, granted him John, and made his wife fertile for him.”

He also says, Most High:

“When they board a ship, they call upon Allah, devoting their worship sincerely to Him. But when He delivers them safely to land, they immediately associate partners with Him.”

And He says, Most High:

“And among His signs are the ships on the sea, like mountains.”

“If He wills, He stills the wind, leaving them motionless on its surface. Indeed, in that

are signs for everyone who is steadfast and grateful.”

“Or He may destroy them for what they have earned, though He pardons much.”

“And those who dispute Our signs will know that they have no escape.”

He thus tells us that, if He wills, He destroys them. His taking them to task for their sins and His pardoning many of those sins are accompanied by the realization among those who dispute His signs that they have no escape. For in such circumstances, the person who raises specious objections against the proofs of the Lord’s lordship, power, will, and mercy knows that he has no escape from the plight in which he finds himself. This is like His saying in another verse:

“Yet they dispute about Allah, while He is mighty in retribution.”

Knowledge that arises in the soul through compelling circumstances is firmer and more deeply rooted than knowledge produced by mere syllogistic reasoning—which vanishes from people’s minds in such circumstances: Is the Lord a cause whose effects follow necessarily from His essence, so that He does not Himself originate events and cannot bring anything into being or change the world, such that He could be invoked and petitioned? Does He know things both in detail and in general, and have the power to alter circumstances, so that He may be asked to bring about a change from one state to another? Or is He not so, as certain philosophizers and other misguided people claim?

Thus, alongside punishment and pardon from the Possessor of Majesty, those given to disputation and argument come to know that they have no escape from what He has inflicted upon those who disputed His signs, for He is mighty in retribution. We have discussed this and similar matters elsewhere, together with the doctrines and religious beliefs connected with them. The point here is to recognize that supplication and petition are a means of attaining what is sought and requested

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

“Do divine decrees entail wisdom or not? If they entail wisdom, has Allah willed that people do what they actually do? And if His will has preceded their actions, what does it mean for there to be an excuse under these circumstances? Please give us a ruling; may you be rewarded.”

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds. Our Lord, glorified and exalted is He, encompasses everything in knowledge, power, and rule; His mercy and knowledge embrace all things. There is not an atom in the heavens or the earth, nor any meaning whatsoever, that does not testify to Allah Most High’s complete knowledge and mercy and His perfect power and wisdom. He did not create creation without purpose, nor has He done anything in vain. Rather, He is wise in His actions and His words—glorified and exalted is He. Some aspects of His wisdom He has disclosed to some of His creatures, while knowledge of others He has reserved for Himself.

His will is of “two kinds”: the will pertaining to command and legislation, and the will pertaining to decree and ordainment.

The first kind pertains only to acts of obedience, not sins, whether those acts occur or not. As He says:

“Allah intends to make things clear to you, guide you to the ways of those before you, and accept your repentance.”

And He says:

“Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you.”

And as for the second kind—the will pertaining to decree—it encompasses all beings and every event. In this sense, rather than the first, Allah has willed that His creatures do what they actually do. As He, Most High, says:

“Whoever Allah wills to guide, He opens their heart to Islam; and whoever He wills to lead astray, He makes their heart tight and constricted.”

And He says:

“My advice will not benefit you, even if I wish to advise you, if Allah wills to lead you astray. He is your Lord.”

Likewise, Muslims say: “Whatever Allah wills happens, and whatever He does not will does not happen.” There are many similar examples.

This will encompasses acts of obedience and disobedience that actually occur, but not those that do not occur. The first will, by contrast, encompasses acts of obedience whether they occur or not. The blessed person is one from whom Allah wills, by His decree, what He wills for him through His legislation. The wretched servant is one for whom He wills, by His decree, what He does not will for him through His legislation. Judgment proceeds in accordance with these two wills. Whoever views deeds with both these eyes sees clearly; whoever considers divine decree without divine legislation, or divine legislation without divine decree, sees with only one eye. Such were the Quraysh, who said:

“If Allah had willed, neither we nor our forefathers would have associated partners with Him, nor would we have forbidden anything.”

Allah Most High said:

“Likewise, those before them denied the truth until they tasted Our punishment. Say, ‘Do you have any knowledge that you can produce for us? You follow nothing but conjecture, and you do nothing but lie.’”

These people believed that everything Allah willed to exist and occur—this being His decretive will—He had also commanded and approved, without regard to His legislative will. Then they saw that their associating partners with Him without any revealed authorization was among the things Allah had willed to exist. They therefore said: “Then He must have approved and commanded it.” Allah said:

“Likewise, those before them denied”—the revealed laws, with their commands and prohibitions—“until they tasted Our punishment. Say, ‘Do you have any

knowledge that you can produce for us?’”—that Allah has prescribed associating partners with Him and forbidding what you have forbidden.

“You follow,” in this matter, “nothing but conjecture”—namely, your supposition that whatever He has decreed, He has also prescribed. “And you do nothing but lie”—that is, you lie and fabricate, thereby setting His law aside.

“Say, ‘Allah’s is the conclusive argument’”—against His creatures, for He sent them messengers who called them to worship Him alone and follow His law. Nevertheless, had He willed, He would have guided all creatures to follow His law. Yet He bestows His favor upon whomever He wills, guiding them out of His grace and kindness, and withholds it from whomever He wills. For one who bestows a favor may either bestow it or refrain from doing so. His withholding His favor from those He deprives of it is just and equitable, and He has consummate wisdom in doing so.

He punishes His creatures for contravening His command and His legislative will, even though their doing so occurs by His decretive will. For just as disobedience occurs by divine decree, so too does its punishment. Likewise, He, glorified be He, may decree that a servant suffer illnesses that bring pain: the illness is by His decree, and the pain is by His decree.

If a servant says, “It was already willed that I should sin, so I will not be punished,” this is like a sick person saying, “It was already willed that I should become ill, so I will not feel pain”; or saying, “It was already willed that I should eat something hot, so my constitution will not become overheated”; or, “It was already willed that the blow should be struck, so the person struck will not feel pain.” Besides being ignorance, this does not benefit the person who says it. Rather, invoking divine decree as an excuse is a second sin for which he will also be punished.

It was Iblīs who invoked divine decree as an excuse when he said:

“Because You have led me astray, I will surely make evil appealing to them on earth.”

Adam, by contrast, said:

“Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves. If You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers.”

When Allah wills blessedness for someone, He inspires him to say what Adam—peace be upon him—said, or words to that effect.

translated_text:
and whoever He wills to be wretched invokes Iblīs’s excuse or something similar. He is thus like someone seeking refuge from scorching ground in fire.

His likeness is that of a man into whose house a spark flies. Sensible people tell him, “Put it out before it burns down the house!” But he begins saying, “Where did it come from? The wind carried it here, and I am not to blame for this fire.” He continues offering such excuses until the fire blazes up, spreads, and burns down the house and everything in it.

Such is the condition of someone who attributes his sins to divine decree rather than counteracting them by seeking forgiveness and offering apologies. Indeed, his condition is worse, because he himself committed the sin, whereas he had no part in causing the spark.

May Allah, glorified be He, grant us, you, and all our brothers success in doing what He loves and is pleased with. For obedience to Him can only be attained through His help, and disobedience to Him can only be avoided through His protection. And Allah knows best.

translated_text:
He was asked—may Allah sanctify his soul—about divine decrees:

“Do they embody wisdom or not? If they embody wisdom, has He willed what people will do or not? If His will has already preceded their actions, what does it mean for an excuse to exist in such circumstances?”

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds. Yes, Allah has perfect wisdom in His decrees and ordainments, even if He has not made it known to His servants. For Allah possesses knowledge that He has taught His servants—or whomever He wills among them—and knowledge that He has not taught His servants:

“They encompass nothing of His knowledge except what He wills. His Kursī extends over the heavens and the earth, and preserving them does not tire Him.”

He, glorified be He, has willed what His servants will do by His creative will. Thus, the Muslims agree that whatever Allah wills happens, and whatever He does not will does not happen. As He says:

“Whoever Allah wills to guide, He opens his heart to Islam; and whoever He wills to lead astray, He makes his heart tight and constricted.”

And as He says:

“They will continue to differ,”

“except those to whom your Lord has shown mercy; and for this He created them.”

And as He says:

“If Allah had willed, they would not have fought one another, but Allah does whatever He wills.”

And as He says:

“Allah makes firm those who believe

with the firm word in this worldly life and in the Hereafter. Allah leads the wrongdoers astray, and Allah does whatever He wills.”

Yet He has not willed acts of disobedience from those who commit them in the sense of commanding or legislating them, loving or approving them, or prescribing them as religion. Rather, this latter kind of will is as expressed in His words, Exalted is He:

“Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you.”

And His words, Exalted is He:

“Allah wishes to make things clear to you and guide you to the ways of those before you.”

“Allah wishes to turn to you in mercy, but those who follow their desires wish you to deviate far from the right path.”

“Allah wishes to lighten your burdens, for mankind was created weak.”

And He, Exalted is He, says:

“Allah does not intend to impose hardship upon you, but He intends to purify you.”

And He, Exalted is He, says:

“I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me.”

By drawing distinctions and explaining matters in detail, confusion is removed and error dispelled. I have discussed this at appropriate length in several places in my writings on fundamental principles, for this is not the place to elaborate on it.

As for the questioner’s words, “What does it mean for an excuse to exist?” the person who is excused, and knows that he is excused, is someone unable to perform an act despite wishing to do so. Examples include a sick person unable to stand in prayer, fast, or take part in jihad, and a poor person unable to spend, and similar cases. Such people are neither obligated to perform these acts nor punished for omitting them. The same applies to those unable to hear and understand, such as a child, a person of unsound mind, and someone whom the call to Islam has not reached.

translated_text: As for someone who has been made to love committing evil deeds, to choose them and to approve of them, and who consequently commits them, he is neither forced to act against his will nor coerced into doing what he willingly accepts. How, then, can he be called excused? Rather, he should be called deluded. But explaining this fully requires discussing the wisdom underlying creation and command. This is discussed in its proper place, and there is no room for it here. Allah knows best, and may Allah bless Muhammad.

translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām Taqī al-Dīn Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—said:

On the distinctions that make clear how good deeds come from Allah and evil deeds from the self (*)

Allah says:
“Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah.”

He also says:
“Say: My Lord has only forbidden shameful deeds, whether committed openly or secretly,”
up to His words:
“and that you say about Allah what you do not know.”

This excludes prohibition from other things and affirms it for those mentioned. But has He affirmed fear of Allah for the class as a whole, or for every individual who possesses knowledge? Compare the saying, “Only Muslims perform Hajj.” The question is whether the category singled out is a cause or a condition. In this verse and others like it, it is a cause, so the statement applies universally: knowledge of what the messengers warned against necessarily produces fear. Since knowledge necessarily produces the fear that prompts one to do good deeds and abandon evil deeds, and every sinner is ignorant, lacking complete knowledge, what we have stated becomes clear: the root of evil deeds is ignorance and lack of knowledge.

That being so, lack of knowledge is not an existing thing. Rather, it is like the absence of ability, hearing or sight. Nonexistence is not a thing; only what exists is a thing—and Allah is the Creator of all things. Pure nonexistence, therefore, is not attributed to Allah Most High, but it may

This treatise is abridged from al-Hasanah wa-l-Sayyi'ah (Good and Evil), 14/229–425. It does not abridge the entire treatise, but only part of it, beginning at the fifth line of p. 294 and continuing to the end of p. 361. Comparing the abridgment with its source reveals the following points:

1. At 8/205: “The soul by its nature moves him, for it is alive.” At 14/294: “The soul by its nature is changeable, for it is alive.” It appears to me that the correct reading in both places is: “The soul by its nature is in motion.”

4. At 8/212: “The Exalted has said: ‘So call upon Allah, devoting religion sincerely to Him’; ‘Praise be to Allah, Lord of all worlds.’” The correct reading is a single verse, not two: “So call upon Him, devoting religion sincerely to Him. Praise be to Allah, Lord of all worlds,” as at 14/311.

13. At 8/234: “These resembled the People of the Book in what had been altered or abrogated, while those resembled people with no scripture. He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—said: ‘Souls are innately endowed with necessary knowledge of the Creator who created the heavens…’”
I say—the speaker here is Shaykh Nāsir al-Fahd—that the words “resembled people with no scripture” mark the end of the abridgment and occur at 14/361. As for the words “He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—said: ‘Souls are innately endowed…,’” these begin a new quotation from the Shaykh—may Allah have mercy on him—taken from somewhere other than the treatise al-Hasanah wa-l-Sayyi'ah. Allah Most High knows best.

translated_text:
be accompanied by something that exists. Thus, when a person lacks knowledge, his soul naturally impels him, for it is alive (*), and voluntary movement is inseparable from life. Hence the names that most truthfully describe a person are al-Hārith and al-Humām. The hadith states:
“The heart is like a feather cast down,”
and so on. Another hadith states:
“The heart changes more rapidly than a pot at a rolling boil.”

Such being its condition, if Allah guides the soul, He teaches it what benefits it and what harms it, so that it desires what benefits it and abandons what harms it. Allah, glorified be He, has favoured the children of Adam with two things that form the foundation of happiness:

First: Every child is born upon the natural disposition, as recorded in the two Sahīh collections. Muslim also records, from ‘Iyād ibn Himār, a report traced back to the Prophet:
“I created My servants as pure monotheists,”
and the hadith continues. Thus, if left to its natural disposition, the soul would love Allah and worship Him without associating anything with Him. It is corrupted, however, by those devils among humans and jinn who make evil alluring to it. Allah Most High says:
“And when your Lord took from the children of Adam—from their backs—their descendants,”
and the verse continues. The explanation of this verse is set out at length elsewhere.

Second: Allah Most High has granted people general guidance through the reason He has endowed them with, the scriptures He has sent down to them, and the messengers He has sent to them. Allah Most High says:
“Read in the name of your Lord who created,”
up to His words:
“what he did not know.”

Allah Most High also says:
“The Most Merciful taught the Quran, created man, and taught him speech.”

Allah Most High also says:
“Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High, who created and fashioned, and who determined and guided.”

He also says:
“And We guided him to the two ways.”

Within every person, therefore, is that which calls for recognizing the truth and loving it. Allah has guided each person to kinds of knowledge through which he can attain happiness in the Hereafter, and has placed a love for this within his natural disposition.

translated_text:
But a person may turn away from seeking knowledge of what benefits him. This turning away is a privation. Yet will and movement are inseparable from the soul, for it possesses natural life. Its happiness, however, lies in living a beneficial life by worshipping Allah. Whenever it fails to live this life, it is dead, while the natural life it possesses becomes a cause of its torment. Thus, it is neither alive and enjoying life nor dead and relieved of torment. Allah Most High says:

“Then he will neither die therein nor live.”

The recompense corresponds to the deed: since, in this world, he neither lived a beneficial life nor was dead and without sensation, his condition in the Hereafter is likewise.

If the soul knows the truth and desires it, this is part of Allah’s complete favour upon it. Otherwise, its very nature necessarily leads it to have an object of desire and worship other than Allah, as well as evil objects of desire. This state arises from its failure to know Allah and worship Him, and this is a privation.

The Qadariyyah acknowledge this, and acknowledge that Allah created man with a will. However, they regard him as possessing will only potentially, as a capacity—that is, as capable of willing this or that. As for his actually willing this particular thing or that particular thing, they hold that this is not created by Allah. They are mistaken. Rather, Allah is the Creator of all of this, and He is the One who inspired the soul with its wickedness and its piety. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to say:

“O Allah, grant my soul its piety,”

and so on.

Allah, glorified be He, made Abraham and his household leaders who called by His command, and made Pharaoh’s people leaders who called to the Fire. But this … (1) (*) to Allah on two grounds: in terms of its final cause, and in terms of its causal origin:

أَمَّا الْعِلَّةُ الغائية:
 فَإِنَّهُ إنَّمَا خَلَقَهُ لِحِكْمَةِ هُوَ بِاعْتِبَارِهَا خَيْرٌ، وَإِنْ كَانَ شَرًّا إضَافِيًّا، فَإِذَا أُضِيفَ مُفْرَدًا تَوَهَّمَ الْمُتَوَهِّمُ مَذْهَبَ جَهْمِ بْنِ صَفْوَانَ أَنَّ اللَّهَ خَلَقَ الشَّرَّ الْمَحْضَ الَّذِي لَا خَيْرَ فِيهِ لِأَحَدِ، لَا لِحِكْمَةِ وَلَا لِرَحْمَةِ، وَالْكِتَابُ وَالسُّنَّةُ وَالِاعْتِبَارُ يُبْطِلُ هَذَا،
 كَمَا إذَا قِيلَ:
 مُحَمَّدٌ وَأُمَّتُهُ يَسْفِكُونَ الدِّمَاءَ وَيُفْسِدُونَ فِي الْأَرْضِ كَانَ هَذَا ذَمًّا لَهُمْ، وَكَانَ بَاطِلًا، وَإِذَا قِيلَ يُجَاهِدُونَ لِتَكُونَ كَلِمَةُ اللَّهِ هِيَ الْعُلْيَا وَيَقْتُلُونَ مَنْ مَنَعَهُمْ مِنْ ذَلِكَ كَانَ هَذَا مَدْحًا لَهُمْ وَكَانَ حَقًّا.
 فَإِذَا قِيلَ:
 إنَّ الرَّبَّ تَعَالَى حَكِيمٌ رَحِيمٌ أَحْسَنَ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ خَلَقَهُ وَهُوَ أَرْحَمُ الرَّاحِمِينَ، وَالْخَيْرُ بِيَدَيْهِ وَالشَّرُّ لَيْسَ إلَيْهِ، لَا يَفْعَلُ إلَّا خَيْرًا، وَمَا خَلَقَهُ مِنْ أَلَمٍ لِبَعْضِ الْحَيَوَانِ، وَمِنْ أَعْمَالِهِ الْمَذْمُومَةِ، فَلَهُ فِيهِ حِكْمَةٌ عَظِيمَةٌ وَنِعْمَةٌ جَسِيمَةٌ، كَانَ هَذَا حَقًّا وَهُوَ مَدْحٌ لِلرَّبِّ. وَأَمَّا إذَا قِيلَ يَخْلُقُ الشَّرَّ الَّذِي لَا خَيْرَ فِيهِ، وَلَا مَنْفَعَةَ لِأَحَدِ، وَلَا لَهُ فِيهِ حِكْمَةٌ وَلَا رَحْمَةٌ وَيُعَذِّبُ النَّاسَ بِلَا ذَنْبٍ لَمْ يَكُنْ مَدْحًا لَهُ بَلْ الْعَكْسُ، وَقَدْ بَيَّنَّا بَعْضَ مَا فِي خَلْقِ جَهَنَّمَ وَإِبْلِيسَ وَالسَّيِّئَاتِ مِنْ الْحِكْمَةِ وَالرَّحْمَةِ وَمَا لَمْ نَعْلَمْ أَعْظَمُ، وَاَللَّهُ سُبْحَانَهُ وَتَعَالَى يَسْتَحِقُّ الْحَمْدَ وَالْحُبَّ وَالرِّضَا لِذَاتِهِ وَلِإِحْسَانِهِ هَذَا حَمْدُ شُكْرٍ، وَذَاكَ حَمْدٌ مُطْلَقًا. وَقَدْ ذَكَرْنَا فِي غَيْرِ هَذَا أَنَّ مَا خَلَقَهُ فَهُوَ نِعْمَةٌ يَسْتَحِقُّ عَلَيْهَا الشُّكْرَ،
 وَهُوَ مِنْ آلَائِهِ وَلِهَذَا قَالَ فِي آخِرِ سُورَةِ النَّجْمِ:
 
{فَبِأَيِّ آلَاءِ رَبِّكَ تَتَمَارَى}
translated_text:
As for its final cause:

He created it only for a wise purpose in light of which it is good, even though it is evil in relative terms. If evil is attributed to Him in isolation, someone might imagine the doctrine of Jahm ibn Safwān: that Allah created pure evil containing no good for anyone, with no wise or merciful purpose. The Quran, the Sunnah, and reasoned reflection refute this.

For example, saying, “Muhammad and his community shed blood and spread corruption on earth,” would disparage them and would be false. But saying, “They fight so that Allah’s word may be supreme, and kill those who prevent them from achieving that,” would praise them and would be true.

Likewise, the following statement is true and constitutes praise of the Lord: “The Lord Most High is Wise and Merciful. He has perfected everything He created, and He is the Most Merciful of those who show mercy. Good is in His hands, and evil is not ascribed to Him. He does nothing but good. Whatever He has created of pain in some living creatures, or of their blameworthy deeds, contains great wisdom and immense blessing.”

But saying, “He creates evil containing no good or benefit for anyone, with no wisdom or mercy in it, and punishes people without their having sinned,” would not praise Him, but rather the opposite.

We have already explained some of the wisdom and mercy in the creation of Hell, Iblīs, and evil deeds; what we do not know is greater still. Allah, glorified and exalted be He, deserves praise, love, and contentment with Him, both for who He is and for His beneficence. Praise for His beneficence is praise in gratitude, while praise for who He is is unqualified praise.

Elsewhere, we have explained that whatever He has created is a blessing for which He deserves thanks. It is among His favours. Hence He says at the end of Sūrat al-Najm:

“Then which of your Lord’s favours will you doubt?”

original_footnote:
(*) قال الشيخ ناصر بن حمد الفهد (ص ٧١):
والصواب: (ثم التفت إليه فقال: " فَبِأَيِّ آَلَاءِ رَبِّكَ تَتَمَارَى " كما في ١٤/ ٣٠٢، وكما يقتضيه السياق.
translated_text:
And in Sūrat al-Rahmān He mentions:

“Everyone upon the earth will perish,”

and similar statements, after which He says:

“Then which of your Lord’s favours will you both deny?”

A group of scholars offered the following explanation—the wording is al-Baghawī’s. Then, after citing His words,

“They will go back and forth between it and scalding water,”

he said: “Everything Allah, Mighty and Majestic, mentions from His words, ‘Everyone upon the earth will perish,’ onwards consists of admonitions. This is a blessing, because it deters people from sins.”

Others, including al-Zajjāj and Ibn al-Jawzī, explained these verses as meaning: “Then which of your Lord’s favours will you both deny?”—referring to these things, for they are all blessings: they point you to His oneness, and through them He provides you with what sustains you. This is what they said concerning Sūrat al-Rahmān.

Regarding His words,

“Then which of your Lord’s favours will you doubt?”

they said: “Which of your Lord’s blessings, pointing to His oneness, do you call into question?” Another explanation is: “You doubt and dispute.” Ibn ‘Abbās said: “You deny.”

I say: The word tatamārā (“you dispute”) incorporates the meaning of tukadhdhib (“you deny”); hence He made it transitive with tā. It follows the tafā‘ul pattern, derived from mirā (disputation). One says, “We disputed about the crescent moon,” and, “Disputing about the Quran is disbelief.” Such disputation can involve denial and casting doubt.

It is also said that, since the address was directed to them, He said tatamārā (“you dispute”), meaning yatamārawna (“they dispute”), rather than tamtarī (“you doubt”), because the tafā‘ul form involves two parties.

Concerning His words,

“And that a person will have only what he strives for,”

they said: “It has been said that this refers to al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah.” For He said:

“Or has he not been informed of what is in the Scriptures of Moses,”

“and of Abraham, who fulfilled his obligations,”

“that no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another?”

[Then He turned to address him, saying: “And that a person will have only what he strives for.”] (*)

Likewise, He said:

“He created man from clay like pottery,”

“and He created the jinn from a smokeless flame of fire.”

“Then which of your Lord’s favours will you both deny?”

Thus, everything He has created contains kindness towards His servants for which He is to be thanked, and He has in it a wise purpose that pertains to Him
translated_footnote:
(*) Shaykh Nāsir ibn Hamad al-Fahd states (p. 71):
The correct reading is: “Then He turned to address him and said, ‘Then which of your Lord’s favours will you doubt?’” as in 14/302 and as the context requires.

 الْآيَةَ، وَكِلْتَا النِّعْمَتَيْنِ تَحْتَاجُ مَعَ الشُّكْرِ إلَى الصَّبْرِ، أَمَّا الضَّرَّاءُ فَظَاهِرٌ، وَأَمَّا نِعْمَةُ السَّرَّاءِ فَتَحْتَاجُ إلَى الصَّبْرِ عَلَى الطَّاعَةِ فِيهَا،

 اُبْتُلِينَا بِالضَّرَّاءِ فَصَبَرْنَا، وَابْتُلِينَا بِالسَّرَّاءِ فَلَمْ نَصْبِرْ، فَلِهَذَا كَانَ أَكْثَرُ مَنْ يَدْخُلُ الْجَنَّةَ الْمَسَاكِينُ، لَكِنْ لَمَّا كَانَ فِي السَّرَّاءِ اللَّذَّةُ، وَفِي الضَّرَّاءِ الْأَلَمُ، اشْتَهَرَ ذِكْرُ الشُّكْرِ فِي السَّرَّاءِ وَالصَّبْرِ فِي الضَّرَّاءِ،
 قَالَ تَعَالَى:
 
{وَلَئِنْ أَذَقْنَا الْإِنْسَانَ مِنَّا رَحْمَةً ثُمَّ نَزَعْنَاهَا مِنْهُ}
 - إلَى قَوْلِهِ - 
{إلَّا الَّذِينَ صَبَرُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَاتِ}
 الْآيَةَ.
translated_text:
for which He deserves to be praised in His own right. Thus, all created things contain blessings for His servants—including humankind and jinn, addressed in His words:

“Then which of your Lord’s favours will you both deny?”

This is because they are signs through which His servants are guided, pointing to His oneness and the truthfulness of His prophets. Hence He says immediately afterwards:

“This is a warner like the warners of old.”

Some say this refers to Muhammad; others say it refers to the Quran. The two are inseparable. The meaning is: this is a warner who warns of what the earlier messengers and scriptures warned of. His words, “like the warners of old,” mean that it is of their kind. The greatest blessing is therefore the blessing of faith, and every created thing is among the signs through which something of this blessing is attained. Allah Most High says:

“There is certainly a lesson in their stories for people of understanding.”

And He says:

“As insight and a reminder for every servant who turns to Him.”

Whatever befalls a person, if it pleases him, is an evident blessing. If it distresses him, it is also a blessing, because it expiates his sins and he is rewarded for bearing it patiently. It is also a blessing because it contains wisdom and mercy unknown to the servant:

“Perhaps you dislike something which is good for you, and perhaps you love something which is bad for you,”

and the rest of the verse. Both kinds of blessing require patience as well as gratitude. In adversity, the need for patience is obvious. As for the blessing of prosperity, it requires steadfastness in obedience amid that prosperity. As one of the early generations said: “We were tested with adversity and remained patient; we were tested with prosperity but did not remain patient.” This is why most of those who enter Paradise are the poor. However, since prosperity brings pleasure and adversity brings pain, gratitude has commonly been associated with prosperity, and patience with adversity. Allah Most High says:

“And if We give man a taste of mercy from Us, then withdraw it from him”

—up to His words—

“Except those who remain patient and do righteous deeds,”

and the rest of the verse.

" سُورَةِ النَّحْلِ "
، وَتُسَمَّى 
" سُورَةَ النِّعَمِ "
 كَمَا قَالَهُ قتادة وَغَيْرُهُ، وَعَلَى هَذَا فَكَثِيرٌ مِنْ النَّاسِ يَقُولُ الْحَمْدُ أَعَمُّ مِنْ الشُّكْرِ مِنْ جِهَةِ أَسْبَابِهِ؛ فَإِنَّهُ يَكُونُ عَلَى نِعْمَةٍ وَغَيْرِهَا، وَالشُّكْرُ أَعَمُّ مِنْ جِهَةِ أَنْوَاعِهِ فَإِنَّهُ يَكُونُ
translated_text:
Moreover, those enjoying prosperity have greater need of gratitude, while those facing adversity have greater need of patience. Gratitude is obligatory for the former, and patience for the latter. Patience in prosperity, however, may be recommended, and gratitude may be recommended for someone facing adversity. Gratitude and patience can be combined amid both pain and pleasure, though this is a state many find difficult. A fuller discussion belongs elsewhere.

The point is that Allah Most High bestows blessings through all of this, even if most people do not recognize it at first. Allah knows, and you do not know. A person’s sins, however, come from himself. Nevertheless, when accompanied by a good outcome, even these are a blessing. They are also a blessing for someone else because of the lessons he draws from them. An example of this is the saying:

“O Allah, do not make me a cautionary lesson for others, and do not let anyone else benefit more than I do from what You have taught me.”

Among the supplications in the Quran is:

“Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people.”

Likewise, it says:

“And make us leaders for the righteous.”

Make us leaders for those who follow our example, and do not make us a trial for those who go astray through us.

In Arabic, ālā’ means blessings, which also imply power. In the Quran, Allah Most High mentions His signs that demonstrate His power and lordship, His signs that contain His blessings to His servants, and His signs that reveal His wisdom. These are inseparable. Yet the blessing of benefiting from food, drink, dwellings, and clothing is evident to everyone. Hence these are cited as evidence in Surah al-Nahl, also called “the Surah of Blessings,” as Qatāda and others stated.

On this basis, many people say that praise is broader than gratitude in terms of its grounds, since it may be offered for a blessing or for something else, whereas gratitude is broader in terms of its forms, since it is expressed

translated_text:
through the heart, the tongue, and the hand. If, then, every created thing contains a blessing, praise can only be for a blessing. And praise belongs to Allah in every circumstance. Yet this is understood only by those who recognize the blessings within created things. The Jahmiyya and the Jabriyya are far removed from this, as are the Qadariyya, who say: “Wisdom concerns not Him, but only the benefit of created beings.”

Their position therefore leaves room only for gratitude, just as the position of the Jahmiyya leaves room only for power. Power devoid of blessing and wisdom displays nothing praiseworthy. The reality of their doctrine is that He does not deserve praise: His is sovereignty without praise. Likewise, according to the Mu'tazila, His is a kind of praise without sovereignty. According to the early generations, however, His are both sovereignty and praise in their entirety.

Allah Most High says:

“Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him—as do the angels and those endowed with knowledge—while He upholds justice. There is no deity except Him, the Almighty, the All-Wise.”

He alone is worthy of worship, and to Him belong justice, might, and wisdom. These four are affirmed only by the early generations and their followers. Whoever falls short in knowledge of the Sunnah denies the Lord some of what is rightfully His.

The Jahmī-Jabrī affirms neither justice nor wisdom, nor His oneness as the sole object of worship; rather, he affirms only His oneness as Lord. The Mu'tazilī affirms neither His oneness as the sole object of worship, nor justice, might, or wisdom. Even if he says that he affirms some wisdom, understood as pertaining to others rather than Him, that is not wisdom. Anyone who acts, not for a purpose pertaining to himself but for one pertaining to another, is not wise in the judgment of all rational people.

Since praise is offered only for a blessing, it has been established that it is the foremost part of gratitude; it is therefore the beginning of gratitude and praise,

and even when it is offered for both blessing and wisdom, gratitude expressed through deeds is for His blessing, and is worship of Him on account of His divinity, which encompasses His wisdom. Thus, all these matters fall within gratitude. This is why the Quran attaches such great importance to gratitude, rather than to praise alone, since praise is one form of gratitude. Praise, which is gratitude expressed in words, has been prescribed at the beginning of every address, together with the affirmation of Allah’s oneness. Thus, al-Fātiha combines gratitude with the affirmation of His oneness, and prescribed sermons must include both.

The enduring righteous deeds are of two kinds:

“Glory and praise be to Allah” expresses gratitude, declares His freedom from imperfection, and magnifies Him; “There is no deity except Allah” and “Allah is the Greatest” affirm His oneness and greatness.

[Allah Most High has said:

“So call upon Allah, sincerely devoting your religion to Him.”

“All praise belongs to Allah, Lord of all worlds.”] (*)

Is praise confined to matters of choice, as has been said regarding resolve, or is it broader in scope? This requires consideration, but this is not the place for it. An authentic report states that when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, raised his head from bowing, he would say:

“Our Lord, to You belongs all praise, filling heaven, filling the earth, and filling whatever else You will. You are worthy of praise and glory—the truest words a servant has said, and we are all Your servants. None can withhold what You give, and none can give what You withhold; nor can worldly fortune avail its possessor against You.”

This is the wording of the hadith. Ahaqq (“truest”) is a superlative. Some have mistakenly said:

“What the servant says is true.”

This is not sound, for a servant speaks both truth and falsehood. Rather, it is what the Lord says that is true, as He has said:

“The truth—and I speak the truth.”

Ahaqq, however, is the predicate of an omitted subject: that is, “Praise is the truest thing a servant has said.” The hadith thus establishes that praise is the truest thing a servant has said, which is why it is obligatory in every prayer.

translated_text:
If it is said that He creates what is pure evil, this would not inspire His servants to love and praise Him, but rather the opposite. Hence many of these people utter blame and abuse in poetry and prose. Many of their shaykhs and scholars express such sentiments; even when one does not voice them, his heart is filled with them, but he sees no benefit in expressing them, or fears the Muslims. Similar sentiments appear in the poetry of some shaykhs, and they advance the arguments of Iblīs and his followers against Allah.

This contradicts how He describes Himself in His words:

“Your Lord is never unjust to His servants.”

“We did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves.”

Thus the words, “The truest words a servant has said,” imply that praising Him is the truest thing a servant has said, because He, glory be to Him, does nothing but good. And He, glory be to Him, … (1) (*).

And man’s soul is naturally active in a manner that inevitably involves evil, in accordance with consummate wisdom and as an abundant blessing.

If it is asked, “Why, then, did He not create it differently?” the answer is that this would have meant creating a being other than man, and the wise purpose of his creation would not have been fulfilled. This was the angels’ question when they said:

“Will You place in it someone who will spread corruption there and shed blood?”

—through to His words—

“Indeed, I know what you do not know.”

He thus knew aspects of the wisdom in creating this being that the angels did not know. How, then, could individual human beings know them? And the human soul was created as the Most High has said:
