translated_text:
whatever is subject to His will is also subject to His power, for whatever Allah wills comes to pass, and nothing comes into being except through His power. Likewise, whatever exists through His power is also subject to His will, for nothing comes into being except through His power and will. Whatever can be subject to His power can also be subject to His will, and vice versa; whatever cannot be subject to one cannot be subject to the other. Hence His saying:

“Indeed, Allah has power over all things.”

The word shay’ (thing) was originally the verbal noun of shā’a, yashā’u, shay’an (to will), just as naylan is the verbal noun of nāla, yanālu (to obtain). The verbal noun was then used in place of the object: what is willed was called a shay’, just as what is obtained is called nayl. Thus they speak of nayl al-ma‘din (the yield of a mine). Similarly, what is brought about by power is called qudra (power), and what is created is called khalq (creation). Thus His saying:

“has power over all things”

means that He has power over everything He wills. This includes what He has willed and has therefore come into existence, and what He has not willed but which is an object of will in knowledge, in the sense that it is capable of being willed. His words:

“over all things”

include whatever is a thing both in external reality and in knowledge, or in knowledge alone. This excludes what cannot be subject to the will—namely, the Most High, the True One, and His attributes, or what is intrinsically impossible. None of these falls within the general scope of the statement.

For this reason, people have agreed that what is intrinsically impossible is not a thing, but they have disagreed concerning what does not exist yet could exist. A group of speculative theologians among the Mu‘tazila and the Rāfida, together with some misguided Sufis who agreed with them, held that it is a thing in external reality because will and power relate to it. This is an error. It is merely known to Allah and, if it is among the things that will come into existence, willed by Him. In itself, it has neither death nor existence nor any reality whatsoever. Rather, its existence, its established being, and its actuality are one and the same. Its essence and reality in the external world are identical with its existence, actuality, and established being; there are not in

Once this is understood, the present question rests upon “the question of Allah’s speech and other such attributes of His”: are they eternal attributes inseparable from His essence, none of which relates to His action, will, or power? Or should it be said that He speaks when He wills and remains silent when He wills, and that these are also attributes of action? Our companions and other adherents of Ahl al-Sunnah hold two positions on this.

I said: This supplication offered by Shaykh Abū Zakariyyā is transmitted from Imam Ahmad, and that is where the shaykh learned it—Allah knows best. He had great love for Ahmad and the reports transmitted from him, and devoted much attention to accounts of his virtues and life. They have included this supplication in accounts of his virtues, and the hadith master al-Bayhaqī narrated it in Manāqib Ahmad (The Virtues of Ahmad). Shaykh Abū Zakariyyā was authorized to transmit this work by the hadith master ‘Abd al-Qādir al-Ruhāwī. They heard it read before him, with his transmission from al-Ruhāwī being by authorization.

Al-Bayhaqī said: Among the reports Abū ‘Abd Allāh, the hadith master, conveyed to me by authorization was the following: Abū Bakr Muhammad ibn Ismā‘īl ibn al-‘Abbās related to me: Abū Muhammad ‘Abd Allāh ibn Ishāq ibn Ibrāhīm al-Baghawī related to me: Abū Ja‘far Muhammad ibn Ya‘qūb al-Saffār related to us, saying:

We were with Ahmad ibn Hanbal and said, “Pray to Allah for us.” He said:

“O Allah, You know that we know that, in most respects, You are toward us as we would wish. So make us toward You as You love.”

He said: Then I sat for a while, and someone said to him, “Abū ‘Abd Allāh, give us more.” He said:

“O Allah, we ask You by the power with which You said to the heavens and the earth, ‘Come, willingly or unwillingly,’ and they said, ‘We come willingly.’ O Allah, guide us to what pleases You. O Allah, we seek refuge in You from being in need of anyone but You, and we seek refuge in You from being humbled before anyone but You. O Allah, do not give us so much that we transgress, nor give us so little that we forget

translated_text:
What do you scholars of Islam, firmly rooted in theology and eminent in the science of legal rulings, say? May the All-Knowing greet you with honour in the foremost places of the Abode of Peace, and may the Ever-Sustaining favour you with clarifying what minds find obscure concerning the creed of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿah. May Allah bless the souls of their predecessors, increase the numbers of their successors, and sustain them with every kind of gracious favour.

Concerning the belief that the voluntary acts of servants occur through Allah Most High’s creation and the servant’s creation: what exactly is the servant’s acquisition of an act? Furthermore, does this acquisition have any effect in bringing the act into existence, or does it not?

If it does, the servant becomes a partner of the Creator in creating the act. He would then be not one who acquires an act, but a partner who creates—and the righteous people of the Sunnah are innocent of this claim. If it has no effect in bringing the act into existence, then the act has been brought into existence entirely by the True One, glorified and exalted is He, with the servant having no part in it. This necessarily entails compulsion, which sweeps away the very foundation of religious law. Yet the adherents of the radiant Sunnah and the clear path shun this monstrous assertion and defective belief. Nor, on that basis, could obedience and disobedience, disbelief and faith be attributed to the servant such that he deserves wrath or good pleasure.

How, then, are we to proceed along the straight path and the sound way, O guides who show the way? Both extremes flanking the middle course are blameworthy. Give us an explanation that frees our minds from these shackles and heals our hearts of this intractable disease. May He to whom belong the attributes of perfection strengthen you with the Holy Spirit.

translated_text:
The shaykh, imam and godly scholar, into whose heart divine light had been cast, who united in himself manifold virtues, the mufti of the Muslims, Taqī al-Dīn Ahmad ibn Abd al-Halīm ibn Abd al-Salām ibn Abī al-Qāsim ibn Muhammad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—replied as follows. He said, may Allah be pleased with him:

The answer, in brief, is that acquisition is an act that brings its doer benefit or harm, as Allah Most High says:

“Each soul will have the good it has earned and will bear the evil it has earned.”

He, glorified is He, thus explains that a soul’s acquisition counts either in its favour or against it. People say, “So-and-so has gained wealth, praise or honour,” since he benefits from these things. Because servants attain perfection and become upright through their acts, having initially been created deficient, it is valid to affirm this causal relationship: their perfection and uprightness result from their acts.

As for Allah, glorified and exalted is He, His acting and making proceed from His perfection and majesty. His acts proceed from His names and attributes and are derived from them, as He, glorified and exalted is He, says:

“I am al-Rahmān (the Most Merciful). I created al-rahim (the bond of kinship) and derived its name from My name.”

The servant’s names and attributes, by contrast, result from his acts. He comes to be called knowledgeable or accomplished after knowledge or accomplishment has arisen within him.

This is where the Qadariyyah went astray: they likened His acts—glorified and exalted is He, far above what they say—to the acts of servants. Thus, it was they who likened Allah to His creation with regard to acts. They believed that whatever was good on their part was necessarily good on His part, and whatever was bad on their part was necessarily bad on His part, according to the measure of their knowledge and reason. Or did they not know that those acts were good on their part only because they lead to their well-being

and success, and bad because they lead to their corruption? Allah, glorified is He, is exalted above being affected by anything unbefitting His glory.

As for his question:

“Is it causally effective in bringing the act into existence, or not?”

This must be discussed in two respects.

(The first)

Taken at face value, this question is unsound, because the servant’s acquisition is his very act and deed. How, then, can one ask whether his acquisition has a causal effect upon his act, or whether something can have a causal effect upon itself? Even if someone supposes that acquisition means engaging in something, undertaking it directly, intending it and attempting it, these are all acts to which the same discussion applies as to bodily acts such as standing and sitting.

I think the questioner understood it in this sense and seized upon the statement of those who say:

“The servant’s act comes about through Allah’s creation—mighty and majestic is He—and the servant’s acquisition.”

The precise formulation is:

“The servant’s act is Allah’s creation—mighty and majestic is He—and the servant’s acquisition.”

An exception would be if the intended meaning were that his bodily acts come about through his acquisition—that is, through his intention and deliberate pursuit. This would amount to saying that his outward acts come about through his inward acts.

It is hardly surprising that this question has not been formulated afresh, for it is a place where feet slip and minds go astray. A well-posed question is half of knowledge, if the questioner has formed a clear conception of the question and seeks only to affirm or deny the matter in question. Were a complete conception attained, one of the two alternatives would be known.

translated_text:
The second respect:

Clarifying the question and its answer. The question is this: Does the servant’s created power have a causal effect in bringing his act into existence? If it does, this entails associating partners with Allah; otherwise, it entails compulsion. This is a familiar issue that has given pause to many investigators, researchers, people of insight, and those possessing spiritual unveiling. Most of them have understood it correctly, but few have expressed it clearly.

We therefore say:

“Causal efficacy” is a term with several meanings. It may mean independently originating something and bringing it into being unaided. If this is the kind of power intended when speaking of the causal efficacy of the servant’s power, then—Allah forbid!—no Sunni has professed it. Rather, it is attributed to the people of misguidance.

If causal efficacy means some kind of assistance, whether concerning one of the act’s qualities or one of its aspects, as many affirmationist theologians have maintained, this too is false, for the same reasons that invalidate such causal efficacy with respect to the act itself. There is no difference between attributing independent causal efficacy to something other than Allah, glorified is He, with respect to a speck or an elephant. Is this anything but a lesser degree of associating partners with Allah, even though the proponent of this view intended only to arrive at the truth?

If, however, causal efficacy means that the act passes from nonexistence into existence through the mediation of the newly created power—in the sense that this created power is a cause and an intermediary through which Allah, glorified and exalted is He, creates the act—just as He creates vegetation through water, rain through clouds, and all effects and created things through intermediaries and causes, then this is true.

and this is the case with all causes and effects. Attributing causal efficacy to the servant’s power in this sense is not associating partners with Allah; otherwise, affirming any causes at all would be associating partners with Him.

The All-Wise, the All-Aware has said:

“Then through it We sent down water, and through it We brought forth every kind of fruit.”

“Then through it We caused gardens of beauty to grow.”

And He, exalted is He, has said:

“Fight them; Allah will punish them by your hands.”

He thus made clear that He is the One who inflicts the punishment, while our hands are causes, instruments, intermediaries, and means by which the punishment reaches them. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“If any of you dies, be sure to inform me so that I may pray over him, for through my prayer over him Allah will bestow blessing and mercy.”

It is Allah, glorified is He, who bestows mercy, and it is through the prayer of our Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that He bestows it. With this clarification, we say:

Allah, glorified is He, creates bodily acts through acts of the heart. In this sense, one of these two acquired acts has a causal effect on the other, and that acquired act forms part of the power involved in the second acquired act.

For power here means nothing other than that through which the act necessarily occurs: intention, will, soundness of the organs, the faculties created in the limbs, and so forth. It must therefore accompany the act and cannot precede it in time. As for the capacity upon which commands and prohibitions depend, that is another matter, which is not our subject here.

وَبِالتَّمْيِيزِ بَيْنَ هَاتَيْنِ الْقُدْرَتَيْنِ يَظْهَرُ لَك قَوْلُ مَنْ قَالَ:

 الْأَفْعَالُ كُلُّهَا تَكْلِيفُ مَا لَا يُطَاقُ، وَمَنْ مَنَعَ ذَلِكَ؛

 بِهِ فَعَلَ وَبِهِ صَنَعَ - وَلِلَّهِ الْمَثَلُ الْأَعْلَى - فَإِنَّ الْأَسْبَابَ بِيَدِ الْعَبْدِ لَيْسَتْ مِنْ فِعْلِهِ وَهُوَ مُحْتَاجٌ إلَيْهَا لَا يَتَمَكَّنُ إلَّا بِهَا وَاَللَّهُ سُبْحَانَهُ خَلَقَ الْأَسْبَابَ وَمُسَبَّبَاتِهَا وَجَعَلَ خَلْقَ الْبَعْضِ شَرْطًا وَسَبَبًا فِي خَلْقِ غَيْرِهِ وَهُوَ مَعَ ذَلِكَ غَنِيٌّ عَنْ الِاشْتِرَاطِ وَالتَّسَبُّبِ وَنَظَمَ بَعْضَهَا بِبَعْضِ لَكِنْ لِحِكْمَةِ تَتَعَلَّقُ بِالْأَسْبَابِ وَتَعُودُ إلَيْهَا وَاَللَّهُ عَزِيزٌ حَكِيمٌ.
وَأَمَّا قَوْلُهُ:
 إذَا نَفَيْنَا التَّأْثِيرَ لَزِمَ انْفِرَادُ اللَّهِ سُبْحَانَهُ بِالْفِعْلِ. وَلَزِمَ الْجَبْرُ، وَطَيُّ بِسَاطِ الشَّرْعِ الْأَمْرُ وَالنَّهْيُ.
 فَنَقُولُ:
 إنْ أَرَدْت بِالتَّأْثِيرِ الْمَنْفِيِّ التَّأْثِيرَ عَلَى سَبِيلِ الِانْفِرَادِ فِي نَفْسِ الْفِعْلِ أَوْ فِي شَيْءٍ مِنْ صِفَاتِهِ فَلَقَدْ قُلْت الْحَقَّ وَإِنْ كَانَ بَعْضُ أَهْلِ الِاسْتِنَانِ يُخَالِفُك فِي الْقِسْمِ الثَّانِي. وَإِنْ أَرَدْت بِهِ أَنَّ الْقُدْرَةَ وُجُودُهَا كَعَدَمِهَا وَأَنَّ الْفِعْلَ لَمْ يَكُنْ بِهَا
translated_text:
By distinguishing between these two kinds of power, you will understand the statements of those who say, “Power accompanies the act,” and those who say, “It precedes it”; those who say, “All acts entail imposing what is beyond one’s capacity,” and those who reject this. You will also grasp the subtleties underlying these positions.

If this explanation remains unclear to you, consider an example from your own experience. When you write with a pen, strike with a stick, or shape wood with an adze, does the pen become your partner, or is any part of the act itself or its attributes ascribed to it? Would it be right, on the other hand, to disregard its effect, dismiss it altogether, and treat its existence as no different from its absence? Or should one say, “He acted through it and accomplished his work through it”?

And to Allah belongs the highest description. The means at the servant’s disposal are not of his own making, and he needs them: he can act only through them. Allah, glorified is He, however, created the causes and their effects, making the creation of some a condition and a cause for the creation of others. Yet He has no need of conditions or causal means. He has linked them to one another for a wise purpose connected with the causes and pertaining to them. Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.

As for his statement, “If we deny causal efficacy, it follows that Allah, glorified is He, alone acts. Compulsion necessarily follows, and the entire framework of the revealed Law—commands and prohibitions—is swept away,” we reply:

If by the causal efficacy you deny you mean independent efficacy with respect to the act itself or any of its attributes, then you have indeed spoken the truth, although some adherents of the Sunnah disagree with you concerning the second category. But if you mean that the existence of power is no different from its absence, and that the act did not occur through it

{كَذَلِكَ قَالَ الَّذِينَ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ مِثْلَ قَوْلِهِمْ فَاللَّهُ يَحْكُمُ بَيْنَهُمْ}

translated_text:
and was not accomplished through it, then this is false, as explained above. Compulsion does not then follow. Rather, the framework of the revealed Law is fully established, knowledge of commands and prohibitions is disseminated, and Allah’s argument is conclusive.

It has thus become clear to you that affirming or denying causal efficacy without qualification, without distinguishing the possibilities and explaining what efficacy means, amounts to embracing ignorance and holding misguided beliefs. Truly did someone say:

“Most disagreement among rational people arises from using the same terms for different meanings.”

It has also become clear to you that the relationship between the created act and created power is that of causes to their effects. This encompasses everything Allah Most High has created in the heavens and the earth, in this world and the Hereafter. Believing that causes operate independently is to enter into misguidance, while denying their effects and disregarding them is to embrace the impossible. Human power does, however, have a distinctive character that other causes do not, as we shall briefly indicate, if Allah Most High wills.

After this explanation, you may perhaps say:

“I do not understand causes; I remain confined to this dichotomy and the demand to choose one of its two alternatives.”

If you say this, multitudes of misguided people have said it before you:

“Those without knowledge have likewise said the same as they did; Allah will judge between them.”

Your position here is a crossroads leading either to Paradise or to the Fire. It is therefore explained to you again that causes have an effect insofar as they are causes, like the effect of a pen, but have no effect in the sense of originating and creating. We offer you examples so that you may understand the true situation. It is explained to you that affirming causes as originators is to associate partners with Allah, whereas affirming them as interconnected causes is precisely what it means to uphold Allah’s oneness. Perhaps Allah will cast into your heart a light by which you may see this

explanation.

“And whoever Allah does not grant light has no light.”

If you say: “Affirming power as a cause is, in reality, to deny its efficacy. Why, then, is the act attributed to the servant? Why is he commanded and forbidden, rewarded and punished? Is this anything but sheer compulsion? If you liken human power to the writer’s pen and the striker’s stick, have you ever seen a pen rewarded or a stick punished?”

I now say to you: Allah willing, your guidance is assured through your Master’s aid, even if your insight into the secrets of divine decree amounts to no more than something like a faint imprint. Listen with an attentive heart; perhaps Allah will sustain you with His support.

Know that the servant truly acts, possesses a real will, has a firm intention, and possesses power suited to action. The Quran explicitly affirms the will of human beings in numerous verses, such as His words:

“For whoever among you wills to take a straight path.”

“But you do not will unless Allah wills, the Lord of all worlds.”

“So whoever wills may take a path to his Lord.”

“So whoever wills may heed it.”

“But they will not heed it unless Allah wills. He alone is worthy of being feared and worthy of granting forgiveness.”

It also explicitly affirms human action throughout the Quran: “they work,” “they do,” “they believe,” “they disbelieve,” “they reflect,” “they observe,” and “they fear Allah.”

Just as we have distinguished ourselves from the Magians of this community by affirming that He, Most High, is the Creator, we have distinguished ourselves from the proponents of compulsion by affirming that the servant is an acquirer of acts, an agent, a maker, and a doer. Compulsion, in the intelligible sense rejected by the early generations of this community and the scholars of the Sunnah, is for an action to be imposed upon something without intention or will

translated_text:
or choice, like the movement of trees when the winds blow, or the movement of … (1) caused by closing the hands. Comparable instances in human beings are the movements of someone suffering from fever, paralysis, or tremors. Every rational person recognizes an obvious difference between a person’s standing, sitting, praying, engaging in jihad, committing illicit sexual intercourse, or stealing, and the trembling of a paralytic or the shivering of someone with a fever. We know that, in the former case, the person has the power to act, intends the act, and chooses it, whereas in the latter he has no power over it, neither intends it nor chooses it.

Jahm and his followers, the “Jabriyyah” (proponents of compulsion), are reported to have claimed that all human acts belong to a single category. This position is plainly false. It is precisely the distinction between these two categories that divides acts into voluntary and involuntary, with commands and prohibitions applying only to voluntary acts. Neither revealed laws nor the words of any wise person contain a command directing a blind man to dot a copy of the Quran, a person unable to walk to run, or someone with a fever to remain motionless, or anything similar. Although people have differed over whether such commands are admissible on rational or revealed grounds, people of sound reason, of every persuasion, unanimously rule out their actual occurrence.

If it is said:

“Granted that the act I intended and chose occurs through my will and intention, are not that intention and that will themselves created by Allah Most High? If He creates that which necessitates the act, is it possible to refrain from acting while that necessitating cause exists? At most, the difference is that the first is compulsion without the mediation of the servant’s will, whereas this is compulsion mediated through his will.”

فَإِنْ قُلْت:

translated_text:
We reply:

The compulsion we deny is the first kind, as we have explained. As for affirming the second kind, those who adhere to the Sunnah and transmitted reports, and those endowed with understanding and insight, have no doubt about it. Nevertheless, it is not called “compulsion,” lest it be confused with the first kind and immediately bring that meaning to mind. It may sometimes be called compulsion when there is no risk of confusion and the intended meaning is understood. In his well-known supplication invoking blessings upon the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

“O Allah, Spreader of the expanses and Creator of the lofty heavens, Compeller of hearts according to their innate dispositions, whether to wretchedness or bliss.”

He thus explained that Allah, glorified is He, compels hearts according to the disposition upon which He created them, whether wretchedness or bliss. This second disposition is not the original disposition. Both dispositions have been used to explain the Prophet’s saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Every child is born upon the natural disposition.”

Interpreting it in terms of the first disposition is straightforward. Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazī—one of the most distinguished and eminent Successors in Medina, sometimes ranked above most of them—expressed this when explaining His name “the Compeller.” He said: “He compelled His servants to what He willed.” This has also been reported from others.

The testimony of the Quran and hadith, together with what those endowed with insight and rigorous reasoning perceive, makes this utterly clear: Allah, glorified and exalted is He, turns His servants’ hearts and directs them, inspires them with their wickedness and their piety, and sends down the inexorable decree from the Almighty, the All-Wise, upon the hearts of all people in less than the blink of an eye, so that their limbs move in accordance with what has been decreed for them and against them. This is clear to everyone except those whose sight and hearts Allah has blinded.

If you say:

“On this understanding, having abandoned the conception of compulsion that they denied and refuted, and holding firmly to what they stated and explained, I ask you: how are reward and punishment based

I reply—and Allah is the Guide to the straight path:

Know that Allah Most High created the servant’s action as a cause that produces praiseworthy or blameworthy effects. A righteous deed—such as a prayer performed with inward and outward attentiveness, sincerity, mindfulness of Allah, and understanding of the good words and righteous deeds upon which it is founded—is immediately followed by light in his heart, ease in his breast, tranquillity in his soul, increased knowledge, firmer certainty, and greater strength of understanding. Other effects include bodily strength, radiance in his face, restraint from indecency and wrongdoing, love for him being placed in people’s hearts, protection from affliction, and further things that He knows but we do not. These effects—the light, knowledge, certainty, and so forth that he has attained—are themselves causes leading to further, higher effects, whether of the same kind or of a different kind, and so on.

Hence it has been said:

“Part of the reward for a good deed is another good deed after it, and part of the punishment for an evil deed is another evil deed after it.”

Likewise, an evil deed—lying, for example—brings immediate punishment upon its perpetrator: darkness and hardness in his heart, constriction in his breast, hypocrisy, turmoil, forgetting what he has learned, the closing of a door to knowledge he had been seeking, diminished certainty and understanding, darkness in his face, hatred for him in people’s hearts, and greater boldness in committing another sin, whether of the same kind or a different kind, and so on—unless Allah comes to his aid with His mercy.

translated_text:
These effects produced by deeds are themselves reward and punishment. Deeds lead to these effects and bring them about just as all the causes that Allah—glorified and exalted is He—has established lead to their effects. When a person eats or drinks, his thirst is quenched and his hunger satisfied. Allah—glorified and exalted is He—has firmly linked the quenching of thirst and the satisfaction of hunger to drinking and eating. Yet, if He willed not to satisfy a person’s hunger or quench his thirst despite his eating and drinking, He would do so: by giving the food no efficacy, by placing a counteracting force in the recipient, or by whatever means He wills—glorified and exalted is He. And if He willed to satisfy his hunger and quench his thirst without eating or drinking, or through eating something unusual, He would do so.

The same applies, in exact parallel, to deeds and their rewards and punishments. Reward is called thawāb because it returns (yathūbu) to the doer from his deed. Punishment is called ‘iqāb because it follows (ya‘qubu) the deed—that is, it comes after it. If Allah willed not to reward him for that deed—whether by giving the deed no property that leads to reward, by the presence of causes that prevent that reward, or otherwise—He would do so, glorified and exalted is He. The same applies to punishments.

To explain: eating and drinking themselves take place through the servant’s choice and will, a will that is itself also brought about by Allah—glorified and exalted is He. Yet the servant has no part whatsoever in bringing about the satisfaction of hunger that follows eating. Even if he wished to prevent that satisfaction after undertaking the causes that produce it, he would be unable to do so. Likewise, the deed itself takes place through his will and choice; but if he wished to avert its effect and reward after the cause producing them had come into existence, he would be unable to do so.

 وَخَلَقَ أَعْمَالَهُمْ وَسَاقَهُمْ بِتِلْكَ الْأَعْمَالِ إلَى رِضْوَانِهِ وَكَذَلِكَ أَهْلُ النَّارِ كَمَا قَالَ:
 الصَّادِقُ الْمَصْدُوقُ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ لَمَّا قِيلَ: لَهُ 
{أَلَا نَدَعُ الْعَمَلَ وَنَتَّكِلُ عَلَى الْكِتَابِ؟
 فَقَالَ:
 لَا اعْمَلُوا فَكُلٌّ مُيَسَّرٌ لِمَا خُلِقَ لَهُ. أَمَّا مَنْ كَانَ مِنْ أَهْلِ السَّعَادَةِ فَيُيَسَّرُ لِعَمَلِ أَهْلِ السَّعَادَةِ وَأَمَّا مَنْ كَانَ مِنْ أَهْلِ الشَّقَاوَةِ فَيُيَسَّرُ لِعَمَلِ أَهْلِ الشَّقَاوَةِ}
 . فَبَيَّنَ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَنَّ السَّعِيدَ قَدْ يُيَسَّرُ لِلْعَمَلِ الَّذِي يَسُوقُهُ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى بِهِ إلَى السَّعَادَةِ وَكَذَلِكَ الشَّقِيُّ. وَتَيْسِيرُهُ لَهُ هُوَ نَفْسُ إلْهَامِهِ ذَلِكَ الْعَمَلَ وَتَهْيِئَةُ أَسْبَابِهِ وَهَذَا هُوَ تَفْسِيرُ خَلْقِ أَفْعَالِ الْعِبَادِ فَنَفْسُ خَلْقِ ذَلِكَ الْعَمَلِ هُوَ السَّبَبُ الْمُفْضِي إلَى السَّعَادَةِ أَوْ الشَّقَاوَةِ. وَلَوْ شَاءَ لَفَعَلَهُ بِلَا عَمَلٍ بَلْ هُوَ فَاعِلُهُ فَإِنَّهُ يُنْشِئُ لِلْجَنَّةِ خَلْقًا لِمَا يَبْقَى فِيهَا مِنْ الْفَضْلِ.
 يَبْقَى أَنْ يُقَالَ:
 فَالْحِكْمَةُ الْكُلِّيَّةُ الَّتِي اقْتَضَتْ مَا اقْتَضَتْهُ مِنْ الْأَسْبَابِ الْأُوَلِ
translated_text:
Such are Allah Most High’s wisdom and will regarding all causes in this world and the Hereafter. Yet knowledge of the deeds that benefit or harm a person in the Hereafter lies, for the most part, beyond the reach of created minds. The same is true of the servants’ destiny and final abode after they depart this world. Allah—glorified and exalted is He—therefore sent His messengers as bearers of glad tidings and warnings, and revealed His books, so that people would have no argument against Allah after the messengers. His wisdom in this parallels His wisdom in creating all causes and their effects. This is only because His eternal knowledge, His unfailing will, and His irresistible power have determined what they have determined and necessitated what they have necessitated: that certain people should enter Paradise through deeds of theirs that lead necessarily to it.

He created their deeds and, through those deeds, led them to His good pleasure. The same applies to the people of the Fire. Thus the truthful one whose truthfulness is confirmed—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—was asked, “Should we not give up acting and rely on the written decree?”

He replied: “No. Act, for everyone is enabled to do that for which he was created. Whoever is destined for bliss will be enabled to perform the deeds of those destined for bliss, and whoever is destined for misery will be enabled to perform the deeds of those destined for misery.”

He—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—thus explained that the one destined for bliss may be enabled to perform the deed through which Allah Most High leads him to bliss. The same applies to the one destined for misery. Enabling him to perform it consists precisely in inspiring him to do that deed and preparing the means for it. This is what is meant by the creation of the servants’ acts: the very creation of that deed is the cause leading to bliss or misery. If He willed, He would bring this about without deeds. Indeed, He does so, for He creates people for Paradise to occupy the space remaining in it.

It remains to ask: what, then, of the all-encompassing wisdom that determined what it did regarding the first causes

original_text: وَحَقَائِقِ مَا الْأَمْرُ صَائِرٌ إلَيْهِ فِي الْعَوَاقِبِ وَالتَّخْصِيصَاتُ وَالتَّمْيِيزَاتُ الْوَاقِعَةُ فِي الْأَشْخَاصِ وَالْأَعْيَانِ إلَى غَيْرِ ذَلِكَ مِنْ كُلِّيَّاتِ الْقَدَرِ الَّتِي لَا تَخْتَصُّ بِمَسْأَلَةِ خَلْقِ أَفْعَالِ الْعِبَادِ. وَلَيْسَ هَذَا الِاسْتِفْتَاءُ مَعْقُودًا لَهَا وَتَفْسِيرُ جُمَلِ ذَلِكَ لَا يَلِيقُ بِهَذَا الْمَوْضِعِ. فَضْلًا عَنْ بَعْضِ تَفْصِيلِهِ. وَيَكْفِي الْعَاقِلُ أَنْ يَعْلَمَ أَنَّ اللَّهَ عَزَّ وَجَلَّ عَلِيمٌ حَكِيمٌ رَحِيمٌ بَهَرَتْ الْأَلْبَابَ حِكْمَتُهُ وَوَسِعَتْ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ رَحْمَتُهُ. وَأَحَاطَ بِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ عِلْمُهُ وَأَحْصَاهُ لَوْحُهُ وَقَلَمُهُ وَأَنَّ لِلَّهِ تَعَالَى فِي قَدَرِهِ سِرًّا مَصُونًا وَعِلْمًا مَخْزُونًا احْتَرَزَ بِهِ دُونَ جَمِيعِ خَلْقِهِ وَاسْتَأْثَرَ بِهِ عَلَى جَمِيعِ بَرِيَّتِهِ؛ وَإِنَّمَا يَصِلُ بِهِ أَهْلُ الْعِلْمِ وَأَرْبَابُ وِلَايَتِهِ إلَى جُمَلٍ مِنْ ذَلِكَ وَقَدْ لَا يُؤْذَنُ لَهُمْ فِي ذِكْرٍ مَا وَرُبَّمَا كَلَّمَ النَّاسَ فِي ذَلِكَ عَلَى قَدْرِ عُقُولِهِمْ وَقَدْ سَأَلَ مُوسَى وَعِيسَى وَعُزَيْرٌ رَبَّنَا - تَبَارَكَ وَتَعَالَى - عَنْ شَيْءٍ مِنْ سِرِّ الْقَدَرِ وَأَنَّهُ لَوْ شَاءَ أَنْ يُطَاعَ لَأُطِيعَ وَأَنَّهُ مَعَ ذَلِكَ يُعْصَى فَأَخْبَرَهُمْ - سُبْحَانَهُ وَتَعَالَى - أَنَّ هَذَا سِرُّهُ. وَفِي هَذَا الْمَقَامِ تَاهَتْ عُقُولُ كَثِيرٍ مِنْ الْخَلَائِقِ وَفِيهِ ضَلَّ الْقَائِلُونَ بِقِدَمِ الْعَالَمِ، وَأَنَّ صَانِعَهُ مُوجِبٌ بِذَاتِهِ وَمُقْتَضِي بِنَفْسِهِ اقْتِضَاءَ الْعِلَّةِ لِلْمَعْلُولِ وَأَنَّهُ لَيْسَ فِي الْإِمْكَانِ أَبْدَعُ مِمَّا صَنَعَ وَدَبَّ بَعْضُ هَذَا الدَّاءِ إلَى بَعْضِ أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ وَأَتْبَاعِ الرُّسُلِ فَقَدْ قَرَّرُوا انْحِصَارَ الْمُمْكِنِ فِي الْمَوْجُودِ وَكُلُّ ذَلِكَ طَلَبًا لِلِاسْتِرَاحَةِ مِنْ مُؤْمِنَةٍ تَعْلِيلِ الْأَفْعَالِ الْإِلَهِيَّةِ وَوُجُودِ الْأَسْبَابِ الْحَادِثَةِ لِلْأُمُورِ الْحَادِثَةِ وَعَلَّلَهُ أَهْلُ الْقَدَرِ بِعِلَلِهِمْ الْعَائِلَةِ فِي التَّعْدِيلِ وَالتَّجْوِيزِ وَوُجُوبِ رِعَايَةِ الصَّالِحِ
translated_text:
and the realities of ultimate outcomes, the particular allocations and distinctions made among individuals and concrete entities, and the other universal aspects of divine decree that are not confined to the question of the creation of the servants’ acts? This request for a ruling does not concern those matters, and this is not the place to explain even their broad outlines, let alone any of their details.

It suffices a person of understanding to know that Allah—mighty and majestic—is All-Knowing, All-Wise, and Merciful: His wisdom has dazzled minds, His mercy encompasses everything, His knowledge embraces everything, and His Tablet and Pen have recorded it all. Allah Most High has, within His decree, a guarded secret and hidden knowledge that He has withheld from all His creatures and reserved exclusively for Himself. People of knowledge and His close servants attain only some broad insights into this. They may not be permitted to mention certain matters, and people may be addressed about it according to their capacity to understand.

Moses, Jesus, and Ezra asked our Lord—blessed and exalted is He—about an aspect of the secret of divine decree: that if He willed to be obeyed, He would be obeyed, yet He is nevertheless disobeyed. He—glorified and exalted is He—informed them that this was His secret.

In this realm, the minds of many creatures have wandered in bewilderment. Here too, those who hold that the world has no beginning went astray, maintaining that its Maker necessarily produces effects by virtue of His essence and necessarily entails them of Himself, as a cause entails its effect, and that nothing more perfect than what He has made is possible. Some of this malady crept into certain People of the Scripture and followers of the messengers, who asserted that what is possible is confined to what actually exists. All this was an attempt to escape the difficulty of explaining divine acts and the existence of originated causes for originated events. The Qadarites explained this through their own unsound rationales concerning judgments of justice and permissibility and the obligation to provide what is beneficial

or what is best. Neither group’s foundational principle proved sound or consistently applicable. From this difficulty, the dualists and adherents of Magianism came to posit two principles and to maintain that light and darkness are eternal.

Most theologians of the affirmationist tradition escaped some of these errors—although their position involved a measure of thinking ill of Allah and a degree of irreverence. They referred the matter to sheer volition and pure will, maintaining that its production of all contingent things and its bringing about of all possible things proceed in one and the same manner, and that its particular determinations and distinctions are intrinsic to it. Had this account incorporated something of the manifestations of mercy and forms of wisdom—whether known or unknown to us—it would have been more acceptable.

In any case, the lām expressing purpose in His acts—glorified and exalted is He—does not bear the meaning that most people understand when it expresses purpose in their own acts. Beyond what these people know and say lies the understanding with which Allah—glorified and exalted is He—has illuminated the hearts of His close servants and which He has cast into the hearts of His chosen ones: those who, in their outward statements, adhere firmly to the path of those devoted to transmitted reports, and, in what they keep hidden from people’s understanding, hold fast to the bond of those endowed with insight.

At this level, people of understanding discern the secret of His words:

“My mercy has preceded My wrath,”

and the words:

“Evil is not ascribed to You,”

and the words:

“In Your hand is all good,”

and the words: “from the evil of what

original_footnote: (١) سقط بالأصل
translated_text:
He has created,” and His words:

“And when I am ill, it is He who cures me.”

“And we do not know whether evil is intended for those on earth, or whether their Lord intends right guidance for them.”

Similar expressions either leave the agent of evil unnamed, attribute evil to its causes, or include it within a general statement. As for singling out evil and attributing it to the Creator of all things, wise speech does not call for this, because of what is required by the reality that demands well-founded propriety, not merely for a distinct … (1).

Here one understands why many creatures enter Paradise without having performed any deeds, and why creatures are brought into being for it. The Fire, however, is entered only on account of deeds, and none will enter it except those who have lived in this world. One also understands the true meaning of:

“Whatever evil befalls you is from yourself,”

and:

“Whatever calamity befalls you is because of what your own hands have earned,”

even though that evil is part of the divine decree; and the statement of al-Siddīq and other Companions:

“If it is correct, it is from Allah; if it is mistaken, it is from me and from Satan.”

There are other such matters in which every thinker has discerned some portion of the truth and grasped some thread of what is correct. Yet none follow the various aspects of truth and believe in the entire Book except those endowed with understanding—and how few they are! This is a brief indication of divine ordainment as a whole.

As for the particular significance of the servant’s capacity and the acts he acquires among all other causes, Allah—Mighty and Majestic—has distinguished the human being by making his knowledge produce in him, in this world, traits of character, states, and effects, as well as other things in the Hereafter. This has not been granted to His other creatures. And the ways in which He has distinguished

بِهَا الْإِنْسَانَ فِي ذَاتِهِ وَصِفَاتِهِ وَأَسْمَائِهِ وَأَفْعَالِهِ شَخْصًا وَنَوْعًا أَكْثَرَ مِنْ أَنْ تُحْصَى وَمَا مِنْ عَاقِلٍ إلَّا وَعِنْدَهُ مِنْهَا طَرَفٌ وَلِهَذَا حَسُنَ تَوْجِيهُ الْأَمْرِ وَالنَّهْيِ إلَيْهِ. وَصَحَّ إضَافَةُ الْفِعْلِ إلَيْهِ حَقِيقَةً وَكَسْبًا مَعَ أَنَّهُ خَلْقُ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ تَعَالَى خَلَقَ الْعَبْدَ وَعَمَلَهُ وَجَعَلَ هَذَا الْعَمَلَ لَهُ عَمَلًا قَامَ بِهِ وَصَدَرَ عَنْهُ وَحَدَثَ بِقُدْرَتِهِ الْحَادِثَةِ. وَأَدْنَى أَحْوَالِ

translated_text:
the human being in his essence, attributes, names, and actions, both individually and as a species, are too numerous to count. Every rational person knows something of these distinctions. Hence it is fitting that commands and prohibitions should be addressed to him, and that an act should truly be attributed to him as something he acquires, even though it is created by Allah Most High. For Allah Most High created the servant and his action, and made that action his own: an action subsisting in him, proceeding from him, and occurring through his created power.

At the very least, an “act” is comparable to the attributes and character traits created in the servant when these are made to lead to further consequences. Can the servant, then, rightly be dissociated from them? Certainly not—and why should he be?

As for the “command,” in the case of the obedient it is among the causes through which their action comes about: it arouses their motivation, then brings about their obedience, wholehearted compliance, and submission. It thus forms part of the prior divine decree leading them to felicity. In the case of the disobedient, it is the cause on account of which disobedience is rightly ascribed to them, since without it the obedient could not be distinguished from the disobedient. “Moreover,” in their case it forms part of the prior divine decree leading them to disobedience, so that He may lead many astray through it and guide many through it.

Concerning the inclusion of commands and prohibitions among divinely decreed matters . . . (1) resolves many a difficulty. This . . . (2) glorified and exalted is He, because of His knowledge of the outcomes. As for commands issued by human beings, the absence is evident . . . (3) of acts of disobedience within their knowledge, and that their intention is the very occurrence of the act from everyone; thus it is . . . (4) in the outward aspect of the religious command conveyed by the messengers through the revealed Books, and Allah
translated_footnote: (1, 4) Thus in the original.

original_text:
كُلَّهُ. . . 
(١)
 مُظْهِرٌ أَمْرٍ وَحُكْمٍ يُمْضِيهِ فَالْإِرَادَةُ وَالْأَمْرُ كُلٌّ مِنْهُمَا مُنْقَسِمٌ. . . 
(٢)
 عَامُّ الْوُقُوعِ جَامِعٌ لِلْقِسْمَيْنِ وَإِلَى شَرْعٍ وَرُبَّمَا بَعُدَ وَرُبَّمَا وَقَفَ. . . 
(٣)
 الْقَدَرُ لَهُ وَالْخَيْرُ كُلُّ الْخَيْرِ فِي نُفُوذِهِ وَهُوَ خَاصُّ الْوُقُوعِ بِفَرْقِ إلَى الْقِسْمَيْنِ وَاضِعُ الْأَشْيَاءِ فِي مَرَاتِبِهَا. وَإِذَا صَحَّ نِسْبَةُ الطَّاعَةِ وَالْمَعْصِيَةِ إلَى مَنْ خُلِقَتْ فِيهِ وَلَوْ أَنَّهُ يَخْلُقُ الصِّفَاتِ.
 أَفَيَحْسُنُ بِالْإِنْسَانِ أَنْ يَقُولَ:
 أَسْوَدُ وَأَحْمَرُ وَطَوِيلٌ وَقَصِيرٌ وَذَكِيٌّ وَبَلِيدٌ وَعَرَبِيٌّ وَعَجَمِيٌّ فَيُضِيفُ إلَيْهِ جَمِيعَ الصِّفَاتِ الَّتِي لَيْسَ لِلْإِنْسَانِ فِيهَا إرَادَةٌ أَصْلًا أَلْبَتَّةَ لِقِيَامِهَا بِهِ، وَتَأْثِيرِهَا فِيهِ تَارَةً بِمَا يُلَائِمُهُ وَتَارَةً بِمَا يُنَافِرُهُ ثُمَّ يُسْتَبْعَدُ أَنْ يُضَافَ إلَيْهِ مَا خَلَقَ فِيهِ مِنْ الْفِعْلِ بِوَاسِطَةِ قَصْدِهِ وَإِرَادَتِهِ الْمَخْلُوقَيْنِ أَيْضًا؟
 ثُمَّ يَقُولُ:
 لَيْسَ لِلْعَبْدِ فِي السَّيِّئِ شَيْءٌ فَهَلْ الْجَمِيعُ إلَّا لَهُ؟ بَلْ لَيْسَتْ لِأَحَدِ غَيْرِهِ؛ لَكِنَّ اللَّهَ سُبْحَانَهُ وَتَعَالَى خَلَقَهَا لَهُ وَإِضَافَةُ الْفِعْلِ إلَى خَالِقِهِ وَمُبْدِعِهِ لَا تُنَافِي إضَافَتَهُ إلَى صَاحِبِهِ وَمَحَلِّهِ الَّذِي هُوَ فَاعِلُهُ وَكَاسِبُهُ وَقَدْ بَيَّنَّا الْجَبْرَ الْمَذْمُومَ مَا هُوَ.
وَنَخْتِمُ الْكَلَامَ بِكَلَامِ وَجِيزٍ فِي سَبَبِ الْفَرْقِ بَيْنَ الْخَلْقِ وَالْكَسْبِ.
فَنَقُولُ:
 الْخَلْقُ يَجْمَعُ مَعْنَيَيْنِ: أَحَدُهُمَا: الْإِبْدَاعُ وَالْبُرْءُ،
 وَالثَّانِي:
 التَّقْدِيرُ وَالتَّصْوِيرُ.
original_footnote: (١، ٣) هكذا بالأصل
translated_text:
all of it . . . (1), manifesting a command and a decree that He carries out. Will and command are thus each divided . . . (2), universal in occurrence and encompassing both categories, and into revealed law. Sometimes it is far off, and sometimes it halts . . . (3) the divine decree for it. All good lies in its taking effect; its occurrence is particular, distinguishing between the two categories and placing things in their proper ranks.

And if obedience and disobedience can rightly be attributed to the person in whom they are created—even if he creates the attributes—can a person reasonably say, “Black, red, tall, short, intelligent, dull, Arab, non-Arab,” thus attributing to someone all these qualities over which a human being has absolutely no choice, because they subsist in him and affect him, sometimes agreeably and sometimes disagreeably, yet then consider it implausible to attribute to him the action created in him through his intention and will, which are also created?

Then he says, “The servant has no part in evil.” Yet is it not all his? Indeed, these things belong to no one else; but Allah, glorified and exalted is He, created them for him. Attributing an action to its Creator and Originator does not preclude attributing it to the one whose action it is and in whom it subsists—the one who performs and acquires it. We have already explained what constitutes blameworthy compulsion.

We conclude this discussion with a brief explanation of the distinction between creation and acquisition.

We say: Creation encompasses two meanings: first, origination and bringing into being; second, determining measure and giving form.
translated_footnote: (1, 3) Thus in the original.

original_text:
فَإِذَا قِيلَ:
 خَلَقَ فَلَا بُدَّ أَنْ يَكُونَ أَبْدَعَ إبْدَاعًا مُقَدَّرًا وَلَمَّا كَانَ - سُبْحَانَهُ وَتَعَالَى - أَبْدَعَ جَمِيعَ الْأَشْيَاءِ مِنْ الْعَدَمِ وَجَعَلَ لِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدَرًا صَحَّ إضَافَةُ الْخَلْقِ إلَيْهِ بِالْقَوْلِ الْمُطْلَقِ. وَالتَّقْدِيرُ فِي الْمَخْلُوقِ لَازِمٌ إذْ هُوَ عِبَارَةٌ عَنْ تَحْدِيدِهِ وَالْإِحَاطَةِ بِهِ وَهَذَا لَازِمٌ لِجَمِيعِ الْكَائِنَاتِ لَا كَمَا زَعَمَ مَنْ حَسِبَ أَنَّ الْخَلْقَ فِي. . . 
(١)
 ذَوَاتِ الْمِسَاحَةِ وَهِيَ الْأَجْسَامُ مُفَرِّقًا بَيْنَ الْخَلْقِ وَالْأَمْرِ بِذَلِكَ فَإِنَّهُ قَوْلٌ بَاطِلٌ مُبْتَدَعٌ وَالْأَمْرُ هُوَ كَلَامُهُ كَمَا فَسَّرَهُ الْأَوَّلُونَ وَالْخَلْقُ مُفَسَّرٌ. . . 
(٢)
 يَجْعَلُ الْخَلْقَ بِإِزَاءِ إبْدَاعِ الصُّوَرِ الذِّهْنِيَّةِ وَتَقْدِيرِهَا وَمِنْهُ تَسْمِيَةُ. . . 
(٣)
 اخْتِلَافًا إذْ هُوَ صُوَرٌ ذِهْنِيَّةٌ لَيْسَ لَهَا حَقِيقَةٌ خَارِجَةٌ عَنْ الذِّهْنِ وَ. . . 
(٤)
 جَعْلُ الْخَلْقِ بِمَعْنَى التَّقْدِيرِ فَقَطْ مَقْطُوعًا عَنْهُ النَّظَرُ إلَى الْإِبْدَاعِ بِمَا قَالَ. . . 
(٥)
 سُدًى مَا خَلَقْت وَكَمَا قَالَ عَلِيٌّ فِي تِمْثَالٍ صَنَعَهُ: أَنَا خَلَقْته وَالْفَرْقُ. . . 
(٦)
 الْأُولَى مِنْ حَيْثُ إنَّ تِلْكَ الصُّورَةَ مُبْتَدَعَةٌ لَكَانَ قَوْلًا. . . 
(٧)
 يَكُونُ إلَّا اللَّهُ سُبْحَانَهُ وَتَعَالَى صَحَّ وَصْفُهُ سُبْحَانَهُ بِأَنَّهُ خَالِقُ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ.
 وَأَمَّا الْكَسْبُ فَقَدْ ذَكَرْنَا أَنَّهُ إنَّمَا يُنْظَرُ فِيهِ إلَى تَأْثِيرِهِ فِي مَحَلِّهِ وَلَوْ لَمْ يَكُنْ لَهُ عَلَيْهِ قُدْرَةٌ حَتَّى يُقَالَ:
 الثَّوْبُ قَدْ اُكْتُسِبَ مِنْ رِيحِ الْمِسْكِ، وَالْمَسْجِدُ قَدْ اكْتَسَبَ الْحُرْمَةَ مِنْ أَفْعَالِ الْعَابِدِينَ وَالْجِلْد قَدْ اكْتَسَبَ الْحُرْمَةَ لِمُجَاوَرَةِ الْمُصْحَفِ وَالثَّمَرَةُ قَدْ اكْتَسَبَتْ لَوْنًا وَرِيحًا وَطَعْمًا فَكُلُّ مَحَلٍّ تَأَثَّرَ عَنْ شَيْءٍ مُؤَثِّرًا وَمُلَائِمًا وَمُنَافِرًا صَحَّ وَصْفُهُ بِالِاكْتِسَابِ بِنَاءً عَلَى تَأَثُّرِهِ وَتَغَيُّرِهِ وَتَحَوُّلِهِ
original_footnote: (١، ٧) بياض بالأصل
translated_text:
Thus, to say that someone “created” necessarily means that he originated something according to a determined measure. Since He—glorified and exalted is He—originated all things from nothing and assigned everything its measure, creation may rightly be attributed to Him without qualification. A created thing necessarily has a determined measure, for this means delimiting and circumscribing it, which necessarily applies to everything that exists. This is contrary to the claim of those who suppose that creation applies to ... (1) things possessing spatial dimensions, namely bodies, thereby distinguishing creation from command. This is a false, innovated view. Command is His speech, as the early scholars explained it, and creation is explained ... (2) makes creation correspond to originating mental forms and determining their measure. This includes calling ... (3) “difference,” since it consists of mental forms with no reality outside the mind; and ... (4) taking creation to mean determining measure alone, disregarding origination, on the basis of the saying ... (5) “In vain is what you have fashioned.” Likewise, ‘Alī said of a figure he had made, “I created it.” The distinction ... (6) the first, insofar as that form is newly originated, would be a statement ... (7) is none but Allah, glorified and exalted is He. It is therefore correct to describe Him, glorified is He, as the Creator of all things.

As for acquisition, we have mentioned that what is considered is its effect upon the subject in which it occurs, even if that subject has no power over it. Thus, one may even say that a garment has acquired something of musk’s fragrance; a mosque has acquired sanctity through the acts of worshippers; leather has acquired sanctity through its proximity to the Quran; and a fruit has acquired colour, fragrance, and flavour. Thus, any subject affected by something that exerts an influence, whether agreeable or disagreeable, may properly be described as acquiring, on account of its being affected, changed, and transformed
translated_footnote: (1, 7) Blank in the original.

original_text:
مِنْ حَالٍ إلَى حَالٍ وَالْإِنْسَانُ يَتَأَثَّرُ عَنْ الْأَفْعَالِ الِاخْتِيَارِيَّةِ وَلَا يَتَأَثَّرُ عَنْ الْأَفْعَالِ الِاضْطِرَارِيَّةِ فَتُورِثُهُ أَخْلَاقًا وَأَحْوَالًا عَلَى أَيِّ حَالٍ كَانَ حَتَّى عَلَى رَأْيِ مَنْ يُطْلِقُ اسْمَ الْجَبْرِ عَلَى مَجْمُوعِ أَفْعَالِهِ فَإِنَّهُ يَسْتَيْقِنُ تَأْثِيرَ الْأَفْعَالِ الِاخْتِيَارِيَّةِ فِي نَفْسِهِ بِخِلَافِ الِاضْطِرَارِيَّةِ اللَّهُمَّ إلَّا مِنْ حَيْثُ قَدْ تُوجِبُ الْأَفْعَالُ الِاضْطِرَارِيَّةُ أَمْرًا فِي نَفْسِهِ فَيَكُونُ ذَلِكَ اخْتِيَارًا. ثُمَّ اعْلَمْ أَنَّ الِاضْطِرَارَ إنَّمَا يَكُونُ فِي بَدَنِهِ دُونَ قَلْبِهِ إمَّا بِفِعْلِ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى كَالْأَمْرَاضِ وَالْأَسْقَامِ وَإِمَّا بِفِعْلِ الْعِبَادِ كَالْقَيْدِ وَالْحَبْسِ وَأَمَّا أَفْعَالُ رُوحِهِ الْمَنْفُوخَةِ فِيهِ؛ إذَا حَرَّكَتْ يَدَيْهِ فَهِيَ كُلُّهَا اخْتِيَارِيَّةٌ وَمِنْ وَجْهٍ قَدْ بَيَّنَّاهُ كُلَّهَا اضْطِرَارِيَّةً فَاضْطِرَارُهَا هُوَ عَيْنُ. . . 
(١)
 وَاخْتِيَارُهَا إنَّمَا هُوَ بِالِاضْطِرَارِ وَحَقِيقَةُ الِاضْطِرَارِ هُوَ أَنَّ اضْطِرَارَ. . . 
(٢)
 وَرُبَّمَا أَحَبَّتْ مِنْ وَجْهٍ وَكَرِهَتْ مِنْ وَجْهٍ آخَرَ وَهَذَا كُلُّهُ لَا يَمْنَعُ وُرُودَ التَّكْلِيفِ وَاقْتِضَاءَ الثَّوَابِ وَالْعِقَابِ.
 هَذَا الَّذِي تَيَسَّرَ كِتَابَتُهُ فِي الْحَالِ:
 
{وَاللَّهُ يَقُولُ الْحَقَّ وَهُوَ يَهْدِي السَّبِيلَ}
 وَالْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ وَحْدَهُ.
original_footnote: (١، ٢) بياض بالأصل
translated_text:
from one state to another. A person is affected by voluntary acts but not by involuntary acts: the former impart character traits and inner states to him. This holds in any event, even according to those who describe all his acts as compelled, for he knows with certainty that voluntary acts affect his soul, unlike involuntary acts—except insofar as involuntary acts may bring about something within his soul, in which case that involves choice.

Know, moreover, that compulsion affects only his body, not his heart, whether through the action of Allah Most High, as with illnesses and ailments, or through the actions of His servants, as with shackling and imprisonment. As for the acts of the spirit breathed into him, when it moves his hands, they are all voluntary. Yet, from a perspective we have already explained, they are all necessitated. Thus, its necessity is identical to … (1), and its choice occurs only by necessity. The reality of necessity is that the necessity of … (2). It may love in one respect and dislike in another. None of this precludes being subject to religious obligations or deserving reward and punishment.

This is what I have been able to write at present:

“Allah speaks the truth, and He guides to the right path.”

All praise belongs to Allah alone.
translated_footnote: (1, 2) Blank in the original.

original_text:
سُئِلَ شَيْخُ الْإِسْلَامِ تَقِيُّ الدِّينِ أَبُو الْعَبَّاسِ أَحْمَد بْنُ عَبْدِ الْحَلِيمِ بْنِ عَبْدِ السَّلَامِ ابْنُ تَيْمِيَّة رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ مَا تَقُولُ السَّادَةُ الْعُلَمَاءُ أَئِمَّةُ الدِّينِ - رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ أَجْمَعِينَ -:
فِي 
" أَفْعَالِ الْعِبَادِ "
: هَلْ هِيَ قَدِيمَةٌ أَمْ مَخْلُوقَةٌ حِينَ خُلِقَ الْإِنْسَانُ؟
 وَمَا الْحُجَّةُ عَلَى مَنْ يَقُولُ:
 إنَّ سَائِرَ أَفْعَالِ الْعِبَادِ مِنْ الْحَرَكَاتِ وَغَيْرِهَا مِنْ الْقَدَرِ الَّذِي قُدِّرَ قَبْلَ خَلْقِ السَّمَوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ؟
 وَفِيمَنْ لَمْ يَسْتَثْنِ فِي الْأَفْعَالِ الْمَاضِيَةِ كَقَوْلِ الْقَائِلِ:
 هَذِهِ نَخْلَةٌ أَوْ شَجَرَةُ زَيْتُونٍ قَطْعًا لَمْ يَقُلْ شَيْئًا إلَّا وَيَسْتَرْجِعُ فِيهِ الْمَشِيئَةَ وَيَسْأَلُ الْبَسْطَ فِي ذَلِكَ.
فَأَجَابَ - رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ -:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ، 
" أَفْعَالُ الْعِبَادِ "
 مَخْلُوقَةٌ بِاتِّفَاقِ سَلَفِ الْأُمَّةِ وَأَئِمَّتِهَا كَمَا نَصَّ عَلَى ذَلِكَ سَائِرُ أَئِمَّةِ الْإِسْلَامِ: الْإِمَامُ أَحْمَد وَمَنْ قَبْلَهُ وَبَعْدَهُ حَتَّى قَالَ بَعْضُهُمْ: مَنْ قَالَ: إنَّ أَفْعَالَ الْعِبَادِ غَيْرُ مَخْلُوقَةٍ،
 فَهُوَ بِمَنْزِلَةِ مَنْ قَالَ:
 إنَّ السَّمَاءَ وَالْأَرْضَ غَيْرُ مَخْلُوقَةٍ وَقَالَ يَحْيَى بْنُ سَعِيدٍ الْعَطَّارُ: مَا زِلْتُ أَسْمَعُ أَصْحَابَنَا يَقُولُونَ أَفْعَالُ الْعِبَادِ مَخْلُوقَةٌ. وَكَانَ السَّلَفُ قَدْ أَظْهَرُوا ذَلِكَ لَمَّا أَظْهَرَتْ الْقَدَرِيَّةُ أَنَّ أَفْعَالَ الْعِبَادِ غَيْرُ
translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islam Taqī al-Dīn Abū al-‘Abbās Ahmad ibn ‘Abd al-Halīm ibn ‘Abd al-Salām Ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

What do the esteemed scholars, the imams of the religion—may Allah be pleased with them all—say concerning human actions: are they eternal, or were they created when man was created? What argument can be advanced against someone who says that all human actions, including movements and everything else, belong to the decree ordained before the creation of the heavens and the earth? And what of someone who does not qualify statements about past events by invoking Allah’s will—for example, saying categorically, “This is a palm tree or an olive tree”—and who says nothing without referring it back to Allah’s will? A detailed explanation of this is requested.

He replied—may Allah be pleased with him:

All praise belongs to Allah, Lord of all worlds. Human actions are created, by agreement of the early generations of the Muslim community and its imams. created by Allah, and claimed that man originates or creates them independently of Allah. The early generations and the imams therefore explained that Allah is the Creator of everything, including human actions and all else.

Later, a group of those who identified themselves with the Sunnah proclaimed that people’s utterances of the Quran were uncreated. Imam Ahmad rejected this and declared anyone who said it an innovator. After his death, his companion Abū Bakr al-Marwadhī took up the matter and composed a work on it, which Abū Bakr al-Khallāl mentioned in his Book of the Sunnah. He also mentioned the case of Abū Tālib, whom Ahmad rebuked for saying, “My utterance of the Quran is uncreated.” The Jahmiyyah were the first to say, “Utterance of the Quran is created.” This was transmitted from Ahmad by his two sons, Sālih and ‘Abd Allāh, his cousin Hanbal, al-Marwadhī, Qūrān, and other eminent companions of his.

The leading scholars among Ahmad’s companions and other scholars of the Sunnah condemned those who said that people’s voices and actions were uncreated. Al-Bukhārī composed a work on this subject. Likewise, they declared those who said that Allah does not speak with a voice, that the letters of the Quran are created, or that utterance of the Quran is created, to be innovators and adherents of the Jahmiyyah. The imams thus refuted this innovation, as we have explained at length elsewhere.

No one—not any of Ahmad’s well-known companions, nor any other recognized scholar—ever said that human actions are eternal. I have encountered this view only among certain later scholars in non-Arab lands and in Egypt who affiliated themselves with the school of al-Shāfi‘ī or Ahmad. I have seen some Egyptians say:

“Human actions, whether good or evil, are eternal.” They say, “By actions, we do not mean the movements themselves; rather, we mean the reward granted for them, as stated in the hadith: ‘The believer sees his deeds in the form of a handsome, sweet-smelling man.’”

They argued that actions are part of divine decree, that divine decree is Allah’s secret and one of His attributes, and that His attributes are eternal. They also argued that the revealed laws are uncreated because they are Allah’s command and speech, and that actions are those revealed laws and must therefore be eternal.

This view is utterly unsound and contradicts the explicit statements of all the imams of Islam, including Imam Ahmad. He and other imams expressly stated that the reward Allah grants for reciting the Quran is created. How much more so, then, the reward He grants for people’s other deeds!

When the Jahmiyyah argued before Imam Ahmad and other scholars of the Sunnah that the Quran was created, citing the Prophet’s words (may Allah bless him and grant him peace):

“Al-Baqarah and Āl ‘Imrān will come as though they were two clouds, or two ghayābahs, or two flocks of birds with outspread wings; and the Quran will come in the form of a pale man,”

and similar reports, they said, “Whatever comes and goes can only be created.” Imam Ahmad answered them by pointing out that Allah Most High had described Himself as coming and arriving, saying:

“Are they waiting for anything but for the angels to come to them, or for your Lord to come, or for some of your Lord’s signs to come?”

He also said:

“And your Lord comes, and the angels, rank upon rank.”

Yet this was no evidence that He is created

This is plain: reward and punishment are what Allah has promised His servants and threatened them with. The reward is Paradise and all that it contains, and the punishment is the Fire and all that it contains. Paradise and all that it contains are created, and the Fire and all that it contains are created.

translated_text:
“The Quran comes in the form of a pale young man. Its companion comes, and it says, ‘Do you recognize me?’ He asks, ‘Who are you?’ It replies, ‘I am the Quran that made you thirsty by day and kept you awake at night.’ He said: ‘Then Allah brings him forward, and he says, “My Lord!”’”

They therefore claimed that the Quran is created. We replied to them: The Quran does not come; the meaning is illustrated by the report:

“Whoever recites ‘Say: He is Allah, the One’ will receive such-and-such.”

Do you not see that when someone recites “Say: He is Allah, the One,” it does not come to him? Rather, its reward comes. For we recite the Quran and say that it does not come or change from one state to another.

Ahmad thus explained that it is the reward that comes, and that this is the created result of the deed. What, then, of the punishment for deeds, which changes from one state to another? If this is the reward for “Say: He is Allah, the One,” and thus the reward for the Quran, what, then, of the reward for anything else?

As for the argument that deeds are Allah’s decree, the response is this: The term “decree” can mean either the act of decreeing or what is decreed. If you mean that people’s deeds are Allah’s very act of decreeing—which is His knowledge, speech, will, and other such attributes—then this is mistaken and false. People’s deeds are not any of Allah Most High’s attributes. But if you mean that they are decreed—that Allah Most High has decreed them—then this is true. They are decreed, just as all other created things are decreed. It is established in the Sahīh:

“Allah decreed the destinies of all creatures fifty thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth.”

All those things decreed are created.

translated_text:
It is also established in the two Sahīhs that ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace—who is truthful and whose truthfulness is attested—told us: ‘The creation of each of you is gathered in his mother’s womb for forty days as a drop of fluid. Then he becomes a clinging clot for a similar period, then a lump of flesh for a similar period. Then the angel is sent to him and instructed to record four things. He is told: “Write down his provision, his lifespan, his deeds, and whether he will be wretched or blessed.” Then the soul is breathed into him.’”

Allah has decreed his provision and lifespan just as He has decreed his deeds. It is well known that the provision he eats is created, even though it is decreed. The same applies to his deeds, and likewise to his blessedness and wretchedness. His blessedness and wretchedness consist in the reward and punishment for his deeds. All of this is decreed, just as his provision is decreed, and what is decreed is created.

As for their claim that deeds are religious prescriptions and that religious prescriptions are uncreated, they should likewise be told: The term “religious law” can refer to Allah’s speech by which He prescribed the religion, or to the deeds He has prescribed. Such expressions can refer either to the act or to its result, as with the word “creation” and similar terms.

If you say that people’s deeds are the religious law that is Allah’s speech, this is plainly false. But if you mean that these deeds are prescribed because Allah has commanded them, this is true. Yet Allah’s command is uncreated, whereas what is commanded—whether brought into being by Allah’s command or carried out in obedience to His command—is created, just as the servant who receives the command is created.

translated_text:
The term “command” can denote either the act of commanding or what is commanded. What is commanded is created, as Allah says:

“Allah’s command has come.”

And He says:

“Allah’s command is a decree firmly ordained.”

Here, what is meant is the thing commanded, not His command that is His speech. This verse, which these people cite as evidence, encompasses both religious law—which is His command—and divine decree. Two groups have gone astray on this point:

The Jahmiyyah, who say that Allah’s speech is created and cite His words, “Allah’s command is a decree firmly ordained,” arguing that whatever is decreed is created; and these misguided proponents of divine indwelling, who hold that the acts of servants are beginningless because they are Allah’s command and decree, and His command and decree are uncreated.

The confusion arises because the terms “decree,” “command,” and “religious law” can denote either the act itself or its result. Thus, in His words, “Allah’s command is a decree firmly ordained,” what is meant is the thing commanded and decreed, which is created. But in His words:

“That is Allah’s command, which He has sent down to you,”

His command is His speech, for He did not send down to us the acts He commanded us to perform; rather, He sent down the Quran. This is like His saying:

“Indeed, Allah commands you to return trusts to their rightful owners.”

This command is His speech.

Thus, when a Jahmī—whose position ultimately leads him to hold that He indwells in created things—cites His words, “Allah’s command is a decree firmly ordained,” he is told: What is meant is the thing commanded, as in His words, “Allah’s command has come, so do not seek to hasten it.” Likewise, concerning events that Allah brings about, one says, “This is a momentous affair.” And when a proponent of divine indwelling, who holds that the Lord’s attributes accompany His essence and indwell in

His command and decree that constitute His attributes, like His will and His speech, are uncreated. But His command that is a firmly ordained decree is created. What is decreed is created, and what is commanded is created, even if they are called “command” and “decree.”

before he himself existed? A servant’s action is the movement that proceeds from him. How, then, could it exist before him?

If someone explains his words by saying, “We did not mean the movement itself; rather, we meant its reward,” he is told: Everything besides Allah is created. His speech and attributes do not fall outside what His name denotes; rather, His speech is included in what His name denotes.

If someone were to say, “Everything besides Allah and His attributes is created,” in order to dispel this misconception, he would have intended a sound meaning. The same applies if he says, as some of the early generations said:

“Allah is the Creator, and everything besides Him is created, except the Quran, for it is Allah’s speech, sent down and uncreated. From Him it came, and to Him it will return.”

They excepted the Quran so that the listener would not mistakenly suppose that the revealed Quran is created.

For the Jahmiyyah used to ask people, “Is the Quran Allah, or is it other than Allah?” Someone who did not understand their intent would answer that it is other than Allah. They would then say, “Everything besides Allah is created.” Those of the early generations who used the wording quoted above did so lest someone unfamiliar with the aims of the Jahmiyyah think that the Quran is created, supposing it to fall within the general scope of the statement, “Everything besides Allah is created.” They therefore explained that it does not fall within the general scope of the statement, “Everything besides Allah is created.” Thus they said, “Except the Quran, for it is not created,” even if someone includes it within the statement, “Everything besides Allah is created.”

Since the expressions “other than” and “besides” are ambiguous—a thing’s attribute is sometimes included under these expressions and sometimes not—and since the person being addressed understands the Quran to be included under “besides,” the early generations explicitly excepted it.

translated_text:
As for the acts of servants, no one has excepted them from the general category of created things other than the Qadariyyah—the Muʿtazilah and others like them—who say that Allah did not create them. Yet even these people maintain that such acts originate in time, coming into existence after not existing. The exception is these proponents of indwelling.

I know of no one among the earlier generations, whether from Ahl al-Sunnah or the people of innovation, who said that servants’ acts, whether good or evil, are beginningless. I know of this view only through reports concerning some later Egyptians, and similar reports have reached me concerning some later non-Arabs. I have also seen some of their Syrian shaykhs suspend judgment on these acts, saying, “We say that they are decreed and predestined, but we say neither that they are created nor that they are uncreated.” Some people drew a distinction on the grounds that good deeds are part of faith. The statements of the early generations concerning “faith” are discussed elsewhere.

These “three positions”—that such acts are beginningless, that good deeds are beginningless, or that judgment should be suspended on the matter—are unsound and false. None of the renowned imams held them, nor would anyone who understands what he is saying. What led these people into such positions was their mistaken understanding of “the question of uttering the Quran,” “the question of recitation and what is recited,” and “the question of faith.”

Elsewhere, we have explained people’s positions on “the question of the Quran” and clarified the true, balanced position held by the early generations and the imams, which accords with both transmitted revelation and reason. We have also explained the deviations of those who went astray among both those who affirm and those who negate.

translated_text:
Some of those who regard certain attributes of the servant as beginningless eventually went so far as to regard the spirit within him as beginningless. They also affirmed the beginninglessness of the light present in the sun and moon, and other such doctrines whose falsity and opposition to the early generations and the imams we have explained elsewhere. These people share the belief that some attributes of the Creator indwell created beings. As for the Jahmiyyah, who are worse than these people, their position ultimately leads them to hold that the Creator Himself indwells all created beings, or that He is identical with the very existence of created beings. The shaykh of these Jahmī proponents of indwelling had met with the shaykhs of those proponents of indwelling who affirm the divine attributes. Because of these innovations, others like them, and other violations of the Sharia, the calamities that befell the imams came to pass.

Imam Ahmad and other imams condemned the doctrine of indwelling and likened its proponents to the Christians. In his Refutation of the Heretics and the Jahmiyyah, he said:

“Among the reports that reached us concerning Jahm, the enemy of Allah, was that he came from Khurāsān, from Tirmidh. He engaged in disputes and argument, and most of his discourse concerned Allah. If our argument prevails over yours, you will enter our religion; and if your argument prevails over ours, we will enter your religion.’ Among the things they said to Jahm in their debate was: ‘Do you not claim that you have a god?’ Jahm said:

translated_text:
calls him a newborn, an infant, a child and a boy. He eats and drinks, is addressed with commands and prohibitions, and is subject to promises and warnings. Moreover, he is among the descendants of Noah and Abraham. We may not say about the Quran what we say about Jesus. Have you ever heard Allah say about the Quran what He said about Jesus? Rather, the meaning of Allah’s words—exalted be His praise—

“The Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, was only the Messenger of Allah and His Word which He conveyed to Mary”

is that the word He conveyed to Mary was His saying to him, “Be.” Jesus thus came into being through “Be”; Jesus is not himself the “Be,” but came into being through “Be.” This “Be” is an utterance from Allah, and Allah’s “Be” is not created.’

The Christians and the Jahmiyyah have lied about Allah concerning Jesus. The Jahmiyyah said, ‘Jesus is Allah’s spirit and His Word, but the Word is created.’ The Christians said, ‘Jesus is Allah’s spirit, from Allah’s very essence, and Allah’s Word, from Allah’s very essence,’ just as one says, ‘This piece of cloth is from this garment.’

We said, ‘Jesus came into being through the Word; Jesus is not himself the Word. As for Allah’s words, “and a spirit from Him,” this means that the spirit came to be within him by His command. This is like His words:

“He has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth—all from Him.”

That is, by His command. The expression “Allah’s spirit” simply means a spirit that Allah created through His word, just as one says “Allah’s servant” and “Allah’s heaven.”’”

translated_text:
“Clarification of the Jahmiyyah’s denial that Allah spoke to Moses. We asked them, ‘Why do you deny this?’

They replied, ‘Allah has not spoken and does not speak. He merely brought something into being that spoke on Allah’s behalf, and created a sound and caused it to be heard.’ They claimed that speech can only issue from a hollow interior, a tongue, and two lips.

We said, ‘Can something brought into being, other than Allah, rightfully say, “O Moses, I am your Lord,” or say:

“Indeed, I am Allah. There is no deity except Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance”?

Whoever claims that this was other than Allah has ascribed lordship to it. If, as the Jahmī claims, Allah had brought something into being, that thing would have said, “O Moses, Allah is the Lord of all worlds.” It could not rightfully say, “Indeed, I am Allah, the Lord of all worlds.” Allah Most High has said:

“And Allah spoke to Moses directly.”

He also said:

“When Moses came to Our appointed meeting and his Lord spoke to him.”

And He said:

“I have chosen you over the people through My messages and My speaking to you.”

This is the explicit wording of the Quran.’

As for their assertion that Allah does not speak or address anyone, how do they account for the hadith narrated by al-Aʿmash, from Khaythamah, from ʿAdī ibn Hātim al-Tāʾī, who said that the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

‘There is not one of you who will not speak to his Lord, with no interpreter between them.’”

He continued his argument against them at length, until he said:

“You have fabricated a monstrous lie against Allah by claiming that He does not speak. You have likened Him to the idols worshipped besides Allah, for idols neither speak nor move nor pass from one place to another. When the proof became clear against him, he said, ‘Allah may speak, but His speech is created.’ We said, ‘The speech of human beings is also created. You have thus likened Allah to His creation when

you claimed that His speech is created. According to your doctrine, there was a time when He did not speak, until He created speech. You have thus combined disbelief with likening Allah to His creation. Exalted is Allah above such a description! Rather, we say: Allah has always spoken whenever He wills. We do not say that He existed without speaking until He created speech.’”

He then cited the remainder of his statement. He thus made clear that human speech is created: Allah created it. This is even more forceful than his explicit affirmation that people’s actions are created, although he explicitly affirmed both.

He also said:

“If you wish to know that the Jahmī lies about Allah when he claims that He is everywhere and is not in one place to the exclusion of another, say: ‘Did Allah not exist when nothing else existed?’ He will say, ‘Yes.’ Then ask him, ‘When He created His creation, did He create it within Himself or outside Himself?’ He must then adopt one of three positions.

“First, if he claims that Allah created creation within Himself, he commits disbelief by claiming that jinn, human beings, and devils are within Him.

“If he says, ‘He created them outside Himself and then entered into them,’ this too is disbelief, since he claims that He entered a desolate, filthy, foul place.

“If he says, ‘He created them outside Himself and did not then enter into them,’ he has abandoned his position entirely. This is the position of Ahl al-Sunnah.”

Ahmad thus made clear that human speech is created, and explicitly stated in several places that people’s actions are created. His explicit statement concerning their speech is more forceful, since the specious arguments concerning it are more apparent.

As for adding “if Allah wills” to statements about known and certain past matters—for example, saying, “This is a tree, if Allah wills,” “This is a human being, if Allah wills,” “The sky is above us, if Allah wills,” “There is no deity worthy of worship except Allah, if Allah wills,” or “Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, if Allah wills”; or refusing to say categorically, “Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah,” or “This is a tree”—this is an innovation contrary to reason and religion.

We have heard of no one among the people of “Islam” doing this except a group of those affiliated with Shaykh Abū ‘Amr ibn Marzūq. Neither the shaykh nor his sensible followers held this view.

However, someone well informed told me that, after his death, two of his followers, Hāzim and ‘Abd al-Malik, fell into a dispute. Hāzim introduced this innovation of adding “if Allah wills” when speaking about past matters known with certainty, and ceased making categorical assertions about them. ‘Abd al-Malik opposed him in this, agreeing with the Muslim community and the imams of the religion. Nevertheless, there are passages in the Judge’s writings in which his statements are inconsistent and contradictory. In one passage, he made a statement from which those who agreed with him developed unsound conclusions. A scholar may make an erroneous statement, and his followers then derive numerous further conclusions from it, as happened regarding the questions of “utterance,” “human speech,” “faith,” and “human actions.”

None of the early generations and imams—Imam Ahmad and others—said that human speech is uncreated, nor did they say that it is eternal, or that human actions are uncreated or eternal. They also prohibited saying, “The letters of the alphabet are created,” because these assertions entail that the Quran is not Allah’s speech and that He did not speak to Moses.

Then some people came and asserted the opposite without qualification. Some said, “My utterance of the Quran is uncreated.” Imam Ahmad and other imams declared those who said this to be innovators. Likewise, some asserted without qualification that faith is uncreated, until this came to be understood as meaning that the “human actions” constituting faith are uncreated. Others then went further, saying, “Human speech consists of letters that are uncreated; therefore, it is uncreated.” Still others said, “All human actions, then, are uncreated.”

The more an innovation is developed and its implications are drawn out, the uglier and more abhorrent it becomes, ultimately leading its proponent to contradict what is necessarily known through reason and religion. We have discussed this at length and explained people’s inconsistencies concerning it in the question of the Quran and other matters.

translated_text:
and that Allah’s speech is nothing but a meaning subsisting in His essence, comprising command, prohibition, and report. This claim is invalid according to sound reason and authentic transmitted evidence. A single meaning cannot constitute the command to perform every commanded act and the report from every informant; nor can the Torah, the Gospel, and the Quran have one and the same meaning. They say: “When that speech is expressed in Arabic, it becomes the Quran, and when expressed in Hebrew, it becomes the Torah.” This is mistaken: the Torah can be expressed in Arabic, yet its meanings are not those of the Quran; and the Quran can be expressed in Hebrew, yet its meanings are not those of the Torah.

The first to introduce this position was Ibn Kullāb. Nevertheless, he and those who followed him in it, such as al-Ashʿarī and others, also say: “The Quran is truly preserved in hearts, truly recited by tongues, and truly written in the codices.”

Some of them illustrate this by saying that it is preserved in hearts just as Allah is known in hearts, recited by tongues just as Allah is mentioned by tongues, and written in the codices just as Allah is written in the codices. This is a mistaken account of the actual position of Ibn Kullāb and al-Ashʿarī. In their view, the Quran is a meaning expressed in words, and realities have four levels of existence: existence in external reality, in knowledge, in speech, and in writing. Thus, knowledge of the meaning does not occupy the second level, nor is its presence in a book like the presence of concrete entities in a book. These people have therefore made the position of Ibn Kullāb and al-Ashʿarī even more repugnant.
